“If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed.” You, her son, her daughter, her uncle, her brother, take care of her, so the church can care for the real widows who have no family. That is who the money Simon betrayed was for.

The high priest Onias told Heliodorus “that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children.” The temple had money in it for the widows. So how come, in the days of the apostles, “there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration”? Why didn’t they just get it from the temple?

Because these were followers of Christ, and the priesthood had already agreed to cast out any man who confessed him. The widows of the disciples were getting nothing from the temple because they believed in Christ.

So the twelve said, “It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.” To serve tables means to take care of the widows, the orphans and all of that. “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.”

This is how the deacons were chosen. “And the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch.” Stephen, the one we always read about, was one of the first deacons chosen. They set them before the apostles, “and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.”

So the care of widows and the fatherless has always been a sacred charge among our people, kept in the temple in Onias’s day and put into the deacons’ hands in the apostles’ day. That is what Simon betrayed to the Greeks.

Onias said there was money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, “and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed”, and that it was “altogether impossible that such wrongs should be done unto them, that had committed it to the holiness of the place.”

There is a scripture that says keeping a man’s earnings from him is like murder: “The bread of the needy is their life: he that defraudeth him thereof is a man of blood. He that taketh away his neighbour’s living slayeth him; and he that defraudeth the labourer of his hire is a bloodshedder.”

What Simon did was no light thing. Taking money from the widows, the orphans, the fatherless and the strangers is murder. That was their livelihood; we took care of them with that money. Simon would rather have Esau come and take it all than help his own people. He is a murderer.

That is why it is never just one sin. All I did was tell them about the money? No, you did worse than you think. Sin is a domino effect: one hits the next and it goes all around. That is why Onias was in such agony, the priests lay on their faces before the altar and the whole city cried to heaven, and why the Lord of spirits sent the horse with the terrible rider and the two young men to scourge Heliodorus.

The temple kept money “laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children”, yet in Acts 6 the widows of the disciples were neglected in the daily ministration. Why couldn’t they get it from the temple? John shows what the priesthood had already decided.

The man born blind was healed, and his parents would not answer plainly: “These words spake his parents, because they feared the Jews: for the Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.”

They were kicking people out left and right. So Peter and them saw that the widows were not getting anything from the temple, because they believed in Christ. Put out of the synagogue, they were cut off from the relief the temple held for widows and the fatherless.

That is why the apostles had to look out seven men of honest report to serve tables and take care of the widows themselves. And that is how the deacons came to be chosen.

Paul says a widow indeed “trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.” Luke gives an example of exactly that.

“And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser: she was of a great age, and had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity; And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.”

She did not depart from the temple. She served God with fastings and prayers, night and day. That is what widows did. She was married to one man, well over threescore years old, and she gave her life to prayer for Israel.

Those were the widows the temple money was laid up to relieve in Onias’s day: sisters who had dedicated themselves to the Lord. To betray that money to the Greeks was to take the bread from women like Anna.

“Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”

That is Simon. He hated Onias, his brother, and his faction committed murders. This is the domino effect: it starts off as coveting; Simon coveted power. From there it turned to anger, from there to slander, and from there to murder. It is never just one sin, and not only are you affected, the people you sinned against are affected too.

Holding on to anger is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to die. You are drinking poison waiting for somebody else to drop dead, and they are not dropping dead. The only one being affected is you. This goes for men and women.

Onias was the opposite. He went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private”. He did not even go there to accuse Simon. That is the difference between a brother and a betrayer.

“There be three things that mine heart feareth; and for the fourth I was sore afraid: the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation: all these are worse than death.”

Simon did all three. The slander of a city: God does not like that thing, and Simon slandered the city. The gathering together of an unruly multitude: Simon had all the Greeks gather together to try to get the money from Jerusalem. And a false accusation: he accused Onias of doing this to Heliodorus. God said all these are worse than death.

Then think about this: don’t tell me what they say about me, tell me why they feel so comfortable telling you. In every school there is that one brother or sister that all the murmurers draw to, and they tell them all the things they don’t like about people. Why do they draw to you? You obviously did not have our back, because they are slandering and they feel so comfortable saying evil to you.

A deacon once pointed out a sister in red shoes with high heels and called her a hoe because of the shoes. The Bishop called Deacon Asaf, Deacon Malachi and the others over and asked them if she was; they said no. And he blew that brother’s spot up in front of them. You cannot come to me with evil. We must train ourselves to hate evil.

“Use not to make any manner of lie: for the custom thereof is not good.”

Use not to make any manner of lie, not a big one and not a small one. The custom of it is not good: when lying becomes your custom, it becomes what you are.

This follows the false witness of Exodus 20:16 and the maul, sword and sharp arrow of Proverbs 25:18. Simon made a custom of lying: he betrayed the money, slandered Onias, and called a man zealous of the law a traitor. These are basic laws, and our people must keep them.

Simon “was he bold to call him a traitor, that had deserved well of the city, and tendered his own nation, and was so zealous of the laws.” He was so bold he called Onias the high priest a traitor, that type of a brother, a man zealous of the law.

The law is plain: “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.” Don’t bear false witness.

These are basic laws, but for some reason in the black community they are so difficult. Just so, so difficult. Simon broke this one outright when he falsely accused Onias before the Greeks, and everything that followed came out of that false witness.

“But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”. Simon hated Onias the third so much that he had one of his men kill one of Onias’s priests. That is why it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins. James shows where it comes from.

“From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain”. Simon wanted the upper hand over Onias, and he could not get it. So what did he do?

“ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.” Because you are not praying to the Lord about it. “Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.” When you pray and still do not receive, it is because you ask for the wrong reasons. You have a lustful purpose behind it, a purpose that is not for the benefit of the nation.

This is a self-examination class for all of us: these are the attributes of Simon.

“Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders.”

Every neighbour will walk with slanders. “And they will deceive every one his neighbour, and will not speak the truth: they have taught their tongue to speak lies, and weary themselves to commit iniquity.”

There are people who love the slander. They teach their tongue to speak lies, and they are very good at it; there are some very good liars out there. You ever see a woman caught in the midst of adultery? She starts crying: this is not what it looks like. And some men will dismiss what they saw with their own eyes. Some of you are such a simp.

Don’t bring anybody like that around. They cannot roll with us. Let them stay over there with those other camps. That is what Simon was: a brother that supplanted, walked with slanders, and would not speak the truth about Onias.

“And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity.”

What does that mean? Whatever the judgment is on that man, you get the judgment. This is why in the hood, in the ghetto, people see murders all the time and say, I’m not saying nothing. Then weeks later, a month, a year, that same person ends up dead, and you say, what did she do, they never killed nobody. No: they were a witness, and they chose not to utter it.

Read on and the law also says “if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good, whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath, and it be hid from him; when he knoweth of it, then he shall be guilty in one of these.” And when he is guilty, “he shall confess that he hath sinned in that thing”.

A story from camp: the brothers were planning who to take traveling, and one brother’s hair was unkempt. He was told to trim it, and he answered, well, I guess I’m not traveling then. A couple of men heard it. A young man from Detroit told what was said, and when the officer who heard it first was questioned the next week, he said, I heard it, I was going to tell you next week. Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me.

Be mindful of brothers. They may seem decent on the outside, but you have to be mindful of the things they say, or don’t say.

“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment”.

It does not start with the murder. It starts with anger at your brother without a cause. “and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council”. Raca means thou fool, vain fellow, and the council there is man’s council.

“but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.” Just continuing the sin, the name calling and all of that, puts you in danger of hell fire. That is when God has to step in.

These are the attributes of Simon, and the class is a self-examination for all of us. Simon’s anger toward Onias turned into slander and name calling, calling him a traitor, and it ended in murder.

“A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow.”

Why is he a maul, a sword and a sharp arrow? Because that man will get people hurt, and will get people killed. A false witness is a weapon.

That is what Simon’s false witness against Onias became. He called the high priest a traitor, and before long “by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”. His lie was a sword in the hands of his faction, and it drew blood among his own people.

“This Simon now, of whom we spake afore, having been a betrayer of the money, and of his country, slandered Onias”. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin revealed the secret of the money to the Greeks and then slandered Onias the third, telling them Onias was the one who did that to Heliodorus. This Simon was no damn good.

Now look at the ones who stand next to that kind of man: “Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not.”

The type of man who is a partner with it hates his own soul. He hears the cursing and does not tell it. He keeps it tucked in. That goes directly against the law in Leviticus 5, where the one who hears and does not utter it bears the iniquity.

So it is not only the Simon who is guilty. The one who stands by, hears the evil, and keeps quiet is partnered with him, and he is hating his own soul.

“Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.”

There is a lot of slander in the Israelite community; Deacon Asaf has been going over it in classes these last two weeks. There are camps that thrive off slander, hatred, name calling, ridicule and false accusations.

God already told you he is going to cut off people who do that. Cut off means he is going to kill them. So for you to join with these people, you are nothing but a fool.

And the high look and the proud heart come from the slander; that is what they do. They think God is with them, and the men and women around them, as stupid as they are, believe God is with them. God is not with them, not according to these scriptures.

Simon slandered Onias the third. So how serious is slander? “For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.”

Slander is not a light thing. It is the first step of a counsel against a man’s life. The ones who slander take counsel together, and what they devise is to take away his life.

That is exactly the road Simon walked. He slandered Onias to the Greeks, and it did not stop at words: “when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”. The slander of many leads to the taking of life.

“Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.”

They may speak against us as evildoers, but they shall behold our good works. Why would they glorify God? Because our people who are living like Gentiles will repent based on your conduct out there in the world.

That is the lesson of Onias in 2 Maccabees 4. His conduct was honest before the nations, and even the Greeks and the king wept for him. Menelaus and Andronicus dealt in flattery, theft and deceit, and they brought reproach. Our conversation outside this truth is how our own people living like Gentiles will see it and come to repentance.

Somebody might say a good report with them that are without is only for somebody that desires the office of a bishop. No: “That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.”

You have to walk honestly toward them that are without the truth. You can't be outside the school, outside this truth, robbing, stealing, lying, using drugs, whatever little secret things you have going on.

Why “lack of nothing”? Because people are going to look out for you out there in the world. They are going to say, now this is a good dude, this is a good sister right here. That is what Onias had: a sober and modest behaviour that even the other nations honored, so that when he was slain without cause, they complained with the Jews.

When Onias was murdered, “not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man”, and even Antiochus “was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead.” The white man was crying for Onias, because other nations respected Onias III.

That is his character. He had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations, and he was not trying to join with the other nations; he said, I'm not joining with you. But he still had a good report among them. “Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.”

“Without” means without the truth. You must have a good report outside this truth. If we are at camp one day and somebody tries to do a drive-by on us because of something you did or said, what the hell is going on here? You have to have a good report within and without, like Onias.

Here is an easier verse to say what Job 34:11 says: “But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons.” You see how God gets down. In the world they call that karma. The Bible says if you do wrong, you shall receive for the wrong you have done.

There is no respect of persons. Jason was the high priest and it did not protect him: he undermined his own brother and was undermined by another. Andronicus was a man in authority, the king's deputy, and it did not protect him either. He came to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, drew him out of the sanctuary and killed him, and the king took away his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city “unto that very place, where he had committed impiety against Onias, there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.” He received for the wrong he had done, in the very place he did it.

“Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.” Walk in wisdom toward them that are without the truth, that don't know the truth.

“Redeeming the time” means be aware of the time you are in.

It goes with the good report of Onias. He had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations without joining himself to the other nations, and when he was unjustly murdered, the Jews and “certain of the Greeks that abhorred the fact also” complained because he “was slain without cause.” That is walking in wisdom toward them that are without: keeping yourself apart from their ways, and still carrying yourself so that they know you are righteous.

When Onias found out Menelaus was stealing vessels of gold out of the temple, he reproved him and had to run for his life, fleeing from Jerusalem up to the sanctuary at Daphne by Antiochia in Syria. Sirach shows what drives a man like that from his place.

“Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to thy neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.” Sometimes brothers and sisters may do something simple. Wink at it. It doesn't always have to be a counsel for small matters. “Abstain from strife, and thou shalt diminish thy sins: for a furious man will kindle strife”, and “A sinful man disquieteth friends, and maketh debate among them that be at peace.”

“An hasty contention kindleth a fire: and an hasty fighting sheddeth blood. If thou blow the spark, it shall burn: if thou spit upon it, it shall be quenched: and both these come out of thy mouth.” Your mouth has the power: you can blow on that spark and it will burn, or you can spit on it, let it go, and quench it.

“Curse the whisperer and doubletongued: for such have destroyed many that were at peace. A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation”. We just read that Onias had to flee from Jerusalem up to Syria. “strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men.” A backbiting tongue overthrew the house of a great man, Onias, the real high priest.

“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” Don't be deceived, brothers and sisters. God is not mocked. Whatsoever you do in this earth, you are going to reap from what you have done.

So if you decide, I'm going to undermine my brother next to me, I'm going to do some deceitful stuff to my sister, it is going to come back to you. It might not be this year; it might be next year, but it is going to come.

That is the history of 2 Maccabees 4. Jason sowed undermining against his own brother and reaped being undermined by another, “compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Menelaus got the principality by flattery and money and went on to steal vessels of gold out of the temple, and Andronicus sowed deceit and murder against Onias and reaped death in that very place. Brothers turning on brothers for position all reap what they sow.

“Then Jason, who had undermined his own brother, being undermined by another, was compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Jason undermined his own brother Onias to become high priest, and then he got undermined by Menelaus, the brother of Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin. Now the high priest is of the tribe of Benjamin. You can't make this stuff up.

That is why Job 34:11 is here: “For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways.” Whatever you do is going to come back on you. However you deal in this earth with your brother, with your neighbor, it is going to come back on you.

Jason sent Menelaus to bear the money to the king, and Menelaus flattered the king and “got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver.” Jason found the same thing he had done to his brother, and had to run. And later in the history the same thing comes back again on Jason and on Menelaus both: all that evil comes back on them.

Simon hated Onias so much that one of his faction murdered one of Onias’s priests, and he got Apollonius, the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice, to rage and “increase Simon’s malice.” Not only did he turn his own group against the high priest; he went to the other nations against him. That is how far your anger goes when you cannot get your way.

That spirit shows up again in 1 Maccabees: “Then came ungodly persons, who hated their own people, went unto the king, and told him that Jonathan besieged the tower.” You will always have that: certain ungodly men and women among us who hate their own people and run to the king.

See how it relates to us today. On the Carmelo Anthony verdict, one black commentator celebrated the guilty verdict and blamed the family for spending the money raised for his defense on houses. Another said he was overjoyed there were no black people on the jury. Whatever happened to a jury of your peers? It is the same thing they did back then: a whole white jury, and a judge who allowed it, with connections to the other family. Whatever the white man did, not guilty; a black man on trial, three or four minutes, guilty.

Then a black woman called black supremacy the most dangerous ideology in the world and said every race is tired of black people, and “we” want y’all gone. Where does black supremacy exist? Nobody has ever seen it. And she is not the only one who thinks like that. There are brothers and sisters calling themselves repented Israelites who think exactly like that; we had a bunch of them leave in 2018.

Onias went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all.” The ungodly who hate their own people go to the king to accuse them. That is the difference between Onias and Simon.

Onias went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private.” Simon was full of malice, envy and evil speaking. Peter tells us what to do with all of that.

“Wherefore laying aside all malice”: when you give yourself to the Lord, one of the first things you must do in repenting is lay aside all malice. “And all guile”: guile means deceit; put it away from you. “And hypocrisies”: don’t be a hypocrite. “And envies”: whatever envies, hatreds and jealousies you have, put them from you. “And all evil speakings.”

“As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.” You cast those sins away and start all over again as newborn babes, desiring the commandments in Christ. That is the only way you can grow in this truth.

If you apply verses 1 and 2, everyone will see a substantial change in your life. But if you are the same grimy brother or sister from last year and the year before that, we know you have not been applying 1 Peter 2:1-2. Our people forget history quickly; we cannot afford to become Simon.

Onias saw “that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto.” We read, blessed are the peacemakers, and if it be possible, live peaceably with all men. But peace doesn’t always work with some people.

Paul says: “Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you: And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith.” Meditate on that. Some men you cannot reason with. There is no, let’s sit down and talk, let’s get two witnesses. Some spirits are grimy. At the end of the day they don’t want peace with you; they want you dead.

There are Israelite camps like that. Brothers were at an event, and one of these camps was walking by; a brother said shalom to one of their men, and he cursed him out for it. These are unreasonable and wicked men.

They have no faith, and here is how we know: they are teaching now that Moses is in a lake of fire, and that John the Baptist was a wicked Israelite. Blasphemous new doctrines. They are filled with hatred, and they are unreasonable. We pray to be delivered from them, just as Onias could not make peace with Simon and had to take it to the king.

Onias’s attributes are the attributes of a man of God. He went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all.” Hebrews tells us to walk the same way: “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.”

Follow peace with all men, and holiness with it. Without them no man shall see the Lord. You cannot see the Lord walking in Simon’s spirit of malice, slander and murder.

Onias followed peace and holiness even when his friend Simon turned on him, and soon after his own blood brother Jason labored underhand to take the priesthood from him. Put yourself in his sandals. He still sought peace, until he saw it was impossible for the state to stay quiet and Simon to leave his folly unless the king looked into it.

Onias the high priest went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private.” He did not even go there to accuse Simon. That shows the character of Onias III, a great and upstanding elder man.

Christ says, “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.” That is the attribute of Onias. His own people had turned on him, Simon had one of his priests murdered, and the governor was raging against him, and still he went seeking the good of all, public and private, not revenge.

That is what a child of God does. Simon’s spirit lusts, envies, slanders and kills to get the upper hand. The peacemaker seeks the good of the whole nation.

Onias sought peace, going to the king seeking the good of all rather than to accuse his countrymen. That is one of his attributes, and Paul gives the rule: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”

Notice the words: if it be possible. As much as lies in you, you live peaceably. But it is not always possible. Onias “saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto.” Simon was causing insurrections in Jerusalem, and Onias wanted the king to look into it.

Blessed are the peacemakers, and live peaceably if at all possible, but peace doesn’t always work with some people. Some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don’t want peace with you. They want you dead. Onias did everything that lay in him; the rest he took to the king.

Jason “forthwith brought his own nation to Greekish fashion.” He built a place of exercise, brought the chief young men under his subjection and made them wear a hat, the hat of Hermes. “Now such was the height of Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish manners.” This is when we became Greek citizens, and we worshiped idols.

That is why Paul says: “Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant. Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.” That goes back to what we just read. We were led by Jason into heathenish manners and carried away unto dumb idols.

Everything Paul writes is referenced in the histories. Paul didn’t just make stuff up; it was based on something. Where in the Bible do we find it? In the book of Maccabees, which Esau conveniently took out, so our people in Christianity are lost and confused.

All you men that teach on the street must know this history. Verses 10 to 16 sum up what Paul constantly referenced when he said there is neither Jew nor Greek: we followed the Greeks’ customs so earnestly and desired to be like them in all things.

Who is it that gives out the crowns? Ezra saw it: “And in the midst of them there was a young man of a high stature, taller than all the rest, and upon every one of their heads he set crowns, and was more exalted; which I marvelled at greatly.”

Christ is a young man. He was crucified at 33, so art department, don’t make him look old. And taller than all the rest doesn’t mean by a couple of inches; it means by feet. You are going to know, that’s the Son of God right there, no question.

“So I asked the angel, and said, Sir, what are these? He answered and said unto me, These be they that have put off the mortal clothing, and put on the immortal, and have confessed the name of God: now are they crowned, and receive palms.” This is what we all want.

“Then said I unto the angel, What young person is it that crowneth them, and giveth them palms in their hands? So he answered and said unto me, It is the Son of God, whom they have confessed in the world. Then began I greatly to commend them that stood so stiffly for the name of the Lord.”

The crown comes from Christ, to those who confessed him and stood stiffly for the name of the Lord. It cannot be bought from a king the way Jason bought the priesthood, or cheated for the way a brother cheated the officer of 50 test.

“For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God.” Sometimes we take God’s laws for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won’t do nothing. Ezra shows otherwise: “Then shall they be in pitiful case, which now have abused my ways: and they that have cast them away despitefully shall dwell in torments.”

“For such as in their life have received benefits, and have not known me.” Look at Jason Whitlock. In the interview he said he is not oppressed because he makes ten million dollars a year. That is a benefit. A lot of our people become doctors and make big money and say, if I can do it, you can do it, and they do not know God. Whitlock once posted Revelation 3:9 on his Instagram with no commentary, all Amalek attacked him, and he quickly deleted it. These people need a wake-up call.

“And they that have loathed my law, while they had yet liberty, and, when as yet place of repentance was open unto them, understood not, but despised it.” They had liberty, because the brothers are out there teaching and the videos are in their feed. They see it, and they hate it.

“The same must know it after death by pain.” So who says that when you die you don’t get punished? You are going to know pain after you die, when Christ returns. Nobody escapes. That is why it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God, as Jason did.

Jason undermined his own brother to become high priest. All of this ties into us today. “And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.” You want to be an officer, a captain, a deacon, a bishop; you want to be moved up. You are not crowned except you strive lawfully.

Just as Jason undermined his brother, we have had brothers in here do the same thing. A brother said, we keep failing the officer of 50 test; I’ll get a copy with the answers and disseminate it. You might think, oh, it’s just cheating. No. It is worse than that. The officers of 50 counsel people. Now you have a brother who couldn’t pass it, who cheated and became an officer of 50, and he is counseling marriages. Y’all don’t see nothing wrong with that?

He is not qualified for that rank yet. The captains and deacons spend time on the exam, with variations on it, to see each man’s level of understanding, and a lot of it is counseling questions. The counselors mostly come from married men, and counsel must be accurate, on point and scriptural, not from your heart.

That is striving unlawfully, the same as Jason buying the priesthood. And a man who strives that way is not crowned.

Paul said a man is not crowned “except he strive lawfully.” What does he mean by crowned? He tells it in the same book: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.”

The crown is not a rank a man buys or cheats his way into, like Jason bribing the king for the high priesthood. It is a crown of righteousness laid up by the Lord, the righteous judge, and given at that day to those who strove lawfully and love his appearing.

So the brother who wants to be moved up, to be an officer, a captain, a deacon, must remember whose crown he is striving for. Jason got the rule in his hand for a time, but the writer of Maccabees still calls him “that ungodly wretch, and no high priest.”

Jason promised the king “by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents.” What is that called? Bribery. He tried to bribe his way to become high priest. He paid money for an office that goes through bloodline.

Amos shows what the Lord thinks of it: “For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right.”

That is what they were doing back then. They take a bribe, they afflict the just, and the poor are turned aside from their right. Jason paid the bribe, the king took it, and Onias, the just high priest, was pushed out. The Lord knows those manifold transgressions and mighty sins.

Jason bought the high priesthood with bribes, and three years later he got a taste of it himself: Menelaus, Simon’s brother, offered the king three hundred talents of silver more than Jason and “got the priesthood to himself.” Jason, who had undermined his own brother, was undermined by another and had to flee into the country of the Ammonites.

Sirach says: “All bribery and injustice shall be blotted out: but true dealing shall endure for ever.” The Most High deals with bribes. Here comes Jason, the brother of Onias the high priest, trying to bribe his way in, and it is blotted out.

Sometimes it is not good enough for a brother to be the support brother. Onias was high priest and his brother should have supported him, but Jason said, I can do a better job, plus have access to all that money. Look at a man’s motives. Bribery does not last; true dealing endures for ever.

“Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest.” This is Onias III’s own blood brother. Not only does Onias have to deal with Simon of the tribe of Benjamin; now his brother is trying to take the priesthood from him. When problems come, they come. Put yourself in his sandals: his good friend Simon turned on him, and now his own brother.

Sirach speaks to it: “Seek not of the Lord preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour.” Why go there? The priesthood fell to Onias III; that was his lot. His brother said, I want it, I should have it, not my brother.

“justify not thyself before the Lord; and boast not of thy wisdom before the king.” Jason went to the king to get what the Lord had not given him, seeking preeminence and the seat of honour, and he bought it.

Sometimes it is not good enough for a brother to be the support brother. Onias was the high priest, and his brother should have supported him. Jason said, I think I can do a better job, and have access to all that money. You have to look at a man’s motives.

When a false rumour went out that Antiochus was dead, Jason took a thousand men and assaulted the city. “But Jason slew his own citizens without mercy, not considering that to get the day of them of his own nation would be a most unhappy day for him; but thinking they had been his enemies, and not his countrymen.” He despised his own people.

“Howbeit for all this he obtained not the principality, but at the last received shame for the reward of his treason.” You think you can be a traitor and be honored and respected? No. Nobody likes a traitor. Even in Rise of the Planet of the Apes, the whole movie is about black people, they spray painted the word donkey on the traitor apes. That is the brothers who were in here in 2018, and some of the brothers who just bugged out in LA. You cannot be trusted.

Christ spoke of what it is to harm his own: “But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.” It would be better for the betrayer to have a millstone hanged about his neck and be drowned.

Jason offended and slew those who belonged to the Lord, and he got his reward: shame, fleeing from city to city, and dying in a strange land.

Jason “received shame for the reward of his treason.” Christ spoke directly about the betrayer: “The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born.” Put that with the millstone about the neck, and both mean the same thing for the traitor: go die.

See how all the evil Jason did came back on him. “In the end therefore he had an unhappy return, being accused before Aretas the king of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws, and being had in abomination as an open enemy of his country and countrymen, he was cast out into Egypt.”

“Thus he that had driven many out of their country perished in a strange land, retiring to the Lacedemonians”, that is Sparta, “thinking there to find succour by reason of his kindred: And he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him, nor any solemn funerals at all, nor sepulchre with his fathers.”

It had been good for that man if he had not been born. That is what the scripture says about the betrayer, whether it is Jason with Onias, Judas with Christ, or those who betray their brethren in this truth today.

Christ prophesied it: “And then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another.” Brothers becoming betrayers. Paul shows where to look to understand it: “For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.” So after reading what Christ said, we go back historically to what was written aforetime about brothers who became betrayers.

The history is in 2 Maccabees 3. The holy city was at peace “and the laws were kept very well, because of the godliness of Onias the high priest, and his hatred of wickedness.” Because of Onias' faith, his strength and love for God's laws, everybody else was inspired, and even the kings honoured the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts. That is the mentality we all must have: “Ye that love the Lord, hate evil.” You don't hate evil as long as you watch pornography at home.

“But one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city.” Onias had the last say; Simon did not agree. “And when he could not overcome Onias, he gat him to Apollonius”, governor of Celosyria and Phenice, up by Damascus. He ran to the other nations against his own brother, “And told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money.” You don't want to do what I say? I'm going to tell the other nations about all the money in the temple. You can't make this stuff up. That money was for the Levites, the strangers, the fatherless and the widows.

Ecclesiasticus names that kind of man: “there is a friend, which is only a friend in name. Is it not a grief unto death, when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy?” He rejoices with you in prosperity, “but in the time of trouble will be against him.” It is the same with those who leave the truth today: “I hate the work of them that turn aside.” It was written for our learning, so that we can see the betrayer Christ spoke of coming and not be moved.

“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able”. The Lord still gives you enough strength not to be overtaken, and always a way out. But it is up to you. Sometimes we are weak in the faith and weak in the spirit: you don't read your four chapters a day, your conversation is not about the scriptures, you are not around the brothers, and Satan gets a hold of you.

When we do not study, we have nothing in our spirits to combat Satan; we are defenseless. Even Christ, when he was tempted, used the word of God: as it is written. We have to be the same way. Sirach: “Blessed is the man that doth meditate good things in wisdom, and that reasoneth of holy things by his understanding.”

When you meditate on good things, you can reason in the scriptures in the moment of temptation: wait, the scripture says this; I can't do that. “He that considereth her ways in his heart” is always asking, what does the scripture say about this? That is how you combat the lust, the demon: you have to have something in your spirit.

When you go before the magistrates you are told not to think about what you will say, but you still have to have something in your spirit for the Lord to work with. If you have no scriptures about lust in your head, where are you going to pull from? Give the Holy Spirit something to work with. When Joseph, our forefather in Egypt, was tempted, he went straight back to the law: I would be sinning against God. That came to his mind first because his mind was always on the scriptures. Temptation always comes with an exit; addiction forms when we stop taking the exit.

Today's traps are the thirst traps. “Flee fornication”: get away from it. Solomon shows how the trap works: “Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.”

A lot of us are weak to the woman, weak to the box. Them eyelashes are there for a reason: batting them, fluffing them, all dainty. You noticed in the cartoons back in the day, in a little love scene, the eyelashes seem to grow. That little dainty look on the eyelids is designed to take you. Don't let it get you. Don't let it take you over.

“For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.” She is hunting, and what she hunts is your life.

That is why Paul says “he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.” Once you go outside of Christ, you are sinning against your own self. It is on you; you put yourself in that predicament. So flee it before the eyes and the heart are taken.

Zorobabel, in the contest to reason out the strongest thing we deal with, says, “it is not the great king, nor the multitude of men, neither is it wine, that excelleth; who is it then that ruleth them, or hath the lordship over them? are they not women?” Then he proves it: “Yea, many there be that have run out of their wits for women, and become servants for their sakes. Many also have perished, have erred, and sinned, for women.”

Negroes have died behind the woman; let that be clear. Negroes have died behind the box. We had a brother whose wife jumped out of a moving car. We told him, bro, you are tripping, she don't believe. And he said, it's so good, I can't leave it. You crazy; it ain't worth it; you are going to go to jail. You can be enticed by so many things, if you cannot help yourself, that you are willing to go through years of demise and despair because of the box. Many have perished, have erred, and sinned for women.

And vice versa. A lot of you sisters are sitting ducks. You follow after a man when you have been told, sis, he ain't right. He is tall, dark and handsome, and you think everything about him is good, but he is a demon. We warned you. So when you decide to lay down with that man and it does not go the way you want, it is not on the counsel to fix your marriage. That is your lord now; you did that. We cannot go against it and come in and dictate his house. Our job is not to change somebody's rules in their own household; our job is to use the scriptures to give wise counsel.

America has dictated everything on the aspect of the woman. Negroes will kill, rob and do all kinds of evil to get the attraction of women. The way they dress, the jewels, the necklace, the car, the money rolled down the arm: that is not for dudes, that is to entice a woman, and it is deceitful as hell. That is how strong the thing Zorobabel named is, and why it rules over kings and wine alike.

“which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith”. A lot of sisters in marriages covet other people's marriages: he's doing this, he's doing that, and you're mad at your husband because he isn't doing what that brother is doing, when he is probably trying to get where he needs to be. Solomon points you somewhere else: “Every wise woman buildeth her house”.

You're looking at the wrong thing. Instead of watching what that husband is doing, study her. Why don't you go ask her: what are you doing? What's the secret? Why is he so happy? Every time you ask for something he gives it; I see you with the new purse, the new shoes. Ask her how she's building her house up.

The wise woman has a mind to what is going on in the house: these are the things I need to fix to make my household better; this is how I assist my husband. That is why Genesis says her desire shall be to her husband. It means you study him: you know his likes and dislikes, what irritates him, when not to mess with him, and when to come say something. You live in the house; you see it all the time.

“but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands.” Your pride, sister, will keep you from doing it. You think he's supposed to give you everything first before you get on board: if he ain't doing this for me, I ain't doing nothing for him. You're out of your damn mind; that isn't what you're in the marriage for. He is out providing, bringing food into the house, clothes for the kids, paying the bills. You do your job and he does his. If he has to do it all before you reciprocate anything, something's wrong, and you might be the reason your marriage is the way it is.

“And after him rose up Nathan to prophesy in the time of David.” So we know who we are talking about: this is David, in the days of Nathan the prophet, the prophet the Lord sent to him after Bathsheba. The next verse carries on: “As is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel.”

That is the same David of 2 Samuel 11. He went out on the roof, “he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.” Bad to the bone. He sent and inquired: I got power, let me send some people over there, let me make this official. One with a spiritual mind made it plain: this is the wife of Uriah the Hittite, this is somebody's wife, bro. “And David sent messengers, and took her” anyway. Wisdom and understanding were right there, and he pushed them aside.

“and she came in unto him, and he lay with her”. She wasn't right either. She didn't resist, she wasn't opposed; she thought she came up. “And the woman conceived, and sent and told David, and said, I am with child.”

You see how Satan can deceive you. Satan put that lust in him to where he just didn't care, and he went the extra mile: he put Uriah in the front of the battle, got him killed, and took the wife. What he saw, the desire, the action, the cover-up, and the consequences: his first child was gone. Yet Sirach remembers David as the one chosen out of the children of Israel, and that leads to what the Lord did with him.

“The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.” The Lord did forgive David. He loved David, and David messed up.

David saw Bathsheba from the roof, took another man's wife, put Uriah in battle to be killed, and lost the child. That is as bad as it gets. But David repented, and the Lord took away his sins, exalted his horn, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel.

And that's another thing. A lot of times we are going to fall and do things that are not comely according to the scriptures. That don't mean you bunker down, go into a fetal position and say woe is me. You get yourself together, you repent, and you move forward. You don't go back. What did Christ say? Go, and sin no more.

You got to pick up the pieces and keep moving. We are all going to make mistakes. It is how you handle the mistake: it happened, so what are you going to do now, moving forward?

The Lord set both harvests before Israel from the beginning: “I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live.”

What you put in, you are going to get; you are going to receive a reward. Life and blessing for the one who sows to the Spirit, death and cursing for the one who sows to his flesh. Heaven and earth are called as witnesses, so no one can say he was not told. God is not mocked.

And the choice reaches past you: choose life “that both thou and thy seed may live.” What a man sows, his children reap with him.

“he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.” When you sow yourself into the scriptures, the Lord is going to give you blessings: he will show you favor, have mercy on you, and give you abundance. That is Joshua 1:8: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night.”

We should meditate on the scriptures day and night, “that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.” Meditating and doing is the sowing.

When we do that, the Lord makes our way prosperous. He gives us the abundance we desire, spiritually, emotionally, all the increases we desire, when we put our mind on the Lord. That is reaping of the Spirit.

“And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve.” You cannot serve two masters. You can't serve the flesh and serve God at the same time. You have to choose; ain't no in between.

That is why he said he would rather you be cold or hot. If you are lukewarm, battling that middle ground and playing games, he will spew you out of his mouth. Sowing to the flesh and sowing to the Spirit cannot be done at once.

“whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.” Choose the Lord, sow to the Spirit, and of the Spirit reap life everlasting.

“whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” What you put in, you are going to reap. When you put in the sin, the consequences are going to happen, period. Paul says it plainly: “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Sin is death. That is the corruption reaped by the one who sows to his flesh: sow that sin to your flesh and you will be judged by it. And the gift of God, eternal life through Christ, is the “life everlasting” reaped by the one who sows to the Spirit.

What you put in, you are going to receive as a reward. Wages for sin, a gift for the one who sows to the Spirit. God is not mocked.

“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.” Enticed means there is some attraction there, something that makes us gravitate toward the elements in us that cause us to sin. It seduces us: it looks like it is right for us, but it is not. Paul warned of it: “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits.”

A seducing spirit looks like it is good for you, but it is going to destroy you. Like drugs: that crack feels real good to the crackhead, but he is not able to see around him, and his whole life is being destroyed.

The only way you are going to see whether it is good for you or not is by filtering it through the scriptures. That is why it is important to be studying, reading your four chapters, being around godly men and godly women, so somebody can have your back. You have to be in the spirit to discern whether a thing is righteousness or Satan’s kiss.

Temptation begins internally; the lust is in you. When temptation presents itself you begin to be drawn to it, sin starts enticing you, and it grows through agreement: you get enticed, then you agree with it. “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.” It becomes action, and it always ends in destruction. “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.” In your own counsel you will always think you are right, and that is how people give heed to seducing spirits and depart from the faith.

“Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life.” You are going to be tried. Sirach tells you to get ready for it: “My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.” You are going to be tempted by Satan; he is going to use devices to tempt you.

“Set thy heart aright”: get your damn mind right, get yourself together, because this is not going to be a fair fight, and it is not going to be easy. “and constantly endure”: you have to constantly endure these temptations, because you have demons in you that you need to purge off, and some of these things keep coming back, and you have to be able to fight and get away from them. Paul in Romans 7 asked the Lord to take it away, and the Lord said no, this is the thorn in your side; this is what you will have to battle. But on the flip side, dealing with those battles is what keeps us going in this truth: always trying to get better with our lives, how we communicate, how we deal in relationships and with one another.

“and make not haste in time of trouble.” Things are going to happen, and you can’t fold up; go full-fledged toward it and knock it out. Life is a fight, and everybody is not going to make it victorious and on top. “Cleave unto him, and depart not away, that thou mayest be increased at thy last end. Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate. For gold is tried in the fire.”

You are going to be tried, so make sure you are on point. Everything in the world is against the person trying to be righteous: the work schedule set up to keep you in sin on the weekend, the holidays you want off based on wickedness. So you have to be around righteous people who will hold you accountable. That is the man who endures temptation and receives the crown of life.

Jeremiah sets two men side by side. The man who leans on his own heart and on flesh “shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.” He is dried up and alone, and he cannot even see good when it comes to him.

Then: “Blessed is the man that trusteth in the Lord”. That is the man who gets counsel, who reads the Bible and applies the commandments. The heart is deceitful above all things; your thoughts, your emotion and your intuition will destroy you. Nobody really cares what you think; it is about what the Bible is saying. So you have to be listening, in the word and studying, and not going and deciding for yourself without counsel.

The Lord set up men to guide us. But Black people hate guidance. When they see a man of the truth, it is low self-esteem: they see themselves in him, so they think, I am not nothing, so I know he ain't nothing. That goes way back, to what was done to us from slavery.

So the deceitful heart of verse 9 is the reason for the curse and the blessing here. The man who trusts himself ends in the salt land; the man who trusts the Lord and takes the counsel of the men he set up is the blessed one.

Judas asked the chief priests, “What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?” and “they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.” Sirach shows what that love of money does: “He that loveth gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.”

“Gold hath been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.” Sometimes money is the ruin of you. You stop making sound decisions; you are willing to do anything for it. That is why so many young women today are on OnlyFans and on these podcasts, doing anything they can to make money, willing to get booed on in another country for money. What morals do you have, and then you go home and kiss your kids? It might look good because of the opportunity, but all things ain't good.

“It is a stumblingblock unto them that sacrifice unto it, and every fool shall be taken therewith.” If money is all you think about and all you talk about, if your existence is based off money, money, money, then that is your god. That is why it says you made a sacrifice to it.

“Blessed is the rich that is found without blemish, and hath not gone after gold.” Why blessed? Because it is hard to have riches and keep the commandments. With money you can be enticed in so many ways; you can buy what you want and do whatever you want, and some feel they are above everybody. But when you are without blemish, you use your finances properly and it don't mess with your head. You have a lot of money, but you ain't made it your god.

Judas walked with Christ. He saw the healing and was around the commandment keeping, but that money lust is never enough, and he desired riches more than anything. Gold was his ruin: money was his demise.

“Seek not death in the error of your life: and pull not upon yourselves destruction with the works of your hands.” Don't seek death. When you put that sin above everything, that is exactly what you are seeking: death. Judas did it with his own hands when he “sought opportunity to betray him” for thirty pieces of silver, and he destroyed himself.

Money can be your destruction. Women can be your destruction. Food can be your destruction. Alcohol and drugs can be your destruction. These are the appetites in us that we constantly want to feed, and we have to stop it.

This is war, and people will give you up for money. It runs through history: the Black Panther Party, Martin Luther King, Malcolm X. We had a whole Israelite camp back in the day break up because of money, and today certain brothers get pushed on every platform as the face of the Israelites while the bishops and deacons really out here teaching are kept off. If you are weak in spirit, betrayal comes with money.

So be wise. A lot of times we are going to fall, but you don't sit down in a fetal position; you repent and move forward and sin no more. The destruction a man pulls on himself comes from the works of his own hands, and the way out is to stop feeding the appetite before it becomes your demise, like it became Judas'.

Matthew 5:28 says whosoever looks on a woman to lust after her “hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.” A lot of you brothers do that, and a lot of you sisters do that. You're scrolling down, you see something that catches your eye, and next thing you know you are going down the rabbit hole, full-fledged, not caring about no consequences, fully convinced and convicted in your sin. How do you fix that? Job 31.

“I made a covenant with mine eyes”. You have to control what you view. You have to control what you desire. “why then should I think upon a maid?” I should not be thinking lustfully upon a maid. Because you see a beautiful woman doesn't mean you should think lustfully about that sister; you made a covenant with your eyes. Especially you married men: you should have a covenant with your eyes with your wife. Why should I even think about it?

“For what portion of God is there from above? and what inheritance of the Almighty from on high?” The one who looks to lust has already committed adultery in his heart, and what portion does he have from God then, what inheritance from the Almighty? Read on and Job answers: “Is not destruction to the wicked?”

That is how the private sin of pornography is fought: not after the eye has wandered, but by making the covenant beforehand, so that the looking that leads to adultery in the heart never begins.

“Pride goeth before destruction”. Where does pride begin? Sirach: “The beginning of pride is when one departeth from God, and his heart is turned away from his Maker.” That means you have a froward mind.

“For pride is the beginning of sin”: the beginning of you falling to sin, falling for your temptation, falling to your lust, falling to feed that appetite. You knew better. You had all the warning signs, all the opportunity, everything placed in front of you. You were given a way out, as 1 Corinthians 10:13 said: God will with the temptation make a way to escape. But pride overcame you. Your mind wasn't on the Lord when your back was against the wall.

“and he that hath it shall pour out abomination”. When you have that pride, a negro is unstoppable; a prideful negro, oh my God. “and therefore the Lord brought upon them strange calamities, and overthrew them utterly.” When pride overtakes you, the Lord adds things to your demise: I'm going to leave you to Satan to gobble you on up, because your mind ain't right; you're too prideful.

That is why pride goes before destruction. Pride removes correction; you don't want to hear it. You think you know it all, you have all the wisdom and understanding. Pride isolates you, and it precedes the collapse.

This is how much the Lord hates pride. Sirach first shows what God loves: “In three things I was beautified, and stood up beautiful both before God and men: the unity of brethren, the love of neighbours, a man and a wife that agree together.”

The unity of brethren the Lord loves; the love of neighbors the Lord loves. And a man and wife that agree together: why is that beautiful? Because it's hard for two different personalities to come together and be on the same accord. That's why marriage takes time, brothers and sisters. It isn't overnight; it takes years and experience.

Now the negative: “Three sorts of men my soul hateth, and I am greatly offended at their life: a poor man that is proud, a rich man that is a liar, and an old adulterer that doateth.” He is offended at their life. A negro that's poor and proud: I hate that negro, I hate his soul, I hate everything about him. How can you be that way?

It means you have no humility whatsoever. Nobody can tell you anything; you have all the answers, but no fruits in your life, no solutions, no shame. That is the pride that goes before destruction, and God's soul hates it.

Sirach says pride begins when one departs from God. The Wisdom of Solomon shows how a man departs: “For froward thoughts separate from God”.

Being froward means you are thinking outside of the Bible. Period. That's what it is.

When your mind is not on the Lord, you are separated from him. You can't be both. So pride starts in the thoughts: the moment your thinking goes outside of the scriptures, you have separated yourself from God, and a haughty spirit is on its way to the fall. That is why the man who meditates on the scriptures has something to pull from when temptation comes, and the froward man doesn't.
blog/2026/2026-06-20-2026-06-20-the-bott:
1 Samuel 10:6 says you “shalt be turned into another man.” 2 Esdras 14:34 tells you what your part is in that turning.

“Therefore if so be that ye will subdue your own understanding, and reform your hearts, ye shall be kept alive and after death ye shall obtain mercy.”

Subdue your own understanding and reform your heart. We have to be transformed in the renewing of our minds. Transformed.

That is what the brother with the addiction runs from. He comes to the table having drunk a whole fifth in one night and says he is not an alcoholic. Even the white man knows the first step of recovery is to admit it: you have to realize you need help, that you are sick. Has he watched the classes on alcohol the Bishops and Deacons go over all the time? No. Why not? Because he is running away from his issues, and you cannot run away from that thing. You have to subdue your own understanding, reform your heart, and let the word turn you into another man, and then you shall be kept alive and after death obtain mercy.

A lot of us are not finding comfort in the scriptures because we lack faith. You don’t believe the Bible can transform you. You don’t believe it can turn you into another man, that you could become a whole different person. But 1 Samuel 10:6 says it: “And the Spirit of the Lord will come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them, and shalt be turned into another man.”

John 3:3 says the same thing to Nicodemus: “Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

Being turned into another man is being born again. The brother who drank a whole fifth in one night, the one who says, I can’t put it down, it’s a part of me, is not stuck being that man. Except he be born again, turned into another man, he cannot see the kingdom. The bottle is the battle, and the Bible is how you are turned into another man and win it.

“Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out”. We have to repent as a nation, and in the context of this class, repent from alcoholism. You have to stop. It is not something you can play with. You cannot play with sin.

That is why God says, “Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent: for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee”. It will bite you. You do not stand close to a serpent and see how long you can last; you flee from it.

“The teeth thereof are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men.” That is sin. It is going into the sins you know you deal with. You know which particular sins you struggle with, and yet you still entertain them.

Deacon Joshua said it: you should be able to go six months. Just drop it for six months. Especially you big brothers: drop the alcohol for six months and watch how fast you get in the green, because every week you take away 4,000 calories. To repent and be converted is to flee from the bottle, not to keep it near and hope it does not bite.

Isaiah 61:1 says the Lord “hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted”. We are the brokenhearted. We are the ones crying out in the streets, to this day. And Job shows what the Lord does with us in that condition: “He delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ears in oppression.”

The Lord is telling you there is going to be so much oppression going on that you are going to have to listen to the word of God. The Carmelo Anthony situation, that's oppression: he is in the prison house for defending himself. And the same week of his verdict, a baby was shot dead in Mississippi. These things are going to continue to happen.

Oppression, persecution, tribulation, all these things are going to arise for God's people to realize who they are. That is how he opens our ears. And yet some want to leave the truth because they got called fat, or because they got demoted. That is some evil stuff: traitors and betrayers.

So Isaiah 61 is proclaimed to the ones whose ears the oppression has opened: liberty to the captives, “the opening of the prison to them that are bound”, because we are yet this day in captivity and we fill the prison houses. What is there to hope for outside of the body of Christ? Only the ones who know who they are can look for “the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God”.

The bottle says, take another drink. You can handle it; drink some more. The Bible says, “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.”

The bottle wants to fill you: drink me and be filled with my love. It says, you're alone, nobody understands us, I love you more than anybody. I love you more than water. You don't need to eat today; I'll make the food taste better. You can't sleep; I can put you to sleep so fast you won't even realize it. The bottle starts talking like scripture: I am that I am, the comfort of them all.

That is excess, and it destroys the body too. Alcohol builds fat around your organs and your belly, raises your risk of heart disease, high blood pressure and type two diabetes, makes you hungrier and drives you to fast food. Four or five shots a drink every day is thousands of calories a week, and then you wonder why you can't lose weight or climb a flight of stairs.

The command is to be filled with something else: the Spirit. Cast your burden on the Lord and be filled with his Spirit, not with the bottle.

The bottle says, forget your pain; the Bible says, “Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee.” The bottle says, numb your sorrow. Christ answers that lie: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”

The bottle offers to carry your burden for you. It talks to you like scripture in a dark room with one light over the table: drink me, I can take away thy sorrows; you're depressed, don't worry about it; you're stressed out, put the kids to bed early and drink me. That is a spirit having a conversation with you.

Christ is the one who actually takes the weight. The labouring and heavy laden are told to come to him, not to the liquor store, and he gives rest. The bottle only numbs the sorrow until tomorrow; casting the burden on the Lord is how he sustains you and keeps the righteous from being moved.

The bottle says, you can't change. You're the same; you're going to be that same person. The Bible says, “The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul.”

The law of the Lord converts the soul: it changes a man. So the lie that you can't change is answered by the perfect law of God. You can repent and become a new man.

That is the other side of casting your burden on the Lord. You don't just hand him the weight; you take on his law, and his law turns you into somebody different. The bottle keeps you drunk and stupid, the way the enemy wants it, with a liquor store in every black neighborhood and weed stores everywhere to keep you high, drunk and stupid. The law of the Lord makes the simple wise and converts the soul out of that.

The bottle says, you are a failure. You ain't nothing. You're going to be the same person you always were. The Bible says: “There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.”

Guess what? You can repent. The bottle says you're a failure; the Bible says you can repent and become a new man.

But it starts with acknowledging it: I'm an alcoholic. I'm a fornicator, an adulterer, a liar, a thief; I deal with envy, covetousness, idolatry. That is where the change happens. And acknowledging it is not enough; you have to work on fixing those things. You can't say, I'm an alcoholic, and keep going out drinking.

No condemnation belongs to those who walk after the Spirit and not after the flesh. The man chained to the bottle is walking after the flesh; the man who casts his burden on the Lord and walks in the Spirit is free of the condemnation the bottle keeps whispering over him.
