“So the people honoured him with ten thousands, and praised him in the blessings of the Lord, in that he gave him a crown of glory. For he destroyed the enemies on every side, and brought to nought the Philistines his adversaries, and brake their horn in sunder unto this day.”

David destroyed the enemies on every side. Those are the wars that were about him on every side, which kept him from building the house, until the Lord put them “under the soles of his feet.” What David fought through, Solomon inherited as rest.
docs/study/1-kings/6.md|1 Kings 6:36-38|:
“And the Lord spake unto Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they offered before the Lord, and died”. He charged “that he come not at all times into the holy place within the vail before the mercy seat, which is upon the ark; that he die not: for I will appear in the cloud upon the mercy seat.”

When Aaron came, he had to come “with a young bullock for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering”, put on “the holy linen coat”, the linen breeches, girdle and mitre, “these are holy garments; therefore shall he wash his flesh in water, and so put them on.” Entrance into the holy place was not to be taken lightly.

The pattern of the house was not invented by Solomon. The Most High had already shown the fashion of the sanctuary to Moses in the mount: the holy place within the vail, the mercy seat upon the ark, and all its parts. Solomon spent seven years building the house “according to all the fashion of it”, the fashion the Most High had given.
docs/study/1-kings/7.md|1 Kings 7:40-47|:
“But into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood, which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people: The Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest, while as the first tabernacle was yet standing”.

It was “a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience; Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.” The time of reformation is the coming of Christ.

That is what all Hiram’s bright brass served: the lavers, the shovels, the basons, the ten bases and ten lavers, the one sea on twelve oxen. They were for the washings and the sacrifices of that service, vessels so many “Solomon left all the vessels unweighed”, all belonging to the carnal ordinances that stood until Christ came.
docs/study/1-kings/8.md|1 Kings 8:41-45|:
“Thus saith the Lord of hosts; In those days it shall come to pass, that ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you.”

That is the same joining of the nations to the house of Jacob that Solomon foresaw when he prayed for the stranger “that is not of thy people Israel, but cometh out of a far country for thy name’s sake”, that “all people of the earth may know thy name, to fear thee, as do thy people Israel”.

The nations come because they have heard that God is with Israel. That hearing of the nations comes only when Israel is right and in rulership, not while Israel is in captivity and sin. The Most High hears the stranger’s prayer out of respect for Israel; he does not hear a prayer aimed against his people. When Israel goes out to battle where he sends them, he will “hear thou in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.”
docs/study/1-kings/9.md|1 Kings 9:1-2|So:
“I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon.” Solomon by his own word is black.

So when Solomon “had finished the building of the house of the Lord”, and the Most High appeared to him the second time as at Gibeon, the man who built the first temple was a black man, and the scripture says so plainly. The so-called Jews boast of the temple and their heritage in a land that does not belong to them, but the builder of that temple was black.
docs/study/1-kings/9.md|1 Kings 9:20-23|:
“And the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel; and he said, Because that this people hath transgressed my covenant which I commanded their fathers, and have not hearkened unto my voice; I also will not henceforth drive out any from before them of the nations which Joshua left when he died: That through them I may prove Israel, whether they will keep the way of the Lord to walk therein, as their fathers did keep it, or not.”

That is why there were still Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites in the land in Solomon’s day, “whom the children of Israel also were not able utterly to destroy”. The Most High left the nations to prove Israel whether they would keep his way as their fathers did.

“Now these are the nations which the Lord left, to prove Israel by them, even as many of Israel as had not known all the wars of Canaan”. These are the nations the Most High left to prove Israel and to teach them war.

Those same nations, their children “that were left after them in the land”, are the ones Solomon put under a tribute of bondservice, while the children of Israel served as his men of war, his captains and the rulers of his chariots and horsemen.

“Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids.” Bondmen and bondmaids are to be taken of the heathen round about.

So when Solomon levied a tribute of bondservice on “all the people that were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, which were not of the children of Israel”, it was lawful by the law.

“But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no bondmen: but they were men of war, and his servants, and his princes, and his captains, and rulers of his chariots, and his horsemen.” Instead of enslaving his own people, he built them up and gave them positions.
docs/study/1-kings/9.md|1 Kings 9:6-9|De:
“But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee”.

This is the same warning Moses gave in the law, and the Most High gives it again to Solomon: “if ye shall at all turn from following me, ye or your children, and will not keep my commandments and my statutes”, “Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them”. Disobedience brings the curse of scattering, and it reaches not only that generation but the seed after them.

The Most High is not all love. When they ask why this came, the answer is, “Because they forsook the Lord their God”, “therefore hath the Lord brought upon them all this evil.”

“And thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword, among all nations whither the Lord shall lead thee.”

The Most High told Solomon the same: “Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people: And at this house, which is high, every one that passeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss”. The house that was high and mighty would astonish everyone who passed by.

They would ask, “Why hath the Lord done thus unto this land, and to this house?” and the answer: Israel forsook the Most High who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and took hold of other gods. The curse of the law and the word to Solomon are one.
docs/study/1-samuel/1.md|1 Samuel 1:12-1:
“And whatsoever we ask, we receive of him, because we keep his commandments, and do those things that are pleasing in his sight.”

Hannah was granted her petition because of what she did before she even asked: she kept his commandments and did those things that are pleasing in his sight. She went up to Shiloh and prayed before the Lord, and Eli said, “the God of Israel grant thee thy petition”.

If we keep the commandments and it be his will, we receive whatsoever we ask, in his time.

“And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him.”

Hannah poured out her soul before the Lord, speaking in her heart so that only her lips moved, and Eli took her for drunken. When she told him, “I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the Lord”, Eli answered, “Go in peace: and the God of Israel grant thee thy petition that thou hast asked of him.” She believed when she heard the word of Eli: she “went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad.”

Why did the Lord grant her petition? It was the will of the Most High for Samuel to come through Hannah; it was just in his time.

Understand this: a lot of us pray for things that the Lord has not given to us. The Most High has the infinite and ultimate wisdom and knows what is best for us, so some things he keeps back from us, and we have to accept that and know that. If it be his will, we receive what we ask, in his time; if it is not his will, we will not receive it.
docs/study/1-samuel/1.md|1 Samuel 1:21|D:
“Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the Lord empty”.

The feast of unleavened bread is known as Passover; the feast of weeks is known as Pentecost; and the feast of tabernacles is also known as the feast of booths.

That is what the yearly sacrifice is going into when “the man Elkanah, and all his house, went up to offer unto the Lord the yearly sacrifice, and his vow.” Elkanah, who lived in mount Ephraim, was applying this law over and over again, going up to the place the Lord had chosen.
docs/study/1-samuel/1.md|1 Samuel 1:24-2:
“When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.”

“Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error”. The angel is your personal angel, your guardian angel for lack of a better word, that watches over you and listens to you. Do not say, I did not mean to say that. Yes you did; the angel recorded it and knew exactly what it was.

Hannah paid her vow. When she had weaned the child she brought him to the house of the Lord in Shiloh and said, “For this child I prayed; and the Lord hath given me my petition which I asked of him: Therefore also I have lent him to the Lord; as long as he liveth he shall be lent to the Lord.” That is great faith right there, and she kept her promise. Hannah was an upright and honest woman.

That is why Christ went on to say, “But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.”

Whatever comes out of your mouth, be upright and honest, and do that which comes out of thy mouth. Hannah said she would give the child to the Lord all the days of his life, and she did: “as long as he liveth he shall be lent to the Lord.” Her yea was yea.
docs/study/1-samuel/1.md|1 Samuel 1:9-11:
“And Delilah said unto Samson, Hitherto thou hast mocked me, and told me lies: tell me wherewith thou mightest be bound. And he said unto her, If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web.”

Samson spoke of the seven locks of his head: the locks of the Nazarite vow. Samson was under that same vow that Hannah made for Samuel, that there should no razor come upon his head. The locks are the hair of the head let grow and locked in, as the law of the Nazarite says.

“All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the Lord, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow.”

Hannah, in bitterness of soul, vowed: if the Lord would “give unto thine handmaid a man child, then I will give him unto the Lord all the days of his life, and there shall no razor come upon his head.” What law is that going back to? The law of the Nazarite. Put that together as you read through Samuel about Samuel: he was given to the Lord under the Nazarite vow.

The locks of a Nazarite are hair braided so that it locks into place as it grows long. When you braid your hair, you are locking it in.
docs/study/1-samuel/10.md|1 Samuel 10:9|:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.”

That is what the Most High did for Saul: “when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart: and all those signs came to pass that day.”
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:12:
Moses saw this coming long before it happened. In the spirit of the Lord he knew exactly what Israel would do once they came into the land, and he wrote it down ahead of time: “When thou art come unto the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, and shalt possess it, and shalt dwell therein, and shalt say, I will set a king over me, like as all the nations that are about me”.

That is what Samuel is rebuking. When Nahash the king of the children of Ammon came against them, Israel said, “Nay; but a king shall reign over us: when the Lord your God was your king.” They wanted a king they could see and touch, because all the nations around them had kings. That demand exposed their disbelief in the Lord, and Moses had already written it down.

The same law that foresaw the demand set its terms: “Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee, whom the Lord thy God shall choose: one from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee: thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother.”

So when Samuel says, “behold, the Lord hath set a king over you”, the king stands under the law Moses wrote ahead of time: one whom the Lord thy God shall choose, one from among thy brethren, never a stranger.

The law of the king ends on the very terms Samuel just laid before the people. The king must walk so “That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and that he turn not aside from the commandment, to the right hand, or to the left: to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he, and his children, in the midst of Israel.”

Samuel says the same: “If ye will fear the Lord, and serve him, and obey his voice, and not rebel against the commandment of the Lord, then shall both ye and also the king that reigneth over you continue following the Lord your God”. If you and your king do not rebel against the voice of the Lord, the ultimate king, you will be all right. The king who turns not aside prolongs his days in his kingdom, he and his children.

Then comes the other side: “But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee”.

Samuel says it again: “But if ye will not obey the voice of the Lord, but rebel against the commandment of the Lord, then shall the hand of the Lord be against you, as it was against your fathers.” He repeats it because Israelites require repetition. The hand of the Lord against you is these curses coming upon you and overtaking you.

Among those curses the king himself is named: “The Lord shall bring thee, and thy king which thou shalt set over thee, unto a nation which neither thou nor thy fathers have known; and there shalt thou serve other gods, wood and stone.”

That is why Samuel puts the people and the king under the same warning. If you and your king disobey, the Lord sends you and your king into subjection to the other nations. The king they demanded so they could be like the nations would go down with them into the hands of the nations.
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:16:
To demonstrate how wicked Israel was for asking a king, Samuel asks, “Is it not wheat harvest to day?” That was the very day they expected clear skies to gather the wheat, and Samuel called unto the Lord, “and the Lord sent thunder and rain that day”.

“The Lord thundered from heaven, and the most High uttered his voice.” Imagine how terrified they were when that voice went off over their harvest: “all the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel.”

“And he sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them.” That is the power the Most High put on display that day.

The thunder and rain came when Samuel called, on the day it should have been clear, “that ye may perceive and see that your wickedness is great, which ye have done in the sight of the Lord, in asking you a king.”
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:20:
Samuel does not tell Israel they did nothing wrong: “Fear not: ye have done all this wickedness: yet turn not aside from following the Lord, but serve the Lord with all your heart”. Yes, you did all this wickedness, but now you get it; after all the wickedness you have done, still serve the Lord. That is heavy.

This is really a precept for “a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.” The fall does not end your service to the Most High. The just man rises up again and keeps following the Lord with all his heart.
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:21:
“And turn ye not aside: for then should ye go after vain things, which cannot profit nor deliver; for they are vain.” Something you make with your own hands is not going to make thunder and rain come on your harvest day to show you how wicked you are. Idols cannot help you or save you.

Samuel warned Israel not to do it, and over a span of time that is exactly what they ended up doing. The Lord asked through Jeremiah, “What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?” They walked after the vain things Samuel named, and became vain themselves.

Our people do the same thing today, icing out crosses and things of that nature that cannot do a thing for them. Those are the vain things our people follow after.
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:22:
“For the Lord will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake: because it hath pleased the Lord to make you his people.” That is part of the comfort of the scriptures: he may purge his people, but he will never exterminate the Israelites, for his name’s sake.

Test that against the doctrine that says the Most High cast off Israel after Christ. Paul, whose writings that doctrine misinterprets, asks the question himself: “Hath God cast away his people? God forbid.” And he gives himself as the proof: “For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.” Paul said the same thing Samuel said.

Paul goes on: “God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew.” The Lord has not cast off Israel.

It pleased the Lord to make Israel his people in Samuel’s day, and after Christ they are still the people which he foreknew. He will not forsake them, for his great name’s sake.
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:23:
Marinate on this verse: “Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way”. Samuel was a leader who loved his nation, and he says that if he stopped praying for them, that itself would put him in sin.

“Yea, thou castest off fear, and restrainest prayer before God.” Restraining prayer shows you are starting to lack fear of the Most High. If you want him in your life, you cannot restrain prayer from him, any more than you would let communication die with someone you wanted to keep.

For those who battle with prayer, meditate on that: ceasing to pray for your nation puts you in sin.
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:6-:
“He made known his ways unto Moses, his acts unto the children of Israel.”

Samuel told the people, “It is the Lord that advanced Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. Now therefore stand still, that I may reason with you before the Lord of all the righteous acts of the Lord, which he did to you and to your fathers.” The righteous acts Samuel rehearses are those acts the Most High made known unto the children of Israel.
docs/study/1-samuel/12.md|1 Samuel 12:8-:
After Gideon led the three hundred, “the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son’s son also: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian.”

Gideon is Jerubbaal, one of the deliverers Samuel names: “the Lord sent Jerubbaal, and Bedan, and Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and ye dwelled safe.” This is the history of the book of Judges. When Israel forgat the Lord their God, he sold them into the hand of Sisera, of the Philistines, and of the king of Moab; when they cried, “We have sinned, because we have forsaken the Lord, and have served Baalim and Ashtaroth”, he sent a deliverer.

The people wanted to make their deliverer a king. But none of those saviors had to wear a crown.

“And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you.”

Gideon refused. He knew that if thrones were set up, the people would put their trust and faith in the king instead of the Most High. It was never the Lord’s intention to set kings in the flesh over Israel; he was to be our king.

That is Samuel’s point in rehearsing the deliverers. Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel delivered Israel on every side, and Israel dwelled safe, without a crown. What Israel needed was not a king but to put away the idols. It is not just about having the ark of the covenant among you, as when Israel went and got the ark against the Philistines, got beat even worse, and lost the ark. You have to put away the idols and stop serving Baalim and Ashtaroth.
docs/study/1-samuel/13.md|1 Samuel 13:11:
Samuel asks, “What hast thou done?” and Saul answers with excuses: “Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash”, so “I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering.” This is part of Saul’s pattern of behavior: he never wants to hold himself accountable; he always deflects onto whoever else.

“Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity”. The Most High says stop playing the blame game if you want him to intervene on your behalf. Pointing the finger is exactly what Saul did.
docs/study/1-samuel/13.md|1 Samuel 13:13:
Samuel does not entertain the excuses: “Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God, which he commanded thee”. Saul thought he was only bending Samuel’s word, but disobeying the instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord. For that one act of foolishness the Lord withdrew what he would have given, Saul’s lineage ruling Israel: “for now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever. But now thy kingdom shall not continue”.

The Lord wants to see whether you will perform what he told you to do even when things do not work out how you planned. “Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness?” Abraham drew down with the knife even when it made no fleshly sense. “Joseph in the time of his distress kept the commandment and was made lord of Egypt.” Joseph was betrayed and tempted, kept the commandment, and was exalted.

Loyalty to the Lord regardless of circumstances is what the trial is for. That is what proves you faithful in temptation and worthy of being exalted, and Saul failed that test in the time of his distress.

Samuel told Saul, “the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people”. Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement.

Paul names him: “And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.” That man is David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures. Saul had not kept that which the Lord commanded; David was the one which shall fulfil all his will.
docs/study/1-samuel/13.md|1 Samuel 13:5-:
“For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” The Lord did not give us the spirit of fear.

As the chosen people, if we really have faith we should be fearless. For the people of the Most High, fearfulness before the enemy is unbelief. The Lord had just defeated the Philistines for Israel; to still fear the enemy shows a lack of faith, that you really do not believe in your God.

“As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers; and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein.” If the ruler is a coward, so goes the rest of the nation.

That is why the leader must be fearless: the hearts of the people depend upon their leadership. Nehemiah understood it and would not flee. In Saul’s camp, “all the people followed him trembling.”

“My brethren, be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation.” That is why the scriptures say the greater condemnation.

If you aspire to leadership, make sure your spirit is right, because if you fold when you are tried, you are accountable for all the souls that fold right along with you.

The Philistines came up with “thirty thousand chariots, and six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand which is on the sea shore in multitude”, far deeper than the three thousand Israel had prepared. The men of Israel saw they were in a strait and hid themselves “in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in high places, and in pits.” The sons of God, the mighty men of valor, saw the enemy coming and started hiding, though the Lord had just defeated the Philistines for Israel in chapter 7.

Nehemiah shows the right spirit. In the Persian captivity he had liberty from the king to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and the enemies Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem plotted to scare him off the work. Shemaiah counseled him to hide: “Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple, and let us shut the doors of the temple: for they will come to slay thee; yea, in the night will they come to slay thee.”

Nehemiah answered, “Should such a man as I flee? and who is there, that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in.” He was the governor the Most High set up for everybody to look up to, and he would not go in.

Nehemiah saw through it: “And, lo, I perceived that God had not sent him; but that he pronounced this prophecy against me: for Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.” And he names the purpose: “Therefore was he hired, that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin, and that they might have matter for an evil report, that they might reproach me.”

Afraid, and do so, and sin: operating in the spirit of fear is sin according to the scripture. Fear in the leader would let the enemy call him weak and unfit to lead. Israel did what Nehemiah refused to do; they hid, and the people that stayed with Saul “followed him trembling.”
docs/study/1-samuel/13.md|1 Samuel 13:8-:
Samuel had instructed Saul in chapter 10: when you get to Gilgal, tarry seven days, make no moves until I arrive. Saul “tarried seven days, according to the set time that Samuel had appointed: but Samuel came not to Gilgal; and the people were scattered from him.” The people were acting frantic, and Saul said, “Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and peace offerings. And he offered the burnt offering.” Saul is not the priest; that is Samuel’s office.

“Set thy heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble.” Saul made haste in a time of trouble. He panicked and did unadvisedly, and he is going to suffer consequences for it. Then, “as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came”: he was barely late, and Saul could not hold his patience.

Brothers do the same thing today: leadership said it would be here at ten, it is five past ten, so we cancel the plan and go home. Be humble and tarry like you were instructed. It may run some minutes over, and the Lord may be testing your patience.
docs/study/1-samuel/14.md|1 Samuel 14:27:
Jonathan had not heard his father charge the people with the oath. He dipped the end of his rod in an honeycomb, “and put his hand to his mouth; and his eyes were enlightened.” Like the first taste after a long fast, he felt like a whole new creature. Then he was told, “Thy father straitly charged the people with an oath, saying, Cursed be the man that eateth any food this day. And the people were faint.”

Jonathan answered, “My father hath troubled the land”, and began to convince the people that eating was the better idea and that the king’s order was folly: “How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? for had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines?”

“My son, fear thou the Lord and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change”. Saul was the king and put out an order. When someone among you tries to change the orders of the king, do not meddle with him, because he will lead you into error, which is exactly what happened next.
docs/study/1-samuel/14.md|1 Samuel 14:36:
“But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear.” Sin and iniquity are what cause the Most High not to hear you, plain and clear.

So when Saul asked counsel of God and “he answered him not that day”, the silence was the answer: iniquity had separated them from their God.

Saul proposed, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night, and spoil them until the morning light”, and the people agreed. Then the priest said, “Let us draw near hither unto God.” Saul asked, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? wilt thou deliver them into the hand of Israel? But he answered him not that day.”

“If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me”. Somewhere in the camp there was iniquity, so the Lord did not hear Saul. If you are spiritual, when the Lord ignores you, you understand at that point what it reveals: it is sin. It has to be; the scriptures give only that reason.
docs/study/1-samuel/14.md|1 Samuel 14:4-:
Between the passages were two sharp rocks, Bozez and Seneh, one facing Michmash and the other Gibeah. Jonathan said, “Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the Lord will work for us: for there is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few.” The Lord put that spirit on Jonathan.

Judas answered in the same spirit: “It is no hard matter for many to be shut up in the hands of a few; and with the God of heaven it is all one, to deliver with a great multitude, or a small company: For the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host; but strength cometh from heaven.” We do not have to come deep to get the victory.

That is how the Most High operates: he loves to show his power by having a small number defeat a very large number. That is why it will be the 144,000 taking over the whole world; that is just how he rolls.

Asa had the same faith: “Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O Lord our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude. O Lord, thou art our God; let not man prevail against thee.”

That is the faith you see in Jonathan and this young servant: “there is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few.” Two men going against an army in the name of the Lord.
docs/study/1-samuel/14.md|1 Samuel 14:45:
The people stood up for Jonathan: “Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the Lord liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not.” They kept him from the wrath of his father.

Think about the contrast, and why the scripture says to get the love of the congregation. In chapter 13 Saul was the one disobeying the voice of the Lord and getting rebuked, while Jonathan was brave and mighty and had just saved Israel out of the hand of its enemies. Now the coward wants to kill the deliverer.

“For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.” Saul had just been shown mercy for his own failure, so passing merciless judgment on his own son would have left no mercy for Saul the next time he fell. In some situations you have to weigh it like the people did: yes, he made a mistake and crossed the order, but he just saved all our lives.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:1-:
“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt.” Generations after the wilderness, the Most High still remembers, and he told Israel to remember too: “Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt; How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.”

The detail is written to stir you up. They preyed on the weak and the tired.

The same law told Israel when to act: “Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.” Israel now had rest and a king; the time had come. The generation of Amalekites had returned, and it was time to fulfil what was written.

So the order to Saul is specific: “Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.” Kill all of them, spare none.

The Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness. That answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers.

“For he said, Because the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.” That war did not end in the wilderness; it was still on in Saul’s day.

It applies to this day. The same war continues from generation to generation, and it is now more spiritual than ever, because the adversary has established the imagination that they are the Jews, and we go out and cast down that imagination every day.

“Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.” Read who it speaks of: the children of thy people. The grudge law is toward your own people, not toward the enemies of Israel whom the Most High has sworn against.

Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember: “thou shalt not forget it.” Against Amalek this is a righteous grudge.

“And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity.” A soul that hears and is a witness must utter it, or he bears the iniquity himself.

Hence if we hear of any violence, we report it and make it known. We do not incite it and we do not condone it.

“Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof.” Edom cheered Babylon on when Jerusalem burned; they were the cheerleaders when Babylon destroyed the temple.

The same Most High who remembered Amalek is called on to remember Edom, and the scripture pronounces the payback.

“O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us. Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones.” The Most High calls him happy that pays her back for everything she has done.

But understand the frame. The day of Psalms 137 has not yet come; it belongs to the return of the Lord. So chill out and relax; none of that is for now.

“And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.” Edom grew up from being the daughter of Babylon into Mystery, Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots. That is why the great woman of Revelation carries Babylon’s name.

The payback pronounced on the daughter of Babylon is part of the same war the Lord swore from generation to generation.

“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” That is the walk commanded now.

Understand the frame: we live peaceably with all men and lay hands on no one. We do not incite or condone any violence. The war from generation to generation is fought now by casting down the imagination of the adversary, and the day of Psalms 137 belongs to the return of the Lord.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:10:
“It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king: for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments.” Mark the language: Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counts it as turning back and not performing his commandments at all. For everybody who says, well, I did do this part: whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you.

“And it grieved Samuel; and he cried unto the Lord all night.” Pride had to be in operation for Saul to transgress on that level, and pride is where the throne is lost: “The beginning of pride is when one departeth from God, and his heart is turned away from his Maker. For pride is the beginning of sin, and he that hath it shall pour out abomination: and therefore the Lord brought upon them strange calamities, and overthrew them utterly. The Lord hath cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.”

That is exactly what happened. Saul’s heart turned from his Maker, he poured out sin upon sin from there, and the Lord cast down the proud prince’s throne and set up the meek in his stead. That is the whole story that follows.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:12:
Samuel rose early to meet Saul, and it was told him that Saul “came to Carmel, and, behold, he set him up a place”, a monument to himself. When your transgression becomes the lesson, be thankful when the correction comes quietly and nobody knows your name. Do not take the spirit of bitterness, because you deserved a lot more.

The first thing out of Saul’s mouth is a fabrication, knowing full well he transgressed: “Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord.” Samuel answers, “What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear?” If you performed the commandment, why do I hear animals?

Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: “They have brought them from the Amalekites: for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed.” Verse 9 already told us Saul and the people spared them; now suddenly it is only the people, and for a good reason, a sacrifice, as though the Lord ought to be pleased.

“What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.” The Most High made a law for the bright ideas that come along the way of following instructions, and it is plain.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:16:
“When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel?” Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance.

That is how Saul started. He had answered Samuel, “Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?” That was the little-in-his-own-sight attitude: he thought nothing of himself, with no confidence to be a ruler, and the Most High still chose him.

Then the Lord sent him on the errand of the vengeance written in Deuteronomy 25: “Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed.” “Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord?” Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:20:
Saul is in denial: “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me”. Samuel breaks down the rebuke, and Saul tells the prophet he is wrong.

In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion. He “brought Agag the king of Amalek”, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted. Then he lays the spoil on the people again: “the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed”.

“If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me: if I say, I am perfect, it shall also prove me perverse.” When you plead your own righteousness against correction, you end up revealing more of your rebellion out of your own mouth, which is exactly what Saul did.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:22:
“Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” Do you think the Lord prefers a sacrifice to atone for broken commandments over you simply keeping the commandments? That is a heavy verse.

“He that sacrificeth of a thing wrongfully gotten, his offering is ridiculous; and the gifts of unjust men are not accepted.” The spoil was wrongfully gotten, taken against the will of the Lord, so the offering is ridiculous. “The most High is not pleased with the offerings of the wicked; neither is he pacified for sin by the multitude of sacrifices.” All those animals were not going to pacify his anger.

“The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination: how much more, when he bringeth it with a wicked mind?” Such a sacrifice does not merely do nothing; it makes the Most High more angry.

Saul probably would have kept those animals to eat had it never been pointed out.

David wrote this in his repentance: “For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”

The true sacrifice is being sorry and remorseful for what you did, not pleading why you were not wrong for doing wrong. That is the spirit Saul does not have.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:23:
“For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.” That is heavy. A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft.

Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross. “Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king”: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in.

“A stubborn heart shall fare evil at the last; and he that loveth danger shall perish therein. An obstinate heart shall be laden with sorrows; and the wicked man shall heap sin upon sin.” Obstinate is another word for stubborn: the mind set on doing what it wants contrary to counsel will be laden with sorrows. Saul heaped sin upon sin, lying, justifying himself and blaming the people, and that is what carried him into the witchcraft and idolatry of rebellion.

This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last. Saul’s end comes in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:24:
Now the confession finally comes, and it is still not sincere: “I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” Even in admitting it he deflects: it is the fault of the wicked people you put me over. Then he asks, “pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord”: take me back to the regular Saul and Samuel connection, as though a fearful excuse settles it.

“The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the Lord shall be safe.” If you fear what the people will say, you will fall into the trap and transgress. That is why a leader cannot fold when the people become too much to handle. Saul would have been safe had he trusted the Lord.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:26:
“They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.” Saul professed, restore me that I may worship the Lord, while every work denied him.

This is the starting point of Saul losing the Spirit and going reprobate. He rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord rejected him.

“I will not return with thee: for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel.” Think it through. Samuel gave Saul the opening at the bleating of the sheep, and Saul would not humble down; he asked why Saul disobeyed the voice of the Lord, and Saul justified himself again. Two admonitions were given and refused before this rejection.

“A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject”. Saul had two chances to repent and confess and still justified himself, so Samuel did exactly what the scripture says and rejected him.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:27:
“Do not bind the counsels of the Lord our God: for God is not as man, that he may be threatened; neither is he as the son of man, that he should be wavering.” The Most High is not as man, that he may be threatened, and he does not waver.

Saul laid hold of the prophet’s mantle, but the sentence on Saul stood: “the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent”.

As Samuel turned about to go away, Saul “laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent.” Samuel said, “The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.” Just as Saul tore the hem of the garment, so the Lord tore the throne from him. Samuel says this still before he has ever met David, the same word he gave in chapter 13.

“And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.” “God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?” What he said over Saul, he will do.

The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan. If a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.
docs/study/1-samuel/15.md|1 Samuel 15:4-:
Saul gathered the people and numbered them in Telaim, “two hundred thousand footmen, and ten thousand men of Judah”, and laid wait in the valley. Then he warned the Kenites: “Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt.”

“And the children of the Kenite, Moses’ father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah”. These are the people of Jethro, whose counsel set up the ranking system over Israel, and whose family was as eyes for Israel in the wilderness. They were always helpful to us.

The Most High discriminates righteously: the people who showed Israel kindness were spared out of the judgment. “So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.”
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:14:
“But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” Simultaneously, as the Most High put his spirit on David, the spirit departed from Saul. Note it well: the evil spirit came from the Lord. That is a teaching the church world leaves out.

Chapter 15 said, “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.” Saul is now headed down that downward spiral. The spirit is leaving him, and the road Saul took ends with him literally at witchcraft: he will eventually become a reprobate and dabble in real witchcraft.

“An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him.” Rebellion is what Saul sought in chapter 15, and now the cruel messenger is sent: “an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” A cruel spirit sent to trouble him is what we see on Saul.
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:15:
“Behold now, an evil spirit from God troubleth thee.” It was evident. Whatever Saul was doing and saying, his servants could tell an evil spirit was on him.

Why did the spirit leave Saul? Wisdom walks with a man by crooked ways at the first and tries him by her laws: “For at the first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him, and torment him with her discipline, until she may trust his soul, and try him by her laws. Then will she return the straight way unto him, and comfort him, and shew him her secrets. But if he go wrong, she will forsake him, and give him over to his own ruin.”

Saul was put through a trial, whether he would keep the commandment given through the mouth of the prophet, and he went wrong. Had he passed the test he would have been elevated, but wisdom forsook him and gave him over to his own ruin, that abyss of jealousy, envy and hatred.

“For froward thoughts separate from God: and his power, when it is tried, reproveth the unwise.” Froward means contrary. Saul set his mind on the contrary of what the Most High commanded.

“For into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter; nor dwell in the body that is subject unto sin. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and remove from thoughts that are without understanding, and will not abide when unrighteousness cometh in.” The holy spirit of discipline fled Saul’s deceit and would not dwell in a body subject unto sin, and his servants could see what came in its place: “an evil spirit from God”.
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:16:
Saul’s servants proposed the remedy: “seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well.” Our people understood back then that music is spiritual. The right playing could relieve an evil spirit.

“Moreover David and the captains of the host separated to the service of the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals”. Musicians prophesying with instruments of music.

“Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.” What is played into the ears works on the spirit.

If a spiritual song can heal, so that Saul “shalt be well” when the harp is played, think what an evil song can do to a good spirit. Be mindful when it comes to music.

“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.” The command is spiritual songs, sung to the Most High.

The songs we make and listen to, now that we know the truth, should be spiritual songs. The psalms were the jams of that day, and every one of them is deep, teaching who the daughter of Babylon is, the crafty counsel taken against us, and that the law was given to Israel.

“For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a strange land?”

In this captivity our people are paid fortunes to sing the opposite of spiritual songs, songs that help destroy one another.
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:18:
“Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Beth–lehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the Lord is with him.” The servant did not say the name, but this son of Jesse who went hard on the instruments was David.

“As is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel.”

David was also a singer: “In all his works he praised the Holy One most high with words of glory; with his whole heart he sung songs, and loved him that made him. He set singers also before the altar, that by their voices they might make sweet melody, and daily sing praises in their songs.”

That is the same service we read of in 1 Chronicles 25, the singers set before the altar. Praises in their songs, not filth.
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:19:
Saul sent to Jesse, “Send me David thy son, which is with the sheep.” Jesse sent David with “an ass laden with bread, and a bottle of wine, and a kid”, and “David came to Saul, and stood before him: and he loved him greatly; and he became his armourbearer.”

These are David’s humble beginnings, serving at the king’s side. Even after the spirit had left Saul, David loved him and served him faithfully. Saul sent again, “Let David, I pray thee, stand before me; for he hath found favour in my sight.” Saul liked the spirit on that young brother, and every king keeps a young soldier always with him.

“The king’s favour is toward a wise servant: but his wrath is against him that causeth shame.” That is what David was as armourbearer. We know him as a mighty king, but he started out a wise servant, and that is how he got the king’s favour.
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:2-:
“And Samuel said, How can I go? if Saul hear it, he will kill me.” Remember the influence and love Samuel had among the people; even so, this shows the power of the king. Saul raised no hand against Samuel yet, but a king had the authority to command a prophet’s death.

The debate before the king of Persia over what is strongest says the same: “O ye men, do not men excel in strength that bear rule over sea and land and all things in them? But yet the king is more mighty: for he is lord of all these things, and hath dominion over them; and whatsoever he commandeth them they do.”

“And yet he is but one man: if he command to kill, they kill; if he command to spare, they spare”. The king is only one man, but if he command to kill, they kill. That is the power Saul held, and why Samuel had cause to be careful.

So the Most High told Samuel, “Take an heifer with thee, and say, I am come to sacrifice to the Lord.” He would go incognito, as if coming only to sacrifice, not letting it be known that he was coming to anoint Saul’s replacement, and the Most High would show him whom to anoint: “thou shalt anoint unto me him whom I name unto thee.”
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:6-:
“Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live?” The Most High is the Father of spirits. He deals with the spirits of men, not the outside.

That is why Eliab’s countenance and the height of his stature meant nothing: “the Lord looketh on the heart.”

The Lord told Samuel why he refused Eliab: “for the Lord seeth not as man seeth”. This scripture is heavy: it is showing the spirit of Christ before Christ walked the earth.

“And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots”. The rod out of the stem of Jesse is prophecy of Christ, out of this same lineage. The word repeated all through the verses is spirit: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord”. And “he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears”.

That is why the Pharisees could not understand why he dealt with the lower class instead of the mighty men. He was looking on the heart. He knew the Pharisees’ hearts were corrupt, while the humble were willing to devote their lives to the Most High.

When Samuel looked on Eliab, he judged through his own lens as a man: “Surely the Lord’s anointed is before him.” The Most High corrected him: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him”. Looking the mightiest and the tallest does not make a man the one the Most High picked.

“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” That is the same standard the Most High gave Samuel in this verse: “man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.”

This still happens today. Brothers will look at a group and assume the biggest one must be the leader, not knowing that brother might be the soldier while the leader is the slim one beside him.

“Let the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, set a man over the congregation, Which may go out before them, and which may go in before them, and which may lead them out, and which may bring them in; that the congregation of the Lord be not as sheep which have no shepherd.”

In the context of selecting a leader over the congregation, the Most High is called the God of the spirits of all flesh. The selection is always spiritual. So when Samuel came to anoint a king among Jesse’s sons, the Lord did not choose by countenance or stature; he looked on the heart.
docs/study/1-samuel/16.md|1 Samuel 16:8-:
“For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty”.

Not many mighty are called. The Most High did not choose the giants that were in the earth; he chose Israel, few in number. He passed over Jesse’s older, bigger sons and chose the youngest, who kept the sheep. That is how he operates.

The same pattern continues through the prophets. The Most High told Elijah, “And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel–meholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.”

As with Samuel at Jesse’s house, the prophet was sent to anoint the one the Most High named.

Elijah “found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.” Elisha was taken from the plow.

“And he left the oxen, and ran after Elijah”. He slew a yoke of oxen, “and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, and gave unto the people, and they did eat. Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him.” He left the care of the literal flock, ministered to Elijah, and eventually became the prophet in his place.

“Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that should come unto you: Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.”

The spirit that was in the prophets when they were selected to feed the flock of Israel was the spirit of Christ. So when “the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward”, it was the spirit of Christ in the one the Most High selected.

Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, the older, bigger, more developed ones, and Samuel said, “The Lord hath not chosen these.” There remained “yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep.” Samuel would not sit down until he was fetched, and the Most High said, “Arise, anoint him: for this is he.”

The Lord sent word to David himself: “Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I took thee from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel”. From literal sheep to shepherd over the sheep of the house of Israel. Taking a keeper of sheep and making him the shepherd of the nation is a pattern with the Most High.

Amos was taken from the herd: “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet’s son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the Lord took me as I followed the flock, and the Lord said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.”

The Lord took him as he followed the flock, as he took David from the sheep, and sent him to prophesy unto his people Israel.

David was not the first. “Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb.” There the Most High called him out of the midst of the bush.

Moses was following a literal flock when he was called, just as David was keeping his father’s sheep.

At the bush the Most High said, “Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt.” Moses was called from the flock of animals to bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt, and he ended up feeding them with the laws of the Most High.

That is the same pattern as David: the keeper of a flock made the shepherd of the nation.

“He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds: From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.” Sheep in the backyard to feeding the nation.

The Most High took leaders and prophets from following literal flocks and set them to feed the flock of Israel. The youngest son who kept the sheep while his brothers passed before Samuel was brought to feed Jacob.

David was young when the spirit came on him. He was the youngest son, and “the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward.” That is nothing new either.

“Therefore when she was led to be put to death, the Lord raised up the holy spirit of a young youth whose name was Daniel”. Another example of the spirit put on a man at a very young age. The Most High does not choose the ones everybody expects.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:20:
David rose early, left the sheep with a keeper, and came to the trench as the host was shouting for the battle. While he saluted his brethren, the champion came up “and spake according to the same words: and David heard them.” The same daily smack talk.

“And all the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him, and were sore afraid.” Think on it: the whole nation’s freedom, everything they possessed, was on the line, and they ran scared. This is why the Most High said in chapter 16 that he had refused David’s brothers. They were there and did not have the spirit to rise up; they were among the ones who fled.

“Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? or who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity?” That is the spirit the Most High looks for, one who will stand up for his people against the workers of iniquity. He is not worried about outward appearance.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:25:
David asked, “What shall be done to the man that killeth this Philistine, and taketh away the reproach from Israel? for who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?”

The soldiers themselves did not understand that they were the armies of the living God; David, a sheep keeper sent on an errand, knew it. The Most High said it in Egypt: “that I may lay my hand upon Egypt, and bring forth mine armies, and my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great judgments.” He calls his people, the children of Israel, his armies.

Israel is the army of the Most High, and every army requires order. That is why there are captains and officers, and despising that order is despising the army of the living God.

The men of Israel said, “the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father’s house free in Israel.” A prize was on Goliath’s head.

Caleb made a like offer: “He that smiteth Kirjath–sepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.” The same kind of offer the king made over Goliath.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:31:
David’s words were rehearsed before Saul, and David told him, “Let no man’s heart fail because of him; thy servant will go and fight with this Philistine.” Nobody panic; I will handle it. Saul answered, “Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth.”

“Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.” The nation had no example of faith that day, so a young youth had to be that example.

Young people coming into this truth: if the Most High is dealing with you in a special way, do not let anybody discourage you or tell you that you are too young to be a mighty man of the Lord. Do not let it deter you.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:34:
David gave Saul his resume. Keeping his father’s sheep, when “there came a lion, and a bear, and took a lamb out of the flock”, he went out after him and delivered it out of his mouth, “and when he arose against me, I caught him by his beard, and smote him, and slew him.” He might have looked small, but he was killing lions and bears behind his sheep.

“He played with lions as with kids, and with bears as with lambs.” David was a mighty young man, and Saul did not know that about him.

“The Lord that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.” Same God, no difference. “And Saul said unto David, Go, and the Lord be with thee.”
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:38:
Saul armed David with his own armor: “he put an helmet of brass upon his head; also he armed him with a coat of mail.” David girded his sword upon it and assayed to go, “for he had not proved it. And David said unto Saul, I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them. And David put them off him.”

Instead of the helmet and the brass, David “took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd’s bag”, and “his sling was in his hand”. What he put on instead was the whole armour of God: “Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”.

David went to the battle believing his God would fight for him, carrying the word instead of carnal armor.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:41:
When the Philistine saw David, “he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance.” “Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?” He cursed David by his gods and promised to give his flesh “unto the fowls of the air, and to the beasts of the field.”

David answered, “Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.” Again the record shows who the army of the Most High is: Israel.

David understood he did not need the sword, the spear or the shield; he had the spirit of the living God. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.” That is the only way Israel overcomes. It is no amount of carnal firepower that overcomes the enemies of Israel; this is spiritual warfare, and our forefather David understood that.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:46:
Here is the fulfillment in Hezekiah's day. The Lord said, “I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.” And that night “the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.”

Not one sword was lifted by Judah. They went to sleep and woke up to the battle already won. That is how the Lord gets down.

It is the same word David gave before he ever slung the stone: “the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord’s, and he will give you into our hands.”

The Lord said it long before: “I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses, nor by horsemen.” That is a prophecy that Judah would be saved without carnal weapons.

David spoke the same thing to Goliath's face: “the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord’s.” He prophesied the outcome before the fight, “This day will the Lord deliver thee into mine hand”, so “that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.”

The Most High fights how he wants to fight, not how man thinks it must be done. Judah is saved “by the Lord their God”, not by bow or by sword.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:48:
“Slew he not a giant, when he was yet but young? and did he not take away reproach from the people, when he lifted up his hand with the stone in the sling, and beat down the boasting of Goliath?” David was but a youth, and he took the reproach off of Israel.

Where did the strength come from? “For he called upon the most high Lord; and he gave him strength in his right hand to slay that mighty warrior, and set up the horn of his people.” It was the Most High who gave David's right hand its strength.

That is why one shot was all it took. The stone left the sling with the velocity of a bullet, and it “sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth.” David “prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone”, and “there was no sword in the hand of David.” He ran, stood upon the Philistine, drew Goliath's own sword “out of the sheath thereof”, and “cut off his head therewith.”

“And when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled.” They ran from a young youth because they knew something supernatural was going on: he was in the spirit of the Lord.
docs/study/1-samuel/17.md|1 Samuel 17:8-:
Goliath cried unto the armies of Israel, “choose you a man for you, and let him come down to me.” If he kills me, we will be your servants; if I prevail and kill him, ye shall be our servants. “I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together.” “When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid.”

They were in a carnal spirit, measuring his height, his armor and his reach. The spirit had departed, and fear is not the spirit of the Most High: “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” The fear in the camp was not his spirit.

The Most High put laws in the book about going to battle: “When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” The priest was to tell the people, “let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them; For the Lord your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.”

This fear showed that Saul and the people lacked faith. The same God that destroyed Pharaoh and the Egyptians who pursued Israel was with them.

“I, even I, am he that comforteth you: who art thou, that thou shouldest be afraid of a man that shall die, and of the son of man which shall be made as grass”. The chosen people of the living God have no business fearing a man who will be made as grass.

A trial of faith was set before them in the form of one big intimidating man with a big mouth, and they were dismayed.
docs/study/1-samuel/18.md|1 Samuel 18:1-:
The body, “by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.” As muscles and joints are knit into one body, so were Jonathan and David of one spirit.

That is the knitting in 1 Samuel 18: not anything unnatural, but hearts joined like joints and bands in one body, on one accord.

In 1 Samuel 18, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.” Address the perversion head on: souls being knit is not talking about anything unnatural between the two men.

The same word describes the church. The will of Christ for the church at Colosse was “That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ”. That is the same knitting of souls.

So when Jonathan and David “made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul”, and Jonathan gave David his robe, his garments, “even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle”, it was two brothers on one accord, with the same spirit.
docs/study/1-samuel/18.md|1 Samuel 18:10:
James says, “the devils also believe, and tremble.” On the morrow “the evil spirit from God came upon Saul”, and this time it came back with more power: “there was a javelin in Saul’s hand. And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it. And David avoided out of his presence twice.”

When Saul saw how quickly David escaped, he saw the spirit on David, and he trembled: “Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him, and was departed from Saul.” The one seeking David's life became the one afraid. That spirit on David made the hunter the scared one.
docs/study/1-samuel/18.md|1 Samuel 18:13:
“For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.” David kept behaving wisely and left Saul nothing to charge him with.

And the people saw it: “all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them.” Everybody knew he was the one really putting his life on the line and doing the work, even though he had no throne.

“Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man’s sake.”

“Saul removed him from him, and made him his captain over a thousand.” He basically demoted the brother, putting his own armourbearer away from his presence for no reason. Saul separated David from his company, and that is a mark of blessing on David.

“Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.”

David's faithful service under a hateful king did exactly that. “David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the Lord was with him. Wherefore when Saul saw that he behaved himself very wisely, he was afraid of him.” David's continued righteousness heaped coals of fire on Saul. When your righteousness makes the wicked afraid, that is how you know you are in the spirit.
docs/study/1-samuel/18.md|1 Samuel 18:28:
“Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.”

That is the same spirit that was on Saul, the root of bitterness that says, I have to take that man's life. Saul's works were evil and David's were righteous, and “Saul was yet the more afraid of David; and Saul became David’s enemy continually.”

Meanwhile David kept on: he “behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul; so that his name was much set by.” Harmless as a dove, wise as a serpent.

“The parables of knowledge are in the treasures of wisdom: but godliness is an abomination to a sinner.” That is why “Saul became David’s enemy continually.”

Put the verses together: “Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with David”, and he chose to be that man's enemy anyway. If you know the Lord is with somebody and you make yourself their enemy, you have made yourself the adversary.

David was righteous, obedient and humble; Saul was envious, wicked and rebellious, and he could not stand him. As sin is an abomination to the Most High, so godliness is an abomination to a sinner: the sinner cannot bear to look at righteousness.
docs/study/1-samuel/18.md|1 Samuel 18:8-:
“And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.” What was behind that eye? Envy. “The envious man hath a wicked eye; he turneth away his face, and despiseth men.” That is the eye Saul eyed David with.

“A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion.” Saul had his thousands and he still had the kingdom, but his eye was on David's portion: “what can he have more but the kingdom?”

Then: “and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.” From that point forward, that iniquity dried up Saul's soul.

“Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” Wroth is the same word used of Saul: “And Saul was very wroth, and the saying displeased him.” Same word, same spirit, kindled against a brother who had done nothing wrong.

Abel had done nothing to Cain but what the Lord required. David likewise did nothing to Saul but what Saul himself asked of him. Instead of appreciating the song and giving credit where it is due, for the labourer is worthy of his reward, Saul was displeased at his brother's praise: “They have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed but thousands.” That is the spirit of envy.

Christ took the law, “Thou shalt not kill”, and went into the spirit of it: “whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment.” That is the same judgment as a murderer. Anger without a cause is counted as murder in the spirit.

That is where Saul was. David had caused him nothing, yet Saul “was very wroth”, and the wrath had somewhere to go: “Saul eyed David from that day and forward.”
