docs/study/1-samuel/19.md|1 Samuel 19:1-:
“I will not be ashamed to defend a friend; neither will I hide myself from him.” Even with his father the king gone crazy, Jonathan would not abandon David.

He stood in the gap for him: “I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where thou art, and I will commune with my father of thee; and what I see, that I will tell thee.”

“A faithfull friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found such an one hath found a treasure.” That is what Jonathan was to David.

“Saul spake to Jonathan his son, and to all his servants, that they should kill David.” The Philistines could not get him, so now he wants Israelites to kill an Israelite; that is how far down the slope this man has gone. “But Jonathan Saul’s son delighted much in David”, and told him, “Saul my father seeketh to kill thee: now therefore, I pray thee, take heed to thyself until the morning, and abide in a secret place, and hide thyself.”

Jonathan would have been next in line for the throne. You would think his loyalty lay with his daddy, but he saw the spirit was not on his father, it was on his brother David. His loyalty exceeded his own desires. That is the kind of friend to look for, and the lesson to learn from Jonathan.
docs/study/1-samuel/19.md|1 Samuel 19:11:
“An harlot shall be accounted as spittle; but a married woman is a tower against death to her husband.” That is what Michal was to David that night.

Saul “sent messengers unto David’s house, to watch him, and to slay him in the morning.” Having tried to turn his son against David, he now leans on his daughter, David's own wife. But Michal warned him: “If thou save not thy life to night, to morrow thou shalt be slain.” She “let David down through a window: and he went, and fled, and escaped.”

She laid an image in the bed with “a pillow of goats’ hair for his bolster”, and told the messengers, “He is sick.” Saul said, “Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may slay him”, and they found the image. Michal covered herself, saying David threatened her, “Let me go; why should I kill thee?”, but she was looking out for her husband.

At this time Michal was a righteous example, a ride or die. She turns sour some chapters down the line, but here she saved his life.

“But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.”

Note Saul's words: “Why hast thou deceived me so, and sent away mine enemy, that he is escaped?” Saul and David were brothers, both Israel, Benjamin and Judah. Saul made his brother his enemy, and David loved him anyway. That is the understanding Christ was going into: David exemplified it with Saul.
docs/study/1-samuel/19.md|1 Samuel 19:4-:
“Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.” That is the law in the book, and Saul was set on breaking it.

Jonathan put it before his father: “Let not the king sin against his servant, against David; because he hath not sinned against thee, and because his works have been to thee-ward very good.” David “did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine”, and Saul saw it “and didst rejoice.” So “wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?”

Without a cause: in chapter 18 it was just a feeling, wrath at David for nothing. As Christ explained in the spirit, that anger without a cause leads to actually wanting to murder, which is why it carries the same judgment.

“These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him: A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood.” That is the boat Saul put himself in when he sought to “sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause.”

For that moment Saul heard it: “Saul hearkened unto the voice of Jonathan: and Saul sware, As the Lord liveth, he shall not be slain.” And Jonathan brought David to Saul, “and he was in his presence, as in times past.”
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:27-2:
Joshua said, “choose you this day whom ye will serve”, and then: “but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.”

Eli did not hold his house to that. The man of God asked him, “Did I plainly appear unto the house of thy father, when they were in Egypt in Pharaoh’s house?” That is talking about Levi, going into Moses. The Lord chose him “out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to offer upon mine altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me”, and gave his father's house “all the offerings made by fire of the children of Israel.” They had need of nothing; they were well taken care of.

“Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering, which I have commanded in my habitation; and honourest thy sons above me”? You are disrespecting me, is what he is saying: I am supposed to be honoured in everything before the children of Israel, and you let your sons disrespect my offerings.

Take that into account: do you honour your children above what the Lord says to do? Can they do no wrong, even when they are doing real wrong against the Lord, keeping no commandments, never showing up on the sabbath day, and still living under your roof grown? If they are of age, they know right from wrong, and they are under your roof while you keep the commandments, then they had better be keeping the commandments: showing up to every feast day, the blowing of trumpets, the day of atonement, the passover, the same as you. When they are of age they can go their own way, but they should not be living under your roof and breaking the commandments of God. You honour your children above God when you allow that. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:30|G:
The Lord told Eli, “them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed.” Lightly esteemed means the Lord is not really looking out for you: you are not thinking about me, so I am not thinking about you; go ahead and see how it works out for yourself.

That is why the Lord dealt with Abraham the way he did. “For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord, to do justice and judgment; that the Lord may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken of him.” The Most High said, I know how Abraham gets down; he is not going to let his kids be out of order. Abraham was not going to choose his kids above the Most High, and they were going to do all that he commanded.

Eli did the opposite. He honoured his sons above the Lord, and so the Lord said of his house, “Be it far from me.”

“Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” This is what was going on in the tent of Abraham as long as he lived. All the laws that applied to Abraham at that time, he kept them, the sabbath day included; other laws would apply after Israel came out of Egypt.

That is honouring the Lord, and “them that honour me I will honour.”
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:31-3:
“I will cut off thine arm, and the arm of thy father’s house, that there shall not be an old man in thine house.” Cutting off the arm means cutting off thy strength, and it was talking about his children. The Lord was going to kill Eli's descendants young: “all the increase of thine house shall die in the flower of their age”, in the full strength and peak of their youth.

Why would the Lord judge the children of future generations of Eli's house? The thought might be, he is killing them for the sins of their forefather; I thought the sons did not die for the fathers. Ezekiel 18 shows what it is talking about: “If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood”, that “hath lifted up his eyes to the idols, hath committed abomination”: “shall he then live? he shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him.”

The judgment falls on the son that continues in the sins of his father, and he dies for his own doings. Eli's descendants were going to follow in the same way of their fathers, the sons of Belial, doing wickedness and evil. Because Eli did not reprove his sons, the generations after would follow right in their footsteps.

“Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father’s sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like”, “he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live.”

Eating upon the mountains is partaking in the heathen's idol worship, the food and the drink that went into it, as when Israel rose up to eat and to play before the calf. The son who “hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel”, who “hath executed my judgments, hath walked in my statutes”, lives.

So the cutting off of Eli's house was not the sons dying for the father. The Lord cut them off in the strength of their youth because they were going to follow in the same way of their fathers.
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:34-3:
“Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.”

The sign to Eli was that his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, “in one day they shall die both of them.” And the Lord said, “I will raise me up a faithful priest, that shall do according to that which is in mine heart and in my mind: and I will build him a sure house; and he shall walk before mine anointed for ever.”

That is the same man we have to be: faithful unto the Lord, doing all that is in his heart and in his mind, not in our own. We cannot lean upon our own understanding, and we cannot lean upon our own emotions and how we feel. In whatever situation, at any given moment, it is what did the Lord say. Do not let the old man guide you and lead you; it should be the spirit of Christ which is in you, the hidden man.
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:3|He:
“Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.” The letters of Paul, the book of Samuel, the book of Genesis, the laws of Moses: everything we read ultimately leads up to the life of Christ and his return, and all of it is the spirit of Christ telling you to do those things.

All of us in this walk, keeping the commandments and the faith in Christ, have taken covenant and proclaimed out of our mouths that we are going to endure to the end. We broke the bread and drank the wine and took the covenant with the Lord. Now the Lord is judging you by your actions, for “by him actions are weighed”: are you going to endure to the end, whether to Christ's return or until you leave this earth, if you truly love him?
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:3|Lu:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” “the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.” What the Lord weighs is actions: if it came out of your mouth, are you going to do it?

You cannot just say you love the Lord, that you believe in the God of Israel, and do nothing of what he says: not loving your neighbour, holding grudges and envy, respecting leadership above your own husband who is Christ in the house.

Saying, I have a personal relationship with God, God knows my heart, God loves me no matter what: that is arrogancy coming out of the mouth. The scripture says he loves you if you keep the commandments. Hannah said, “let not arrogancy come out of your mouth.”
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:3|Ma:
“That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.”

“Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth.” Make sure what comes out of your mouth is calculated. That whole, we were arguing and it just slipped, will not fly on judgment day. Repent, and make a door and a bar for thy mouth, as the scriptures say.
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:4-5|:
David said, “For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall.” David was a mighty man of war.

So when Zechariah says “he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David”, that is the strength in view: “they that stumbled are girded with strength.”

“He maketh my feet like hinds’ feet, and setteth me upon my high places. He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.” His feet were fast like a deer, and a bow of steel was broken by his arms. David bent steel, took down lions and bears, and killed a giant with a rock and a sling.

Zechariah's word, “he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David”, goes right back to Hannah's word, “they that stumbled are girded with strength.” That is the house of Israel.

In the same verses Hannah is talking about herself: “the barren hath born seven; and she that hath many children is waxed feeble.”

The Lord is prophesying through Hannah: “The bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girded with strength.” Zechariah shows who that is.

“The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah.” The inhabitants of Jerusalem were Benjamin and Levi, in there with Judah. That is why you see so many of Judah, Benjamin and Levi in the truth right now, with the northern kingdom trickling in. The Most High gives the head tribes what is most important first: not worldly things, but the truth of who they are, to raise up the twelve tribes of Jacob.

Then: “and he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David; and the house of David shall be as God, as the angel of the Lord before them.” That is all twelve tribes. He that is feeble shall be as David goes right back to “they that stumbled are girded with strength”: that is the house of Israel.
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:6|De:
“See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal: neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand.”

That is Hannah's word: “The Lord killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up.” The Lord decides who wakes up and the Lord decides who passes; that is all of the Lord.

He says, “there is no god with me.” There is no Buddha, there is no Allah, there is no Krishna; all of that is made-up imaginations of men.
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:7|Ec:
“The Lord maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up.” Ecclesiasticus, the book also called Sirach, says the same: “Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of the Lord.”

All of it comes of the Lord, the poverty and the riches, the bringing low and the lifting up.
docs/study/1-samuel/2.md|1 Samuel 2:8|Ec:
“He raiseth up the poor out of the dust.” Out of the dust means out of confusion: he brings the poor out of confusion, “and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory.”

“Many kings have sat down upon the ground; and one that was never thought of hath worn the crown.” How is that possible? It is the Lord: he brings low, and he lifts up one that was never thought of.

Like David. When Samuel looked at the older brother he thought, he has to be the one, he looks like a king. Ruth said to Boaz, “spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman.” That is the dictionary's own example of the skirt. The Zondervan Compact Bible Dictionary (page 136) shows the basic garments in general use among men of biblical times were the inner tunic, the tunic coat, the girdle and the cloak, with the headdress and sandals. The word skirt in the KJV usually refers to an article of male, not female, clothing, with meanings of extremity and corner. The skirt is the extremity of the garment.

docs/study/1-samuel/3.md|1 Samuel 3:2-3|:
Before the Most High even gave the ten commandments, he made this plain to “the house of Jacob”: “Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles’ wings, and brought you unto myself. Now therefore, if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people: for all the earth is mine: And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.”

Obedience is what he desired most from the beginning, not the blood of bulls and of goats. That is why the Lord said, “I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.”

Samuel lay down “ere the lamp of God went out in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was, and Samuel was laid down to sleep.” Ere means before: before the lamp of God went out.

That light in the temple by the ark was never to go out. The children of Israel were to “bring thee pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always.” “Aaron and his sons shall order it from evening to morning before the Lord: it shall be a statute for ever unto their generations on the behalf of the children of Israel.” Yet at a point in time it did go out.

“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” This is what Christ was quoting when he said “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice”, for the New Testament was not yet written.

The knowledge of God is the keeping of the commandments. The sacrifices were added because of transgression, the animal's blood taken in your place so the Most High would not have to kill you; you read of it from Genesis 3, where the Lord took the skins after Adam sinned. Yet there were some things you could not sacrifice for, abominations for which a man's own blood was required.

“For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices: But this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you.”

Sacrifice was never the most important thing to the Lord. What he commanded first was obedience: mercy upon one another and the keeping of the commandments. The sacrifices were added because of transgression.

Christ spoke about that fire in the temple: “Or have ye not read in the law, how that on the sabbath days the priests in the temple profane the sabbath, and are blameless?” Israel was not to kindle a fire on the sabbath when it comes to food, but the priests had to keep that fire burning. They broke the sabbath, yet are blameless, because they were doing thus saith the Lord.

“But I say unto you, That in this place is one greater than the temple. But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.” Sacrifice was never the most important thing to the Lord: not the blood of bulls and of goats, but mercy upon one another and the keeping of the commandments.

“And on the sabbath day two lambs of the first year without spot”: “This is the burnt offering of every sabbath, beside the continual burnt offering, and his drink offering.” The priests sacrificed a lamb in the morning and a lamb in the evening on the sabbath, because the Lord commanded it.

That is how the priests in the temple could “profane the sabbath” and be “blameless”: the fire was kept burning and the offering made on the sabbath because it was thus saith the Lord.

The knowing comes when it is sent. The word comes down in order, from the Most High to Christ, to the angels, and into our spirit when it is time to wake up. Until then, like Samuel, a man can be in the house and not yet know the Lord.

“All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him.”

No one knows the Father until Christ reveals him, because Christ is the mediator. That is why Samuel, though he ran to Eli, saying “Here am I”, “did not yet know the Lord, neither was the word of the Lord yet revealed unto him.”

And that is why our brothers and sisters caught up in Christianity and Islam do not know the Most High: he has not been revealed to them, and they have not been shown who they are.

“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.” Your job is the training; the revealing belongs to the Most High.

“Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, neither was the word of the Lord yet revealed unto him.” Look at that. Samuel had been in the house of the Lord since he was weaned, three or four years old, and he still did not know the Lord. This goes in on those playing church with their children: just because your children come and sit and listen to the teaching does not mean they know the Lord. They are there because you brought them there. They can hear all the words they want, but until the Lord reveals himself to them, they do not know him. “The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John.”

That is the order: from the Most High to Christ, to the angels, to the servants. That is how the word comes down and how Israel wakes up, into our spirit when it is time to wake up. The Most High does not deal with us directly right now, because we are too full of sin.

docs/study/1-samuel/31.md|1 Samuel 31:4-:

docs/study/1-samuel/4.md|1 Samuel 4:3-5|:
The elders of Israel asked the right question: “Wherefore hath the Lord smitten us to day before the Philistines?” But instead of examining the nation, they had an idea: “Let us fetch the ark of the covenant of the Lord out of Shiloh unto us, that, when it cometh among us, it may save us out of the hand of our enemies.”

So what is the ark of the covenant, and what does it contain? “Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first, and come up unto me into the mount, and make thee an ark of wood. And I will write on the tables the words that were in the first tables which thou brakest, and thou shalt put them in the ark.” The ark was made to hold the tables the Lord would write on.

“And I made an ark of shittim wood, and hewed two tables of stone like unto the first.” “And he wrote on the tables, according to the first writing, the ten commandments, which the Lord spake unto you in the mount out of the midst of the fire.” Then Moses “put the tables in the ark which I had made; and there they be, as the Lord commanded me.” The ark of the covenant contained the commandments that God wrote.

The law is spiritual, and the law has literal spiritual power; the commandments have always been our source of power as a nation. The church teaches that the laws are done away with, but watch in these chapters how seriously the Lord regarded the ark that contained his commandments.

When “the ark of the covenant of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel shouted with a great shout, so that the earth rang again.” The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with it. That is how excited and ecstatic Israel was to have the ark among them; they felt their enemies could not destroy them now.

But watch why the ark did not have the effect Israel expected in this battle: there were still Israelites in the midst of idolatry with idols among them, and until those idols were put away we could not be delivered from our enemies. That is the lesson Samuel drives home in chapter 7.

The first tables were broken. Moses came down, and “as soon as he came nigh unto the camp, that he saw the calf, and the dancing: and Moses’ anger waxed hot, and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount.” The people were dancing before the golden calf they had made from their gold earrings.

That is why the Lord told Moses to hew two tables of stone like the first ones he broke, and the Lord rewrote the ten commandments on them with his own finger.
docs/study/1-samuel/4.md|1 Samuel 4:6-9|:

With the ark of the commandments among us, the nations understood they were dealing with something above a regular people.

docs/study/1-samuel/5.md|1 Samuel 5:1-5|:
“And Samson took hold of the two middle pillars upon which the house stood”, and said, “Let me die with the Philistines. The Philistines had the audacity to bring the ark of God “into the house of Dagon, and set it by Dagon”, a fake god the Lord had already exposed. When they arose on the morrow, “Dagon was fallen upon his face to the earth before the ark of the Lord.” This was no little souvenir you could knock over; it was a large statue, and nobody had been in there to touch it.

They “set him in his place again”, as if maybe the wind blew a little harder, and the next morning “the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold; only the stump of Dagon was left to him.” No man did this: that is the power of the ark of God. Therefore the priests of Dagon tread not on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod unto this day.
docs/study/1-samuel/5.md|1 Samuel 5:6|Ps:
The Psalm tells the same history in one line: “And he smote his enemies in the hinder parts: he put them to a perpetual reproach.” That is what happened at Ashdod. “the hand of the Lord was heavy upon them of Ashdod, and he destroyed them, and smote them with emerods.”

Emerods are what we know today as hemorrhoids: swollen veins in the lower rectum that bleed and cause pain. So when the Psalm says the hinder parts, it means exactly that. The Most High was not playing games with the heathen; he literally afflicted them in their behinds for stealing the ark.

And he put them “to a perpetual reproach”: a perpetual embarrassment, for taking the ark of the Lord and sitting it beside their idol.
docs/study/1-samuel/6.md|1 Samuel 6:19-2:
“His confidence shall be rooted out of his tabernacle, and it shall bring him to the king of terrors.” Scripture owns the Most High as the king of terrors, and Beth-shemesh shows why.

It was not just the other nations that had to keep discretion with the ark of the covenant. It was forbidden to touch it or look into it unless the Lord gave you authority, no matter what tribe you were, even Levi. The men of Beth-shemesh got too excited and got nosy, taking a peek to see what the writing of God looked like, and “he smote of the people fifty thousand and threescore and ten men.” He was killing thousands at a time, and his judgments are terrifying.

That is why the people cried, “Who is able to stand before this holy Lord God?” and sent to Kirjath-jearim for someone to come fetch the ark. And it is a lesson for us: we have to have a level of discipline over our eyes. With these devices today it is very easy to take a two second look at what you know you should not be looking at. Guard your eyes.

“Come and see the works of God: he is terrible in his doing toward the children of men.” The children of men here is everybody: heathen and wicked Israelite alike.

The Philistines were smitten for taking the ark, and now the men of Beth-shemesh, Israelites, were smitten for looking into it: “the Lord had smitten many of the people with a great slaughter.” He is terrible in his doing, and being an Israelite did not spare the ones who went where the Lord gave them no authority to go.

So the people lamented and said, “Who is able to stand before this holy Lord God?” That is the right question. Come and see his works, and learn to fear him.
docs/study/1-samuel/7.md|1 Samuel 7:15-1:
“Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.” That is the same circuit the leaders of old kept.

Samuel “went from year to year in circuit to Beth–el, and Gilgal, and Mizpeh, and judged Israel in all those places. And his return was to Ramah; for there was his house.” Ramah was his headquarters. That yearly circuit is leadership making its rounds, establishing the people and coming back to check on them, the same example Paul followed with the churches.

These chapters close with the ark lost and regained, and Samuel rising up for the nation. Prayer is a superpower, and that is how our mighty forefathers rolled, from Moses to Samuel to Judas Maccabeus all the way to Christ.
docs/study/1-samuel/7.md|1 Samuel 7:3-4|:
“Thou shalt have no other gods before me.” That is the first commandment, written in the very ark Israel had been trusting in.

Go back to how we lost the battle even with the ark of God among us: we had strange gods among us. Deliverance is not just having the ark; it is applying the commandments that are in the ark. So Samuel tells all the house of Israel, “If ye do return unto the Lord with all your hearts, then put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, and prepare your hearts unto the Lord, and serve him only: and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.”

And Israel did it: “Then the children of Israel did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the Lord only.” That is repentance: no other gods before him.

“Then all the men which knew that their wives had burned incense unto other gods, and all the women that stood by, a great multitude” answered Jeremiah: “As for the word that thou hast spoken unto us in the name of the Lord, we will not hearken unto thee.”

The men knew what their wives were doing, and they stood with it. The same spirit is on brothers today who know their wives are in the midst of evil and will not check them.

This is the same worship Samuel told Israel to put away. Who is Ashtoreth? Astaroth in demonology is a chief figure of hell, named after the Near Eastern goddess Astarte, and Astarte is the Hellenized form of Ashtoreth, a form of Ishtar, the goddess called the queen of heaven, associated with love, beauty, sex, and war. Samuel was exhorting the people to depart from these fake gods and goddesses of the nations, and to this day there are Israelites that have not put away Ashtoreth from among them.

The people told Jeremiah plainly: “we will certainly do whatsoever thing goeth forth out of our own mouth, to burn incense unto the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her.” And their reason: “for then had we plenty of victuals, and were well, and saw no evil. But since we left off to burn incense to the queen of heaven … we have wanted all things, and have been consumed by the sword and by the famine.”

That is Ishtar worship, the queen of heaven, the same Ashtaroth Samuel told Israel to put away. And it is the same spirit that says, when I was in the world celebrating her holidays I was good, and now in the truth I am catching hell.

Easter is at its roots the celebration of Ishtar, the goddess of fertility and sex. When Constantine set out to merge paganism with the faith of the apostles to bring everything under one empire, pagan rituals like Easter and Saturnalia were dressed up as honoring Christ, and that was the birth of Roman Catholicism. Nothing about it mathematically adds up to Christ rising, the apostles never celebrated it or taught it, and a bunny laying eggs has nothing to do with your Lord and Saviour; it is not of Christ.

So put her away, as Israel did: “Then the children of Israel did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the Lord only.”
docs/study/1-samuel/7.md|1 Samuel 7:5-8|:
This is Samuel's mentality as a leader: “God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way.”

For a leader of Israel to stop praying for the nation is a transgression. So when the children of Israel said, “Cease not to cry unto the Lord our God for us”, they were asking of Samuel the very thing he held himself bound to do. He said, “I will pray for you unto the Lord”, and he did not cease.

“The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.” That is why Israel told Samuel, do not stop praying for us: “Cease not to cry unto the Lord our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines.”

Israel had gathered to Mizpeh, drawn water and poured it out before the Lord, fasted, and confessed, “We have sinned against the Lord.” That is James's order too: “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed.”

When the lords of the Philistines came up again and Israel was afraid, this time they did not run for the ark. They went to the righteous man, because they knew the prayer of a righteous man reaches the ears of the Most High.
docs/study/1-samuel/7.md|1 Samuel 7:9-12:
“The Lord thundered from heaven, and the most High uttered his voice. And he sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them.”

Discomfited: the same word used of the Philistines at Mizpeh, where “the Lord thundered with a great thunder on that day upon the Philistines, and discomfited them.” The thunder is the voice of the Most High, and when he utters it in the battle his enemies are scattered.

Keep the commandments and send up that prayer, and the Most High will come down in thunder against your enemies.

“Samuel, the prophet of the Lord, beloved of his Lord, established a kingdom, and anointed princes over his people.” Samuel was one of the most respected prophets in the whole history of the prophets: he established the kingdom and anointed Saul.

“By the law of the Lord he judged the congregation, and the Lord had respect unto Jacob. By his faithfulness he was found a true prophet.” Faithfulness translates loyalty. He came up under Eli, watched Eli's sons go wicked, Eli die, and the nation take losses, but Samuel stayed loyal to the Most High.

That tried loyalty is why, when “Samuel cried unto the Lord for Israel”, “the Lord heard him.”

The Apocrypha records this very history: “He called upon the mighty Lord, when his enemies pressed upon him on every side, when he offered the sucking lamb. And the Lord thundered from heaven, and with a great noise made his voice to be heard.”

That is Mizpeh. “Samuel took a sucking lamb, and offered it for a burnt offering wholly unto the Lord”, and as he was offering it the Philistines drew near to battle, “but the Lord thundered with a great thunder on that day upon the Philistines, and discomfited them.”

That was no regular thunder; it was the Lord entering the battle himself, his voice made to be heard. Israel had repented and put away the false gods, and the prayer of the righteous man reached his ears, so now the Philistines had to deal with the Most High.

“And it came to pass after these things, that God did tempt Abraham, and said unto him, Abraham: and he said, Behold, here I am.”

The Lord tries his servants to see if they will remain faithful. Abraham's faith was tried again and again, and he remained faithful. Samuel was tried the same way: he came up under Eli, watched Eli's sons go wicked, Eli die, and the nation take losses, and he stayed loyal to the Most High.

That tried loyalty is what marked Samuel as a true prophet, and it is why, when he offered the sucking lamb and cried unto the Lord for Israel, “the Lord heard him.”

“Thou shalt be visited of the Lord of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.”

That is how the Lord of hosts visits his enemies, and that is what fell on the Philistines: “the Lord thundered with a great thunder on that day upon the Philistines, and discomfited them; and they were smitten before Israel.” When that thunder hit, the Philistines knew who had entered the battle.

They were so terrified they put up no fight. The men of Israel went out of Mizpeh and pursued them, and smote them, “until they came under Beth–car.” Then Samuel set up the stone and called it Eben-ezer, “saying, Hitherto hath the Lord helped us.”
docs/study/1-samuel/8.md|1 Samuel 8:1-3|:
“If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they.”

What Samuel's sons did, turning aside after lucre, taking bribes and perverting judgment, is what we see today. Do not marvel at it. The Most High, higher than the highest, regards it all.

“And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.” That gift is what goes into bribes.

Samuel's sons Joel and Abiah, judges in Beer-sheba, broke this very law: they “walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.” The gift perverted their judgment just as the law said it would.

We see that same thing going on now in this political climate, and even in the church system. This is why the churches will not teach us who we are or teach the commandments of the Most High; when riots and unrest break out, it is those same pastors who go out to calm the people down.
docs/study/1-samuel/8.md|1 Samuel 8:10-1:
Under Rehoboam the yoke grew heavier still. He passed over the old men and went to the young men he came up with, and they told him to say, “My little finger shall be thicker than my father’s loins. And now whereas my father did lade you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke: my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”

We rejected the Lord and wanted a king like all the other nations, and this is what we got. “And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the Lord will not hear you in that day.”

“And the king answered the people roughly, and forsook the old men’s counsel that they gave him.”

That is the king Israel chose. And look at our condition today: ruler after ruler, and things do not get any better for us. We are getting what we deserve, because we rejected the Lord. “And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the Lord will not hear you in that day.”

Under Solomon's son the people cried out, as Samuel said they would: “Jeroboam and all the congregation of Israel came, and spake unto Rehoboam, saying, Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore make thou the grievous service of thy father, and his heavy yoke which he put upon us, lighter, and we will serve thee.”

That is the manner of the king come to pass: “ye shall be his servants. And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you.”

The manner of the king came to pass under Solomon: “king Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel; and the levy was thirty thousand men.” He levied a tax, and the tax was men.

“And he sent them to Lebanon, ten thousand a month by courses: a month they were in Lebanon, and two months at home: and Adoniram was over the levy.” Just as men go off to war, he sent them a month on and two months off, to prepare the timber and stones to build the house of the Lord.

That is what Samuel told Israel: “He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself.”

“in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Zif, which is the second month … he began to build the house of the Lord.”

That building is what the levy of Israel's men was raised for: thirty thousand men sent to Lebanon by courses to prepare the timber and stones. The king Israel asked for took their sons for his work, just as Samuel said: they would “ear his ground”, “reap his harvest”, and “make his instruments of war.”

“But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no bondmen: but they were men of war, and his servants, and his princes, and his captains, and rulers of his chariots, and his horsemen.”

That is word for word the manner of the king Samuel described: “He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen”, “And he will appoint him captains over thousands, and captains over fifties.”

“These were the chief of the officers that were over Solomon’s work, five hundred and fifty, which bare rule over the people that wrought in the work.” The king's work, the king's captains, the king's chariots: “and ye shall be his servants.”
docs/study/1-samuel/8.md|1 Samuel 8:4-5|:
Moses prophesied this very moment: “When thou art come unto the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, and shalt possess it, and shalt dwell therein, and shalt say, I will set a king over me, like as all the nations that are about me.”

And that is what the elders said at Ramah: “now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” Your sons are not righteous like you, so instead of them judging us, give us a king like the other nations have. Moses was shown from the beginning to the end; he saw Israel rejecting the Lord, and he wrote it for us to read.

Where do we see that today? Voting. We are saying the same thing today when we vote, looking to a ruler like the nations instead of to the Most High.

The law set the king: “Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee, whom the Lord thy God shall choose: one from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee: thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother.”

Israel asked for a king “like all the nations”, not one whom the Lord would choose. When we rejected the Lord in our own land, that also set us up to be taken out of our own land and set in a land we did not know, under oppressors: strangers over us.

Now you hear people say, well, this one is the lesser of two evils; but they are both evil. We look at our condition now because this is what we sought: we rejected the Lord and said we want a king over us, we want to be like all the other nations.
docs/study/1-samuel/8.md|1 Samuel 8:6-9|:
“God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.”

That is what Joshua meant when he said, serve him “in sincerity and in truth.” To worship in spirit and in truth is to keep what he commanded, not just to say you love the Lord. The ones who say they love him and do none of his commandments are not worshipping him in spirit and in truth.

“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.”

The spirit is the word. So when Christ says they that worship him must worship him in spirit, it means worshipping him according to his words. Serving the Lord in spirit is doing what he spoke.

“And Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem”: the elders, the heads, the judges and the officers, and “they presented themselves before God.”

Joshua rehearsed where we came from: “Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods.” The Most High took Abraham from there, “multiplied his seed, and gave him Isaac. And I gave unto Isaac Jacob and Esau”, and “Jacob and his children went down into Egypt”, where we served four hundred years.

Joshua warned us about the very thing Samuel faced. It was at Shechem that Israel made the covenant with its own mouth to serve the Lord and obey his voice; asking for a king was breaking the choice we ourselves made. So the Lord told Samuel, “According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even unto this day, wherewith they have forsaken me, and served other gods, so do they also unto thee.”

“Now therefore fear the Lord, and serve him in sincerity and in truth: and put away the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood, and in Egypt; and serve ye the Lord.”

How do we serve the Lord in sincerity and in truth? If you are sincere about serving the Lord, you are going to keep the commandments. A lot of people today say they love the Lord, yet they do not do any of his commandments; they do not truly show they have the faith of Christ, because they do not keep the commandments.

Israel at Samuel's time had done the opposite: they “have forsaken me, and served other gods.”

“choose you this day whom ye will serve … but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.”

A lot of us grew up with that plaque in the house, as for me and my house we will serve the Lord, and the house kept not one commandment: still eating pork, still keeping Sunday, still keeping the wicked pagan holidays of our oppressors.

Israel made its choice at Shechem. When they asked Samuel for a king, they were choosing again, and the Lord named it: “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.”

“And the people answered and said, God forbid that we should forsake the Lord, to serve other gods.” They gave the reason with their own mouths: “the Lord our God, he it is that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight.” “therefore will we also serve the Lord; for he is our God.”

That is the very deliverance the Lord pointed to when he spoke to Samuel: “since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even unto this day, wherewith they have forsaken me, and served other gods.” The people who said God forbid we should forsake him are the people who forsook him. Asking for a king was breaking the choice we ourselves made.

“Ye cannot serve the Lord: for he is an holy God; he is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins.”

Joshua warned them what would follow: “If ye forsake the Lord, and serve strange gods, then he will turn and do you hurt, and consume you, after that he hath done you good.”

That is the warning Israel walked past when it asked for a king. The Lord had done them good, bringing them up out of Egypt, and they rejected him “that I should not reign over them.”

“And the people said unto Joshua, Nay; but we will serve the Lord.” Joshua made them witnesses: “Ye are witnesses against yourselves that ye have chosen you the Lord, to serve him. And they said, We are witnesses.”

Then: “put away … the strange gods which are among you, and incline your heart unto the Lord God of Israel. And the people said unto Joshua, The Lord our God will we serve, and his voice will we obey.”

We made that covenant. So when the elders came to Samuel for a king, they were witnesses against themselves. The Lord told Samuel to “Hearken unto the voice of the people”, but they had sworn to obey his voice.

Christ gave the same picture: “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return.” He left his servants pounds and said, “Occupy till I come. But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.”

This is speaking about Christ. The same spirit that said set a king over us says, We will not have Christ to reign over us. When we read Samuel again, that is why the Lord said, “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.”

“But those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me.”

That is how Christ deals with them that reject his reign when he returns. Israel said to Samuel, give us a king, and the Lord said they “have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.” Those that would not that he should reign over them are counted his enemies.

“Thy righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and thy law is the truth.”

The truth is the law. So worshipping him in spirit and in truth, and serving him “in sincerity and in truth”, means keeping his law. The spirit is his word; the truth is his law. That is how you serve the Lord, and that is what Israel forsook when they said, give us a king.
docs/study/1-samuel/9.md|1 Samuel 9:15-1:
“Man’s goings are of the Lord; how can a man then understand his own way?”

Saul thought he was going out to fetch his father's asses, but his purpose was to be led unto Samuel. The Lord had already told Samuel in his ear a day before: “To morrow about this time I will send thee a man out of the land of Benjamin, and thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people Israel.”

Saul did not understand his own way; his goings were of the Lord. “And when Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said unto him, Behold the man whom I spake to thee of! this same shall reign over my people.”
docs/study/1-samuel/9.md|1 Samuel 9:6-10:
When the children struggled together within Rebekah, “she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to enquire of the Lord.”

In that time, going to enquire of the Lord meant going to a seer. That is what Samuel explains: “Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.”

So Saul and his servant went to the man of God, “an honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass”, bringing the fourth part of a shekel of silver, that he might “tell us our way.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/1.md|2 Chronicle:
“So David, and the elders of Israel, and the captains over thousands, went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord out of the house of Obed–edom with joy.”

That is the other account of the ark coming up to Jerusalem, the place David had prepared for it. Line up Second Samuel 6 and First Chronicles 15 and you have the history of how the ark came to be in Jerusalem before Solomon was strengthened in his kingdom.

“And they brought in the ark of the Lord, and set it in his place, in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it: and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord.”

That is the history behind what Chronicles says: “the ark of God had David brought up from Kirjath–jearim to the place which David had prepared for it: for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem.” So in Solomon's day the ark was in the tent David pitched at Jerusalem, while the tabernacle Moses made in the wilderness stood at the high place in Gibeon, where Solomon and the congregation went.

“And the speech pleased the Lord, that Solomon had asked this thing.”

The Most High had said, “Ask what I shall give thee”, and Solomon asked for wisdom and knowledge to judge the people. That request pleased the Lord. Kings supplies this detail that Chronicles leaves out.

First Kings 3 tells the same night, where the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and gives more detail of what was said. Solomon said: “And now, O Lord my God, thou hast made thy servant king instead of David my father: and I am but a little child: I know not how to go out or come in.”

That is what he meant in Chronicles: “Give me now wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people.” He knew he was not able to go out and come in before them on his own. When you read between Kings and Chronicles and line up the history, you get the full detail of what went on with Solomon and David.

“Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people?”

This is the same request as in Chronicles: “Give me now wisdom and knowledge … for who can judge this thy people, that is so great?” Kings shows what the wisdom was for: an understanding heart, to discern between good and bad, and to judge a people “like the dust of the earth in multitude.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/10.md|2 Chronicl:
“And the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the Lord God of Israel, which had appeared unto him twice.” He had commanded Solomon “that he should not go after other gods: but he kept not that which the Lord commanded.”

So the Lord said, “I will surely rend the kingdom from thee, and will give it to thy servant.” That is the prophecy now being fulfilled. When Rehoboam answered the people roughly and hearkened not unto them, “the cause was of God, that the Lord might perform his word, which he spake by the hand of Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.”

“Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”

Rehoboam rejects the safe counsel of the elders: “he forsook the counsel which the old men gave him, and took counsel with the young men that were brought up with him, that stood before him.” He asks them, “What advice give ye that we may return answer to this people”, including them as if they were rulers with him over the nation.

This is the same error seen constantly among the people: one comes to the truth and seeks counsel from a new brother or sister rather than from the elder men and women already established in the congregation. And the young men's counsel was rough: “My little finger shall be thicker than my father’s loins”, “I will put more to your yoke: my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/11.md|2 Chronicl:
“Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” He set one in Beth-el and the other in Dan, “And this thing became a sin.”

That is why the Levites left. Jeroboam “ordained him priests for the high places, and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made”, and cast Levi off from executing the priest's office unto the Lord. So Levi had to return where they could serve: “the Levites left their suburbs and their possession, and came to Judah and Jerusalem.”

The calves drove out true worship and forced the faithful to seek the Lord in Jerusalem. Out of all the tribes, “such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem”, and for three years they strengthened the kingdom of Judah and “walked in the way of David and Solomon.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/12.md|2 Chronicl:
“If they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers … if then their uncircumcised hearts be humbled, and they then accept of the punishment of their iniquity: Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land.”

Humbling brings deliverance. That is what happened under Rehoboam: “They have humbled themselves; therefore I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance; and my wrath shall not be poured out upon Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.”

“Nevertheless they shall be his servants; that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries.” They had to learn the difference between serving the Most High and serving the kingdoms of the countries.

The people today must likewise humble themselves, relearn to obey the commandments, and accept their condition as righteous judgment from the hand of the Most High: accept the punishment of our iniquity, and he remembers his covenant.
docs/study/2-chronicles/13.md|2 Chronicl:
“The one lamb shalt thou offer in the morning, and the other lamb shalt thou offer at even.”

That is the pattern of the daily sacrifice, and Judah kept it: “they burn unto the Lord every morning and every evening burnt sacrifices and sweet incense.” They set the shewbread in order and lit the golden candlestick every evening. “for we keep the charge of the Lord our God; but ye have forsaken him.”

“Bring the tribe of Levi near, and present them before Aaron the priest, that they may minister unto him.” The Levites “shall keep his charge, and the charge of the whole congregation”, and “thou shalt give the Levites unto Aaron and to his sons.”

“And thou shalt appoint Aaron and his sons, and they shall wait on their priest’s office: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.”

That is the order Judah kept: “the priests, which minister unto the Lord, are the sons of Aaron, and the Levites wait upon their business.” “for we keep the charge of the Lord our God; but ye have forsaken him.” Jeroboam made priests of whoever would consecrate himself, the very strangers the law said must not come nigh.

“And the Levite that is within thy gates; thou shalt not forsake him; for he hath no part nor inheritance with thee.”

The great sin the account underlines is Jeroboam casting off the Levites, and this is a law the Most High was very specific about. Thou shalt not forsake the Levite. Jeroboam did, and Abijah, who stood on the covenant and kept the priests of the Lord, “waxed mighty.”

Abijah names Jeroboam as “the servant of Solomon the son of David” who “is risen up, and hath rebelled against his lord.” To understand that rebellion, go back to 1 Kings 11: “Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda, Solomon’s servant … even he lifted up his hand against the king.”

He was industrious: “the man Jeroboam was a mighty man of valour: and Solomon seeing the young man that he was industrious, he made him ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph.”

Then the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him in the field, took the new garment, “and rent it in twelve pieces: And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee.”

Against that, Abijah stands on mount Zemaraim and declares that “the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt.”

“Rehoboam was one and forty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem.”

So when Abijah says Rehoboam “was young and tenderhearted, and could not withstand them”, young and tenderhearted does not mean a small child. Rehoboam was forty and one years old when he began to reign; he simply knew nothing of war, for the land had rest in Solomon's days. That is how “vain men, the children of Belial” gathered unto Jeroboam and strengthened themselves against him.

“For the Levites left their suburbs and their possession, and came to Judah and Jerusalem: for Jeroboam and his sons had cast them off from executing the priest’s office unto the Lord.”

That is what Abijah throws at Jeroboam: “Have ye not cast out the priests of the Lord, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and have made you priests after the manner of the nations of other lands?” Jeroboam ordained his own priests for the high places and the devils, and made priests of any man who came to consecrate himself “with a young bullock and seven rams”, so that the same might “be a priest of them that are no gods.”

The great multitude trusted in the “golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods”, and in priests after the manner of the nations.
docs/study/2-chronicles/14.md|2 Chronicl:
“So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and made Rehoboam the son of Solomon strong, three years: for three years they walked in the way of David and Solomon.”

Walking in the way of David and Solomon is what strengthens the kingdom. Asa walked that way: he “did that which was good and right in the eyes of the Lord his God”, took away the altars of the strange gods, the high places, the images and the groves, and “commanded Judah to seek the Lord God of their fathers, and to do the law and the commandment.” And “the kingdom was quiet before him.”

“And it came to pass, when Rehoboam had established the kingdom, and had strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him.”

The pattern of Rehoboam warns what happens when a strong king forsakes that law. Asa did the opposite: he commanded Judah “to do the law and the commandment”, and “In his days the land was quiet ten years.”

“And he shall besiege thee in all thy gates, until thy high and fenced walls come down, wherein thou trustedst, throughout all thy land.”

That is a curse on the seed: the enemy besieging the gates until the high and fenced walls come down. Asa's day was the other side of it. “because we have sought the Lord our God, we have sought him, and he hath given us rest on every side.” So the walls went up, “So they built and prospered”, and Asa had an army of 300,000 out of Judah and 280,000 out of Benjamin, “all these were mighty men of valour.”

“By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through.”

Rest is not idleness. Asa “had no war in those years; because the Lord had given him rest”, and he spent that rest building up, not idling: walls, towers, gates, and bars, “while the land is yet before us.” “So they built and prospered.”

“And the suburbs of the cities, which ye shall give unto the Levites, shall reach from the wall of the city and outward a thousand cubits round about.”

The law measures from the wall of the city, for the cities of Israel have walls. So Asa built fenced cities: “Let us build these cities, and make about them walls, and towers, gates, and bars, while the land is yet before us.”

An host compassed the city with horses and chariots, and Elisha's servant cried, “Alas, my master! how shall we do? And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” Elisha prayed, “And the Lord opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.” And the Lord smote the enemy with blindness “according to the word of Elisha.”

Asa faced the same: Zerah the Ethiopian, a Cushite, came out “with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots.” And Asa cried, “Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power.”

“So the Lord smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled.” They were destroyed “before the Lord, and before his host”, and Judah carried away very much spoil. Faith in the Most High, not the numbers of the enemy, wins the battle.
docs/study/2-chronicles/15.md|2 Chronicl:
“So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.”

“when Asa heard these words, and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage”, put away the abominable idols out of Judah, Benjamin, and the cities he took from mount Ephraim, “and renewed the altar of the Lord.” Hearing the word gave him courage to act.

Hearing the word gives courage still, for we teach our people who they are, that the Israelites and the Christ are black. Faith comes by hearing.
docs/study/2-chronicles/16.md|2 Chronicl:
“Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for the uses which ye may have of him: for the Lord hath created him. For of the most High cometh healing.”

Asa “was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians.” The rebuke is not against physicians. The Lord created the physician, and he is to be honoured. The rebuke is against seeking them in place of the Most High, from whom healing cometh.

“My son, in thy sickness be not negligent: but pray unto the Lord, and he will make thee whole. Leave off from sin, and order thine hands aright, and cleanse thy heart from all wickedness.”

That is the order: in sickness pray to the Most High and leave off from sin, then seek the physician. Asa did it backwards: “in his disease he sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians.” And “Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/17.md|2 Chronicl:
“Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city.”

Teaching the law had a real effect on the nations. After the book of the law went through the cities of Judah, “the fear of the Lord fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were round about Judah, so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat.” Wisdom strengthened Judah more than mighty men could.

“There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it: Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city.”

Wisdom delivers where strength cannot. Judah taught the law in all its cities, and the fear of the Lord fell upon the kingdoms round about, so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat. Wisdom disarmed his enemies.

“Wisdom is better than weapons of war: but one sinner destroyeth much good.”

Wisdom disarmed Jehoshaphat's enemies. He did not win by weapons of war; the fear of the Lord fell on the kingdoms round about, “so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat.”

“And Asa slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father: and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his stead.”

Kings tells the same succession: Jehoshaphat reigned in the place of his father Asa, taking the throne after him. And Chronicles adds what he did first: he “strengthened himself against Israel”, setting himself apart from the northern kingdom's ways.

“And thou shalt teach them ordinances and laws, and shalt shew them the way wherein they must walk, and the work that they must do.”

The way we must walk is defined by the ordinances and laws we are taught. Jehoshaphat walked that way: he “sought to the Lord God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not after the doings of Israel.”

“Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.”

That is what Jehoshaphat's princes and Levites did. They “had the book of the law of the Lord with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.” It is the same pattern we follow, going out into the streets to teach.

“Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?”

Wisdom cries out to the people. That is what the teachers Jehoshaphat sent out did: they carried the book of the law of the Lord through all the cities of Judah “and taught the people”, putting forth the voice of understanding where the people were.

“She standeth in the top of high places, by the way in the places of the paths. She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors.”

Wisdom does not stay hidden; she goes where the people are, to the gates and the entry of the city. So did the princes and Levites who “went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people”, and so do we, going out into the streets to teach.

“Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man.”

Wisdom's call is unto men, a rally cry for men. Jehoshaphat sent men, his princes, Levites and priests, to teach in the cities of Judah with the book of the law of the Lord.
docs/study/2-chronicles/18.md|2 Chronicl:
“To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.”

The messenger told Micaiah, “the words of the prophets declare good to the king with one assent; let thy word therefore, I pray thee, be like one of theirs, and speak thou good.” But one assent does not make it true. If they speak not according to the word, there is no light in them, however many there are.

Micaiah answered as a true prophet: “As the Lord liveth, even what my God saith, that will I speak.”

“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.”

“For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.”

That was Ahab. He had heaped to himself prophets that told him what he wanted to hear, and he hated the one man who spoke the truth: “he never prophesied good unto me, but always evil.”

“That this is a rebellious people, lying children, children that will not hear the law of the Lord: Which say to the seers, See not; and to the prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things, speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits.” They even say, “cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us.”

That is Ahab. Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there not here a prophet of the Lord besides, that we might enquire of him?” and Ahab answered, there is Micaiah, “but I hate him; for he never prophesied good unto me, but always evil.” Always evil means he told the truth. Ahab wanted smooth things, not right things.
docs/study/2-chronicles/2.md|2 Chronicle:
“Then David gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the porch, and of the houses thereof, and of the treasuries thereof, and of the upper chambers thereof, and of the inner parlours thereof, and of the place of the mercy seat.”

Solomon did not come up with the house on his own. David charged him to build it and gave him the pattern. So when “Solomon determined to build an house for the name of the Lord”, and told out threescore and ten thousand men to bear burdens, fourscore thousand to hew in the mountain, and three thousand six hundred to oversee them, he was carrying out what his father had given him.

“And thou, Solomon my son, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind: for the Lord searcheth all hearts.” And David warned him: “if thou seek him, he will be found of thee; but if thou forsake him, he will cast thee off for ever.”

“Solomon determined to build an house for the name of the Lord.” Where did Solomon get this understanding and this vision? It came from his father David, who charged him to build the house.

“He was a widow’s son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass: and he was filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass.”

Chronicles says the same workman was “The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre.” There is no contradiction. His mother was of the tribe of Naphtali, but she was of the city of Dan, which lay within the land of Naphtali. This is cleared up by using the Bible dictionary and the maps, and by chasing the references.

He was “skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving.”

“And the coast of the children of Dan went out too little for them: therefore the children of Dan went up to fight against Leshem, and took it, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and possessed it, and dwelt therein, and called Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their father.”

Leshem is Laish, the same city. Joshua and Judges together show how a city named Dan came to stand within the borders of Naphtali, and why Huram's mother is called “of the daughters of Dan” in Chronicles and “of the tribe of Naphtali” in Kings.

“And they called the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father, who was born unto Israel: howbeit the name of the city was Laish at the first.”

That is the city of Dan the workman's mother came from. The children of Dan took Laish and renamed it after their father. Israel had put the nations to tribute rather than driving them out as the Lord commanded, but the city itself sat in the borders of Naphtali, so a woman there could be spoken of both ways: a widow “of the tribe of Naphtali”, and “a woman of the daughters of Dan.”

“Now, behold, in my trouble I have prepared for the house of the Lord an hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver; and of brass and iron without weight; for it is in abundance: timber also and stone have I prepared; and thou mayest add thereto.”

David had prepared for the house long before. Solomon did not begin empty-handed; his father had provided the workers and the materials. Even the numbering of the strangers was “after the numbering wherewith David his father had numbered them.”

“Behold, a son shall be born to thee, who shall be a man of rest; and I will give him rest from all his enemies round about: for his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quietness unto Israel in his days.”

The Lord promised David a son who would be a man of rest, with peace and quietness given to Israel in his days. In that rest Solomon built, setting the strangers in the land to work, “threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work.”

“Be in pain, and labour to bring forth, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail: for now shalt thou go forth out of the city, and thou shalt dwell in the field, and thou shalt go even to Babylon; there shalt thou be delivered; there the Lord shall redeem thee from the hand of thine enemies.”

Solomon was a man of rest, and in his days Israel had peace and quietness, and the strangers in the land were set to Israel's work. Israel is told to go forth out of the city, for this is not our rest while our enemies still afflict us. There the Lord shall redeem us from the hand of our enemies.

“They that are delivered from the noise of archers in the places of drawing water, there shall they rehearse the righteous acts of the Lord, even the righteous acts toward the inhabitants of his villages in Israel.”

The offerings Solomon named, “morning and evening, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts of the Lord our God”, are “an ordinance for ever to Israel.” That is why we keep them in the land of our captivity: in the places of drawing water we rehearse the righteous acts of the Most High, according to the law given through Moses.

“In the fourteenth day of the first month at even is the Lord’s passover.”

At even: the day is reckoned from even to even. So the passover is kept at even on the fourteenth, and the feast of unleavened bread begins the fifteenth day. These are among the solemn feasts Solomon named, ordained forever to Israel.

“And in the beginnings of your months ye shall offer a burnt offering unto the Lord; two young bullocks, and one ram, seven lambs of the first year without spot.”

The beginning of the months is the new moon, and it had its own burnt offering. Solomon named it with the rest: “on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts of the Lord our God. This is an ordinance for ever to Israel.” That is why we keep them in the land of our captivity, according to the law given through Moses in the book of Numbers.

“And in the fourteenth day of the first month is the passover of the Lord.”

After the daily, sabbath and new moon offerings come the solemn feasts, beginning with the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, and the feast of unleavened bread beginning the fifteenth day. These are “the solemn feasts of the Lord our God” Solomon built the house for, and “This is an ordinance for ever to Israel.”

“This is the offering made by fire which ye shall offer unto the Lord; two lambs of the first year without spot day by day, for a continual burnt offering.”

The daily offering was two lambs, one in the morning and one in the evening. That is what Solomon named: “the burnt offerings morning and evening.” “This is an ordinance for ever to Israel.”

“And on the sabbath day two lambs of the first year without spot, and two tenth deals of flour for a meat offering, mingled with oil, and the drink offering thereof.”

The sabbath offering added two more lambs beside the continual burnt offering. Solomon built the house for the burnt offerings “on the sabbaths” as well, and “This is an ordinance for ever to Israel.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/21.md|2 Chronicl:
“For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep.”

Because of disobedience many are weak and sickly, and many sleep. Sickness follows coming out from under the commandments. Jehoram had not walked “in the ways of Jehoshaphat thy father, nor in the ways of Asa king of Judah”, and the word to him was “great sickness by disease of thy bowels.”

“Also every sickness, and every plague, which is not written in the book of this law, them will the Lord bring upon thee, until thou be destroyed.”

That is what came on Jehoram. Elijah's writing charged him with walking “in the way of the kings of Israel”, making Judah and Jerusalem “to go a whoring, like to the whoredoms of the house of Ahab”, and slaying his brethren “which were better than thyself.” So: “with a great plague will the Lord smite thy people, and thy children, and thy wives, and all thy goods.”

And his own body was struck: “thou shalt have great sickness by disease of thy bowels, until thy bowels fall out by reason of the sickness day by day.” This is what it looks like to mess with the Most High.

Isaac's blessing to Esau: “by thy sword shalt thou live, and shalt serve thy brother; and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck.”

It is fulfilled here: “In his days the Edomites revolted from under the dominion of Judah, and made themselves a king.” “So the Edomites revolted from under the hand of Judah unto this day.” Libnah revolted at the same time, “because he had forsaken the Lord God of his fathers.”

When we obey the Most High the nations are subject to us; when we come out from under the commandments, that is when the other nations rise up and revolt against us and keep us in sin. Jehoram “made high places in the mountains of Judah, and caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, and compelled Judah thereto.” Dealing with other gods is spiritual fornication, but physical fornication is built into these false worships; the pagan holidays passed down to our people, whatever the season, are built on fornication, and that is what draws the people to follow them.
docs/study/2-chronicles/23.md|2 Chronicl:
Deborah speaks of a time when “The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel.” She arose a mother in Israel, yet she set her heart toward the governors and worked with the men of Israel rather than ruling over them.

That is the measure for Athaliah. Being the king’s mother did not make her the ruler, and she had no place ruling Israel. Even Deborah, a mother in Israel, did not take the rule over the men.

So when Jehoiada made the covenant “between him, and between all the people, and between the king, that they should be the Lord’s people”, and set Joash “upon the throne of the kingdom”, order was restored. Joash was king in rank, yet still a learner under Jehoiada, for before a king is set in his position he is under tutors and governors; even kings had to be taught. And once Athaliah was slain, “all the people of the land rejoiced: and the city was quiet.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/24.md|2 Chronicl:
The prophet went out to meet Asa and said, “The Lord is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.” If we seek the Most High he will be found, but if we forsake him he will forsake us.

That is the very charge Zechariah brought against Judah: “because ye have forsaken the Lord, he hath also forsaken you.” They transgressed the commandments, so they could not prosper.

And as Zechariah died, he said, “The Lord look upon it, and require it.” He prayed for vengeance on his murderer, and this is scripture. It is right to pray for the downfall of enemies who do much wickedness, even while we pray for the recovery and repentance of our own people.
