“And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.” The Most High sends the prophet to turn the hearts of the fathers and the children, lest he come and smite the earth with a curse. Our people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.

Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was that kind of prophet: “the Spirit of God came upon” him, and he stood above the people and asked, “Why transgress ye the commandments of the Lord, that ye cannot prosper?” He came to correct the king and turn the people back.

But they “stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the Lord.” The king had him killed for telling him the truth. Joash “remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son.” That is the same spirit our people show today when a laborer brings the medicine and is met with violence.

“When a righteous man doth turn from his righteousness, and commit iniquity, and I lay a stumblingblock before him, he shall die”, and “his righteousness which he hath done shall not be remembered.” He shall die in his sin. That is exactly how it went for Joash.

Joash began by doing right under Jehoiada’s guidance, repairing the house and clearing out the idols. But after he was warned he turned to wickedness and killed Zechariah, and none of that good was remembered in the end.

So judgment came: “For the army of the Syrians came with a small company of men, and the Lord delivered a very great host into their hand, because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers. So they executed judgment against Joash.” They left him “in great diseases”, and “his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and slew him on his bed.” He was buried “in the city of David, but they buried him not in the sepulchres of the kings.”

“This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.” When a man keeps the law, meditates on it and does it, he makes his way prosperous and has good success.

That is why the willing work on the temple succeeded. They brought in “the collection that Moses the servant of God laid upon Israel in the wilderness”, doing what was written, and “all the princes and all the people rejoiced, and brought in, and cast into the chest, until they had made an end.” They “gathered money in abundance”, and “the work was perfected by them, and they set the house of God in his state, and strengthened it.”

Money was a defense here, because it paid the skilled brothers who got the temple work done. Not everyone had the same task: masons, carpenters, and such as “wrought iron and brass” each had their charge, and every man had to listen to a manager, for business requires order and submission to authority. So we must deal righteously with our people today, treating a brother’s business as a place to help the family and the body. The good success came even to the rest of the money, “whereof were made vessels for the house of the Lord”, and “they offered burnt offerings in the house of the Lord continually all the days of Jehoiada.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/25.md|2 Chronicl:
The parallel account in Kings tells the same thing: “as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in his hand, that he slew his servants which had slain the king his father. But the children of the murderers he slew not.”

Amaziah did this “according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses, wherein the Lord commanded, saying, The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children be put to death for the fathers; but every man shall be put to death for his own sin.”

So in this he did “that which was right in the sight of the Lord”, even though it was “not with a perfect heart.” He punished the murderers, and kept the law by sparing their children.

This is the law Amaziah followed, straight from Moses: “The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.”

It is a foundational law. A man answers for his own sin, not for the sin of his father or his child. That is why Amaziah slew the servants that killed the king his father, “But he slew not their children”, doing “as it is written in the law in the book of Moses.”

“And the Lord said, Who shall persuade Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth–gilead?” A spirit came forth and said, “I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And the Lord said, “Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so.” The Most High put a lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab’s prophets to draw him to his fall.

The king who trusts false counsel over the true prophet is set up for destruction. That is Amaziah. The Most High gave him the victory over the children of Seir, and he responded by grabbing the idols of the people he had just defeated: he “brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down himself before them, and burned incense unto them.” That is the divided heart in action.

This is why counsel is important. The prophet asked him, “Why hast thou sought after the gods of the people, which could not deliver their own people out of thine hand?” He was trying to counsel Amaziah to destroy the idols, and instead Amaziah threatened him: “Art thou made of the king’s counsel? forbear; why shouldest thou be smitten?” Be quiet. The prophet forbore, but said, “I know that God hath determined to destroy thee, because thou hast done this, and hast not hearkened unto my counsel.”

Peter said, “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation.” It was counted unlawful for a man that is a Jew to keep company with one of another nation, and the split between the kingdoms ran that deep.

The two kingdoms had real animosity, calling each other another nation. Amaziah, lifted up after he had “smitten the Edomites”, sent to Joash king of Israel, “Come, let us see one another in the face.” Joash answered with the parable of “The thistle that was in Lebanon” and “the cedar that was in Lebanon”, and told him, “thine heart lifteth thee up to boast: abide now at home; why shouldest thou meddle to thine hurt”.

“But Amaziah would not hear; for it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom.” “Judah was put to the worse before Israel, and they fled every man to his tent.” Joash “brake down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits”, and took “all the gold and the silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God”, the treasures of the king’s house and the hostages, and returned to Samaria. Brother stealing the vessels out of his own brother’s temple.
docs/study/2-chronicles/26.md|2 Chronicl:
The law set the king’s duty plainly: “when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites: And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the Lord his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them”.

The king was to write himself a copy of the law and read in it all his life, that he learn to fear the Most High and not lift himself above his brethren. Uzziah did the opposite: “his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the Lord his God”. Had he kept the law before him, he would have known the incense was not his to burn.

The Most High said to Aaron, “thou and thy sons with thee shall keep your priest’s office for every thing of the altar, and within the vail”, and “I have given your priest’s office unto you as a service of gift: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.” The priesthood was given to Aaron and his sons as a gift, and the office was never the king’s to seize.

That is what Azariah and the fourscore priests told Uzziah: “It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the Lord, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed”. He came nigh where he did not belong, and “the Lord had smitten him.”

“Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.” The brother became prideful and high, and it brought him to a fall.

“But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction”. Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense upon the altar of incense, which was not his office. When the priests withstood him, “Uzziah was wroth”, and while he was wroth, with a censer in his hand, “the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests”. He “was a leper unto the day of his death, and dwelt in a several house”, “cut off from the house of the Lord”.

The lesson to all of us is to stay in the spirit, stay humble, and never forget who put you in the position you are in. When a man becomes lifted up he loses his humility and forgets who set him where he is.
docs/study/2-chronicles/28.md|2 Chronicl:
“For the children of Judah have done evil in my sight, saith the Lord”. “And they have built the high places of Tophet, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart.”

That is what Ahaz did. He “burnt incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and burnt his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen whom the Lord had cast out before the children of Israel.” This was witchcraft and child sacrifice, the practice called Tophet, in the high places “and under every green tree.”

Ahaz “did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord, like David his father”. He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and “made also molten images for Baalim”, a thing the Most High commanded not, neither came it into his heart.

The Most High “shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” Then “The envy also of Ephraim shall depart”, and “Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.”

Ahaz ran the other way: “in the time of his distress did he trespass yet more against the Lord”. He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that smote him, saying, “Because the gods of the kings of Syria help them, therefore will I sacrifice to them, that they may help me. But they were the ruin of him, and of all Israel.” He cut in pieces “the vessels of the house of God, and shut up the doors of the house of the Lord, and he made him altars in every corner of Jerusalem.”

That is the pattern of running to a nation that cannot save, the same spirit that trusts in the systems of the world instead of the Most High. The Most High is the only one who can bring the people out of their condition, then and now: it is he who assembles the outcasts, gathers the dispersed, and ends the envy between Ephraim and Judah.

It was “in the days of Ahaz” that “Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.” It was told the house of David, “Syria is confederate with Ephraim”, and the heart of Ahaz and his people was moved “as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.”

The Most High sent Isaiah to tell Ahaz, “Take heed, and be quiet; fear not”, for the evil counsel of Syria and Ephraim “shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass.” He foretold that “within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.” And he warned, “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.”

These are the same two kings in Chronicles. Because Judah “had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers”, the Most High delivered Ahaz “into the hand of the king of Syria”, who carried captives to Damascus, and “into the hand of the king of Israel”. “Pekah the son of Remaliah slew in Judah an hundred and twenty thousand in one day, which were all valiant men”. Zichri, “a mighty man of Ephraim”, slew the king’s son, the governor of the house and the man next to the king, and “the children of Israel carried away captive of their brethren two hundred thousand” to Samaria. This was brother against brother, one nation of Israel captiving the other.

The law said, “if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant: But as an hired servant, and as a sojourner, he shall be with thee, and shall serve thee unto the year of jubile”. Then “shall he depart from thee, both he and his children with him, and shall return unto his own family”. A brother was never to be made a bondservant.

That is why Oded rebuked the host that came to Samaria. The Most High had delivered Judah into their hand because of his wrath, but they had “slain them in a rage that reacheth up unto heaven”, and now they purposed “to keep under the children of Judah and Jerusalem for bondmen and bondwomen unto you”. That is against the law, and it added to their own sins: “are there not with you, even with you, sins against the Lord your God?”

Certain heads of the children of Ephraim stood up too: “we have offended against the Lord already, ye intend to add more to our sins and to our trespass”. So the armed men left the captives and the spoil, and the men named by name clothed the naked, shod them, gave them “to eat and to drink, and anointed them, and carried all the feeble of them upon asses, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brethren”. Even in the middle of the division, these men feared the Most High and would not treat their brethren as slaves.
docs/study/2-chronicles/29.md|2 Chronicl:
The Most High commanded “pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamps to burn continually”, “a statute for ever in your generations.” Aaron was to “order the lamps upon the pure candlestick before the Lord continually.” The twelve cakes of the showbread were set “in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the Lord”, with “pure frankincense upon each row”, and “Every sabbath he shall set it in order before the Lord continually, being taken from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant.”

The oil for the lamps and the showbread were to be kept continually, an everlasting statute, and the fathers abandoned it. Hezekiah names the sin plainly: “they have shut up the doors of the porch, and put out the lamps, and have not burned incense nor offered burnt offerings in the holy place unto the God of Israel.” They “have forsaken him, and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the Lord, and turned their backs.”

So Hezekiah, who “did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done”, went straight to it: “in the first year of his reign, in the first month”, he “opened the doors of the house of the Lord, and repaired them”, and charged the Levites, “sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the Lord God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place.”

“For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.”

Under the law, atonement required animal sacrifice. Hezekiah brought “seven bullocks, and seven rams, and seven lambs, and seven he goats, for a sin offering for the kingdom, and for the sanctuary, and for Judah.” The priests sprinkled the blood upon the altar, “and they made reconciliation with their blood upon the altar, to make an atonement for all Israel”.

But the reconciliation the Most High provides now is through the death of his Son. And you cannot be reconciled to someone you were never joined to, so the reconciliation is for the house of Israel, his people, just as Hezekiah’s offering was made “for all Israel.”

“And these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, who remaining in the chambers were free: for they were employed in that work day and night.” The singers among the Levites were employed in that work day and night. That is the ordained pattern of temple music, and Hezekiah restored it.

He “set the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, with psalteries, and with harps, according to the commandment of David, and of Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet”. And “when the burnt offering began, the song of the Lord began also with the trumpets, and with the instruments ordained by David king of Israel. And all the congregation worshipped”, “until the burnt offering was finished.”

Then the king and the princes “commanded the Levites to sing praise unto the Lord with the words of David, and of Asaph the seer. And they sang praises with gladness, and they bowed their heads and worshipped.” The singers were back at the work they were set to.

“Let all things be done decently and in order.” That is the same standard by which the temple service was restored.

Once the people were consecrated, they brought so many sacrifices and thank offerings that “the priests were too few, so that they could not flay all the burnt offerings: wherefore their brethren the Levites did help them, till the work was ended”, “for the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests.” Everyone took his place, and the burnt offerings were “in abundance, with the fat of the peace offerings, and the drink offerings for every burnt offering.”

“So the service of the house of the Lord was set in order. And Hezekiah rejoiced, and all the people, that God had prepared the people: for the thing was done suddenly.” It was done suddenly, and it was done decently and in order.

The same warning was spoken over Solomon: “if ye shall at all turn from following me, ye or your children, and will not keep my commandments and my statutes”, “Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have hallowed for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people”.

At this house “every one that passeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss”, and they will ask why. The answer: “Because they forsook the Lord their God, who brought forth their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and have taken hold upon other gods”.

Hezekiah saw it come to pass: “the wrath of the Lord was upon Judah and Jerusalem, and he hath delivered them to trouble, to astonishment, and to hissing, as ye see with your eyes.” And, “our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this.” That is exactly how the nations look at scattered Israel today: a proverb and a byword, an astonishment to all who pass by.
docs/study/2-chronicles/3.md|2 Chronicle:
“Then the angel of the Lord commanded Gad to say to David, that David should go up, and set up an altar unto the Lord in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.” This is the threshingfloor read of a few days ago in First Chronicles 21.

That same ground is where Solomon built. He “began to build the house of the Lord at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the Lord appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.” The altar David set up at the angel’s command marked the place of the house of God.

Solomon began “in the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign”, and these “are the things wherein Solomon was instructed for the building of the house of God”: threescore cubits long, twenty cubits broad, the porch twenty cubits by the breadth of the house, “and the height was an hundred and twenty: and he overlaid it within with pure gold.” Chronicles mixes here what is in First Kings 6 and 7, and Kings goes into much more detail on the building.

Kings gives the fuller picture of the walls: “he carved all the walls of the house round about with carved figures of cherubims and palm trees and open flowers, within and without.” That is what Chronicles means when it says he “graved cherubims on the walls”.

Solomon cieled the greater house “with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains.” He “garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim.” He overlaid “the house, the beams, the posts, and the walls thereof, and the doors thereof, with gold”, real gold through and through, not the counterfeit metal of today.

So the house of the Lord itself was carved round about with figures, by the king who built it for the Most High. Solomon was not bowing down to the cherubims and images he made.

“Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image, an abomination unto the Lord, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and putteth it in a secret place.” The curse falls on the image made and put in a secret place, a hidden thing worshipped in secret.

A wall in a man’s house is not a secret place. It is seen plainly when a man enters the home; it is not hidden. Solomon’s cherubims were graved on the walls of the house of the Lord, open for all to see, not hidden away to be worshipped in the dark.

“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth”. Our unlearned Christian brothers and sisters, and some in other doctrines, say from this that a man cannot have images at all. But that is not what the Bible says.

The command forbids making a graven image to bow down thyself to it and serve it. It forbids the worship, not the mere carving of a figure. That is why Solomon could grave “cherubims on the walls” of the house of the Lord and not break the law: he was not bowing down to them.

Behind that hidden door the Lord showed the prophet “what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The Lord seeth us not; the Lord hath forsaken the earth.”

That is the abomination: worshipping images in secret, in the dark, thinking the Lord does not see. It is not the goodly images made openly for the house of the Lord. The ancients of Israel hid their idols in chambers; Solomon graved his cherubims on the walls for everyone to see, and did not bow to them.

“Son of man, dig now in the wall: and when I had digged in the wall, behold a door.” The Lord had the prophet dig through a wall, and there was a hidden door leading to a chamber of secret idolatry.

That is what a secret place is: something hidden behind the wall, that has to be dug into to be found. It is the opposite of cherubims graved openly on the walls of the house of the Lord.

“Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.”

According to the goodness of the land, Israel made goodly images, and these goodly images are the very ones read of here in the building of the house of the Lord: the cherubims graved on the walls, the palm trees and chains, the house garnished “with precious stones for beauty”. They were made openly for the house of the Lord, and Solomon was not bowing down to them.

And the house was rich with the goodness of the land: in the most holy house he “overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents. And the weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/30.md|2 Chronicl:
In the wilderness “they kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month at even”. But “there were certain men, who were defiled by the dead body of a man, that they could not keep the passover on that day”, and they asked, “wherefore are we kept back, that we may not offer an offering of the Lord in his appointed season”?

The Lord answered: “If any man of you or of your posterity shall be unclean by reason of a dead body, or be in a journey afar off, yet he shall keep the passover unto the Lord. The fourteenth day of the second month at even they shall keep it, and eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.” A man defiled or on a far journey may keep the Passover in the second month.

That is the provision Hezekiah relied on. Now that the temple was cleansed, the king and congregation took counsel “to keep the passover in the second month. For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently, neither had the people gathered themselves together to Jerusalem.” So he sent letters “to all Israel and Judah”, even “to Ephraim and Manasseh”, with a proclamation “from Beer–sheba even to Dan”, “for they had not done it of a long time in such sort as it was written.”

“Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.” Speak the same thing, be of one mind and one judgment, with no divisions.

That is the same unity that gave Israel one heart to serve the Most High. “Also in Judah the hand of God was to give them one heart to do the commandment of the king and of the princes, by the word of the Lord.” And “there assembled at Jerusalem much people to keep the feast of unleavened bread in the second month, a very great congregation.”

Not everyone received it. The posts “passed from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh even unto Zebulun: but they laughed them to scorn, and mocked them”, the same mockery Israel meets today when the truth is preached. “Nevertheless divers of Asher and Manasseh and of Zebulun humbled themselves, and came to Jerusalem.” And being of one mind, the congregation “took away the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for incense took they away, and cast them into the brook Kidron.”

“And at that time Solomon held a feast, and all Israel with him, a great congregation, from the entering in of Hamath unto the river of Egypt, before the Lord our God, seven days and seven days, even fourteen days.” That is the earlier pattern Hezekiah’s congregation repeated.

They “kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness”, and then “the whole assembly took counsel to keep other seven days: and they kept other seven days with gladness.” Fourteen days in all, all in one mind and one heart. Hezekiah gave “a thousand bullocks and seven thousand sheep”, the princes “a thousand bullocks and ten thousand sheep”, and all the congregation, the priests, the Levites and “the strangers that came out of the land of Israel” rejoiced together.

So it fits that “there was great joy in Jerusalem: for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there was not the like in Jerusalem.” The priests and Levites blessed the people, “and their prayer came up to his holy dwelling place, even unto heaven.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/31.md|2 Chronicl:
“Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son. For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods”. Make no marriages with the nations, for they turn the heart to other gods.

Instead: “thus shall ye deal with them; ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire.”

That is the law Israel obeyed directly when the feast was finished. They “went out to the cities of Judah, and brake the images in pieces, and cut down the groves, and threw down the high places and the altars out of all Judah and Benjamin, in Ephraim also and Manasseh, until they had utterly destroyed them all.” Then every man returned “to his possession, into their own cities”, the reformation now reaching beyond the temple into the whole land.

“Thou shalt truly tithe all the increase of thy seed, that the field bringeth forth year by year.” The tithe of “thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the firstlings of thy herds and of thy flocks” was brought “that thou mayest learn to fear the Lord thy God always.” And the charge ends: “the Levite that is within thy gates; thou shalt not forsake him; for he hath no part nor inheritance with thee.”

Hezekiah restored exactly that. He appointed the priests and Levites “after their courses, every man according to his service”, set “the king’s portion of his substance” for the morning and evening, sabbath, new moon and feast offerings, “as it is written in the law of the Lord”, and “commanded the people that dwelt in Jerusalem to give the portion of the priests and the Levites, that they might be encouraged in the law of the Lord.” The Levite was not forsaken.

“And as soon as the commandment came abroad, the children of Israel brought in abundance the firstfruits of corn, wine, and oil, and honey, and of all the increase of the field; and the tithe of all things brought they in abundantly.” They laid it by heaps from the third month to the seventh, “And when Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the Lord, and his people Israel.”

David charged Solomon: “be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man; And keep the charge of the Lord thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself”.

Keeping the charge is what brings the prospering. Hezekiah “wrought that which was good and right and truth before the Lord his God”, sought his God “in the law, and in the commandments”, “and prospered.”

So it is for us: keep his laws and do the work with all your heart, or it will not be blessed.

“And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men”. That is Hezekiah: “in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law, and in the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered.”

This is the charge on every one of us. Do the work with everything you have, as unto the Lord, or it will not be blessed. You cannot halfway walk in the truth and expect to grow.
docs/study/2-chronicles/32.md|2 Chronicl:
Kings records “the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city”. Hezekiah had built a water system for Jerusalem, and now he used it against the siege.

When “Sennacherib king of Assyria came, and entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities”, Hezekiah took counsel “to stop the waters of the fountains which were without the city”, and the people “stopped all the fountains, and the brook that ran through the midst of the land, saying, Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water?” The water came into the city, and the enemy outside found none.

He also “built up all the wall that was broken, and raised it up to the towers, and another wall without, and repaired Millo in the city of David, and made darts and shields in abundance.” Our people are resourceful and skilled, doing the work themselves.

“Thus saith the Lord; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord.” That is the opposite of Hezekiah’s trust in the Most High.

Hezekiah set captains over the people and spake comfortably to them: “Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude that is with him: for there be more with us than with him: With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the Lord our God to help us, and to fight our battles.”

Sennacherib made flesh his arm; Hezekiah trusted the Lord. “And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.”

Kings gives the fuller account of the sickness. “In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death.” Isaiah came and said, “Set thine house in order; for thou shalt die, and not live.” Hezekiah “turned his face to the wall, and prayed unto the Lord”, “I beseech thee, O Lord, remember now how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart”, “And Hezekiah wept sore.”

Before Isaiah was out of the middle court the word came: “I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will heal thee”. “And I will add unto thy days fifteen years; and I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria; and I will defend this city for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.”

That is the benefit done to him. And yet “Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem.” When things go well, do not get puffed up and make it about yourself. “Notwithstanding Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord came not upon them in the days of Hezekiah.”

Chronicles says only that the Lord “gave him a sign.” Kings shows what it was. Hezekiah asked, “What shall be the sign that the Lord will heal me”? Isaiah answered, “shall the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees?”

Hezekiah said, “It is a light thing for the shadow to go down ten degrees: nay, but let the shadow return backward ten degrees.” “And Isaiah the prophet cried unto the Lord: and he brought the shadow ten degrees backward, by which it had gone down in the dial of Ahaz.” The shadow returning backward on the sundial of Ahaz was a thing only the Most High could do.

That was the benefit Hezekiah was shown, and it is why his lifted-up heart afterward brought wrath, until he humbled himself.

“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.” The enemy still seeks to deceive Israel out of the truth.

That is what Sennacherib’s servants were doing at the wall of Jerusalem. “Whereon do ye trust, that ye abide in the siege in Jerusalem?” They claimed Hezekiah was persuading the people “to give over yourselves to die by famine and by thirst”. They mocked that he had “taken away his high places and his altars, and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, saying, Ye shall worship before one altar”, twisting obedience to the commandment into a weakness.

Then the argument: “no god of any nation or kingdom was able to deliver his people out of mine hand”, so “how much less shall your God deliver you out of mine hand?” “Now therefore let not Hezekiah deceive you, nor persuade you on this manner, neither yet believe him”. This is the same seed the world plants to make Israel weary and turn a people off one accord.
docs/study/2-chronicles/33.md|2 Chronicl:
“And for our sins and our fathers’ we with our brethren and our kings and our priests were given up unto the kings of the earth, to the sword, and to captivity, and for a prey with shame, unto this day.”

The kings were not spared. Manasseh, king in Jerusalem, was taken “among the thorns”, bound “with fetters”, and carried “to Babylon”, because he and his people “would not hearken.” For their sins and their fathers’ sins, the kings of Israel were given up into the hands of the kings of the earth.

The curse said: “The Lord shall bring thee, and thy king which thou shalt set over thee, unto a nation which neither thou nor thy fathers have known; and there shalt thou serve other gods, wood and stone.”

That came upon Manasseh. “And the Lord spake to Manasseh, and to his people: but they would not hearken.” So the Lord “brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon.” The kings of Israel that were once kings were brought down into captivity, exactly as the curses warned.

“The graven images of their gods shall ye burn with fire: thou shalt not desire the silver or gold that is on them, nor take it unto thee, lest thou be snared therein: for it is an abomination to the Lord thy God.” The graven images of the nations were to be destroyed and not desired, for they are an abomination to the Most High.

That is the example Manasseh followed once he was humbled. “And he took away the strange gods, and the idol out of the house of the Lord, and all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the Lord, and in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city.” He kept none of it.

Then “he repaired the altar of the Lord, and sacrificed thereon peace offerings and thank offerings, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel.” He also built the wall of the city of David and “put captains of war in all the fenced cities of Judah.” The people still sacrificed in the high places, “yet unto the Lord their God only.”

“O Lord, Almighty God of our fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of their righteous seed”. This is the prayer of Manasseh king of Judah, his cry to the God of his fathers when he was held in Babylon.

Chronicles points right to it: “the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer unto his God”, and “His prayer also, and how God was intreated of him, and all his sin, and his trespass”, “behold, they are written among the sayings of the seers.” That prayer is a writing of the Apocrypha, found before the books of Maccabees, and it is part of the Bible.

God was intreated of him, and the wicked king was humbled. “So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his own house: and Amon his son reigned in his stead.”

“Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.”

That is why Amon’s evil increased. He saw his father’s idols stand and took up serving them, and with no sentence executed speedily his heart was fully set to do evil: he “humbled not himself before the Lord”, “but Amon trespassed more and more.” He reigned only “two years in Jerusalem” before “his servants conspired against him, and slew him in his own house.”

“O Lord, Father and Governor of all my whole life, leave me not to their counsels, and let me not fall by them. Who will set scourges over my thoughts, and the discipline of wisdom over mine heart? that they spare me not for mine ignorances, and it pass not by my sins”. A humble man asks the Most High to scourge his thoughts and discipline his heart when he errs, so his ignorance does not increase and his sins do not abound to his destruction.

Amon never asked. He “did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, as did Manasseh his father”, sacrificing “unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made”, “And humbled not himself before the Lord, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more.”

His sins abounded to his own destruction: “his servants conspired against him, and slew him in his own house.” The people of the land slew the conspirators “and made Josiah his son king in his stead.”

“It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife.” Doing worse than the heathen is the same rebuke Paul gives: a sin found among the people that is not so much as named among the Gentiles.

That is Manasseh. He set “a carved image, the idol which he had made, in the house of God”, the very house of which God said to David and Solomon, “In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen before all the tribes of Israel, will I put my name for ever”. “So Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen, whom the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel.”

“There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For all that do these things are an abomination unto the Lord”. And: “Thou shalt be perfect with the Lord thy God.”

Manasseh did every one of them: “he caused his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom: also he observed times, and used enchantments, and used witchcraft, and dealt with a familiar spirit, and with wizards”. Every one of these things is a commandment he broke. Passing children through the fire is child sacrifice, the same spirit as abortion today.

The law says “because of these abominations the Lord thy God doth drive them out from before thee.” Manasseh brought those same abominations into the house of the Lord: he “built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord”, and “wrought much evil in the sight of the Lord, to provoke him to anger.”
docs/study/2-chronicles/34.md|2 Chronicl:
“Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished.” That is the very lesson of these young kings.

Compare the ages. Manasseh began at twelve, Amon at twenty two, and Josiah “was eight years old when he began to reign”, yet the youngest was the wisest. Josiah “did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and walked in the ways of David his father”.

“For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David his father: and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem from the high places, and the groves, and the carved images, and the molten images.” The wise child sought the Most High while the older kings before him would no more be admonished.

The charge to Joshua: “Only be thou strong and very courageous, that thou mayest observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded thee: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest.” And “thou shalt meditate therein day and night”, “for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.”

Josiah is that charge kept. He “walked in the ways of David his father, and declined neither to the right hand, nor to the left.” He observed to do according to the law, turned not from it, and so he reigned “in Jerusalem one and thirty years.”

“And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel”. That is the same book of the law that was found in the house of the Lord.

“And when they brought out the money that was brought into the house of the Lord, Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses.” The very Bible. He said, “I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord”, and delivered it to Shaphan the scribe.

Shaphan carried the book to the king and reported that “All that was committed to thy servants, they do it”, and the money was delivered “to the hand of the workmen.” Then he told the king, “Hilkiah the priest hath given me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king.” The law Moses set before Israel was set before the king again.

“Yea, all Israel have transgressed thy law, even by departing, that they might not obey thy voice; therefore the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses the servant of God, because we have sinned against him.” The Lord “hath confirmed his words, which he spake against us”, “for the Lord our God is righteous in all his works which he doeth: for we obeyed not his voice.”

Josiah saw the same thing when he heard the book: “it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the law, that he rent his clothes”, and said, “great is the wrath of the Lord that is poured out upon us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the Lord, to do after all that is written in this book.”

All Israel had transgressed the law, so the curse and oath written in the law of Moses was poured out upon them, and the Most High is righteous in it. Josiah knew it, so he sent to “enquire of the Lord for me, and for them that are left in Israel and in Judah”.

“Call now, if there be any that will answer thee; and to which of the saints wilt thou turn?” To inquire of the Lord, one must go to a saint, a chosen prophet who has the word. To learn the Bible you must go to one of the chosen.

That is what Josiah did. He had the book read before him, but he did not stop there: he “commanded Hilkiah, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Abdon the son of Micah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah a servant of the king’s, saying, Go, enquire of the Lord for me”, “concerning the words of the book that is found”. He turned to one who could answer.

“My son, go on with thy business in meekness; so shalt thou be beloved of him that is approved. The greater thou art, the more humble thyself, and thou shalt find favour before the Lord. Many are in high place, and of renown: but mysteries are revealed unto the meek. For the power of the Lord is great, and he is honoured of the lowly.”

Humble yourself before the Most High and you find favour, and the mysteries are revealed to the meek and lowly, as they were to tender-hearted Josiah. The king was great, and he humbled himself the more.

Huldah the prophetess declared evil upon Jerusalem, “even all the curses that are written in the book”, “Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods”. But to the king: “Because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God, when thou heardest his words against this place”, “and didst rend thy clothes, and weep before me; I have even heard thee also, saith the Lord.” That is the favour found by the humble.

“The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart: and merciful men are taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come.”

That is why Josiah is gathered in peace. The Lord said through Huldah, “Behold, I will gather thee to thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered to thy grave in peace, neither shall thine eyes see all the evil that I will bring upon this place, and upon the inhabitants of the same.”

The wrath was coming upon Jerusalem and “shall not be quenched”, and the righteous king was taken away from the evil to come.

“They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine’s flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the Lord.” That is the same garden and grove worship Josiah tore down.

“And they brake down the altars of Baalim in his presence; and the images, that were on high above them, he cut down; and the groves, and the carved images, and the molten images, he brake in pieces, and made dust of them, and strowed it upon the graves of them that had sacrificed unto them.” “And he burnt the bones of the priests upon their altars, and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.”

He did the same “in the cities of Manasseh, and Ephraim, and Simeon, even unto Naphtali”, and when he “had beaten the graven images into powder, and cut down all the idols throughout all the land of Israel, he returned to Jerusalem.” Those who worshipped in the groves were consumed together, as the Lord said.
docs/study/2-chronicles/35.md|2 Chronicl:
The Lord spake to Moses and Aaron in Egypt: “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you.” Every man was to take a lamb “according to the house of their fathers”, “without blemish, a male of the first year”, and keep it “until the fourteenth day of the same month: and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it in the evening.”

Josiah kept it exactly. “Josiah kept a passover unto the Lord in Jerusalem: and they killed the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month.” He kept the laws pertaining to the Passover, in the month the Most High made the beginning of months.

He set it in order: he “set the priests in their charges, and encouraged them to the service of the house of the Lord”, told the Levites to “Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon the son of David king of Israel did build”, and to “prepare yourselves by the houses of your fathers, after your courses”, so the whole congregation could do “according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses.”

“And this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the Lord throughout your generations; ye shall keep it a feast by an ordinance for ever.”

The Passover is a memorial kept as a feast to the Lord throughout all generations, an ordinance for ever. That is why Josiah kept it, and why he charged the Levites, “serve now the Lord your God, and his people Israel”, and to “kill the passover”, “that they may do according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses.”

“For I am the Lord your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.”

You sanctify yourselves and are holy by keeping the word of the Lord, here the dietary laws, for he is the Lord your God and he is holy. That is what Josiah commanded the Levites: “So kill the passover, and sanctify yourselves, and prepare your brethren, that they may do according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses.” Sanctifying yourself is doing what the word says.
docs/study/2-chronicles/36.md|2 Chronicl:
Israel said in their mind, “We will be as the heathen, as the families of the countries, to serve wood and stone.” The Most High answers, “that which cometh into your mind shall not be at all.”

That is what the chief of the priests and the people did in Zedekiah’s days: they “transgressed very much after all the abominations of the heathen.” They wanted to be like the nations. But he will not let his people become the heathen: “As I live, saith the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, will I rule over you.”

So the wrath that arose against his people, till there was no remedy, is that fury poured out. The Most High rules over Israel with a mighty hand until his people acknowledge him.

The Most High “saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” It grieved him at his heart, and he said, “I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth.”

That is the pattern behind the fall of Jerusalem. Zedekiah did evil in the sight of the Lord his God, humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet, stiffened his neck and hardened his heart. The chief of the priests and the people transgressed very much after all the abominations of the heathen and polluted the house of the Lord.

A repeated pattern of evil brings his judgment. The Most High sent his messengers, rising up betimes, because he had compassion; but they mocked the messengers, despised his words and misused his prophets, “until the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.” As in the days before the flood, when the wickedness is great and continual, destruction comes.

The curses of the law said it before it happened: “The Lord shall bring a nation against thee from far, from the end of the earth, as swift as the eagle flieth; a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand; A nation of fierce countenance, which shall not regard the person of the old, nor shew favour to the young.”

That nation is the king of the Chaldees. He slew their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and “had no compassion upon young man or maiden, old man, or him that stooped for age.” No regard for the old, no favour to the young, exactly as written.

The Most High gave them all into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand. The vessels of the house of God, the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king and his princes, were brought to Babylon; the house of God was burnt and the wall of Jerusalem broken down. This is the fierce nation the curses warned of, come upon Judah.

The same Most High who gave Judah into the hand of the Chaldees will plead for them. “I will also gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people and for my heritage Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations, and parted my land.”

The nations “have cast lots for my people; and have given a boy for an harlot, and sold a girl for wine.” They took his silver and his gold and “carried into your temples my goodly pleasant things”, just as all the vessels and treasures of the house of the Lord were carried to Babylon. And “The children also of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Grecians, that ye might remove them far from their border.”

So the carrying away is not the end of the matter. The nations that scattered Israel, parted his land and sold his people will be judged: “swiftly and speedily will I return your recompence upon your own head.”

“A wise judge will instruct his people; and the government of a prudent man is well ordered. As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers; and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein. An unwise king destroyeth his people”. As the ruler is, so are his people.

Jehoiakim “did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord his God”, and he destroyed his people. “Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and bound him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon.” Nebuchadnezzar “also carried of the vessels of the house of the Lord to Babylon, and put them in his temple at Babylon.”

“The power of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and in due time he will set over it one that is profitable.” The Most High set a wicked king over the land because his own people would not do what he said. When Israel will not rule in righteousness, he raises a Nebuchadnezzar. Israel’s purpose was never to be wicked and rule at the same time.
docs/study/2-chronicles/6.md|2 Chronicle:
“And ye shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and none else: and my people shall never be ashamed.”

No other nation has this. When the heaven is shut up and there is no rain because Israel sinned, if they pray toward this place, confess his name and turn from their sin, the Most High promised to hear, forgive, teach them the good way wherein they should walk, and “send rain upon thy land, which thou hast given unto thy people for an inheritance.”

When he answers that repentance and sends the rain in due season, Israel knows he is in their midst, their God and none else, and they are not ashamed.

Christ told the Canaanite woman, “It is not meet to take the children’s bread, and to cast it to dogs.” She did not fight it. She said, “Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” She owned herself a dog and submitted under Israel, and that faith moved him: “O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt. And her daughter was made whole from that very hour.”

That is the stranger Solomon prayed for, “which is not of thy people Israel, but is come from a far country for thy great name’s sake.” The Most High hears the stranger who submits and fears him, “that all people of the earth may know thy name, and fear thee, as doth thy people Israel.”

He does not honor a prayer prayed against Israel or for dominion over his people. The stranger is heard in the place of the dog under the master’s table, not in the place of the children.

“The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come.” The sceptre and the lawgiver stay with Judah, and Judah is the line David came from.

That is why, after bringing Israel out of Egypt and choosing no city and no man, the Most High says, “I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there; and have chosen David to be over my people Israel.” The choosing of David, a man of Judah, to rule over his people is the sceptre of Judah that Jacob spoke of, and Jerusalem, the city of David, is where his house would be built.
docs/study/2-chronicles/7.md|2 Chronicle:
“O Lord, have mercy upon the people that is called by thy name, and upon Israel, whom thou hast named thy firstborn.”

The people called by his name is Israel, his firstborn. That is who the Most High speaks to when he says, “If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” The mercy and the healing are promised to Israel, not to all nations.

“Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not: thou, O Lord, art our father, our redeemer.” The Most High is Father and Redeemer to Israel, “the tribes of thine inheritance.”

Then the line that settles who “my people, which are called by my name” are: “We are thine: thou never barest rule over them; they were not called by thy name.” Other nations were never called by his name.

So the promise of 2 Chronicles 7:14 belongs to Israel, the same people read through these chapters. The Most High controls the rain, the locust and the pestilence, and the healing of the land follows Israel’s humbling, praying, seeking his face and turning from their wicked ways. It is not a general love for all nations.

Solomon had already prayed it back to the Most High: “keep with thy servant David my father that which thou hast promised him, saying, There shall not fail thee a man in my sight to sit upon the throne of Israel; yet so that thy children take heed to their way to walk in my law.”

Now the Most High answers with the same word: if Solomon will walk before him as David walked and observe his statutes and judgments, “Then will I stablish the throne of thy kingdom, according as I have covenanted with David thy father, saying, There shall not fail thee a man to be ruler in Israel.”

The promise means every king of Israel would come through David’s lineage. But it carries a condition: the kingdom continues so long as the house keeps the covenant and his children walk in his law.
docs/study/2-chronicles/8.md|2 Chronicle:
“Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the Lord empty.”

That is the commandment of Moses Solomon kept. He offered burnt offerings on the altar he built “on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles.” The place the Lord chose was the house in Jerusalem, and there the three feasts were kept as written, with the priests, Levites and porters in their courses by the order of David.
docs/study/2-chronicles/9.md|2 Chronicle:
“Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred threescore and six talents of gold.” Kings records the same yearly weight of gold that Chronicles gives: six hundred sixty and six talents.

Chronicles is the compressed retelling of the fuller history in Kings. The same gold, beside what the merchants and the kings of Arabia and the governors brought, went into the two hundred targets and three hundred shields of beaten gold that Solomon put in the house of the forest of Lebanon.
docs/study/2-kings/1.md|2 Kings 1:1|2 Sa:
David “smote Moab, and measured them with a line, casting them down to the ground”, and “so the Moabites became David’s servants, and brought gifts.” Those gifts are tribute. Moab was subdued under Israel when Israel served the Lord.

So when “Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab”, it shows the change. Nations that had been subdued under David and brought under tribute begin to break away, because Israel no longer walks in the blessing that came from serving the Most High.
docs/study/2-kings/1.md|2 Kings 1:1|Deut:
The law says, “if thou shalt hearken diligently unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe and to do all his commandments”, then “the Lord thy God will set thee on high above all nations of the earth.”

That is what happened under David, when Moab and the other nations were brought under Israel. Being set on high above the nations depends on hearkening to the voice of the Lord. After Ahab, Israel was not hearkening, and so Moab no longer stayed beneath them.

“But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee.”

The same chapter that promised to set Israel on high above all nations promised the curses if they would not hearken. Under Ahab they did not, and the curses began to overtake them. Moab breaking away is part of that.

“The Lord shall cause thee to be smitten before thine enemies: thou shalt go out one way against them, and flee seven ways before them: and shalt be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth. And thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away.”

This is the blessing of verse 7 turned around. Instead of the enemy fleeing seven ways before Israel, a disobedient Israel flees seven ways before the enemy and is scattered. And the carcase given as meat for the fowls of the air is the same judgment pronounced on the house of Ahab. After Ahab’s death Moab rebels, and the curse is on its way.

“The Lord shall cause thine enemies that rise up against thee to be smitten before thy face: they shall come out against thee one way, and flee before thee seven ways.”

When Israel keeps his commandments, the enemies that rise up are smitten before them, as Moab was smitten under David. Moab rising up and rebelling after the death of Ahab shows that the nation was no longer under that blessing.
docs/study/2-kings/1.md|2 Kings 1:2-8|1:
When the ark of God was sent to Ekron, “the Ekronites cried out, saying, They have brought about the ark of the God of Israel to us, to slay us and our people.” They begged to send it away, “for there was a deadly destruction throughout all the city; the hand of God was very heavy there.”

The god of Ekron could not even defend his own people against the God of Israel. That is Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, the lord of the flies, the one Ahaziah sent to when he fell through the lattice and was sick.

Ahaziah should have known that history, and it would have kept him from trusting the god of Ekron. That is why Elijah asks, “Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baal–zebub the god of Ekron?” He turned to an idol rather than the Most High, and the word came: “thou shalt not come down from that bed on which thou art gone up, but shalt surely die.”
docs/study/2-kings/10.md|2 Kings 10:18-2:
“The graven images of their gods shall ye burn with fire.” The silver and gold on them is not to be desired, “for it is an abomination to the Lord thy God.” It is not to be brought into the house, “lest thou be a cursed thing like it: but thou shalt utterly detest it, and thou shalt utterly abhor it; for it is a cursed thing.”

That is the law Jehu carried out. He gathered all the worshippers of Baal in subtilty, filled the house of Baal, and after the sacrifice sent in the guard to slay them. Then “they brought forth the images out of the house of Baal, and burned them. And they brake down the image of Baal, and brake down the house of Baal, and made it a draught house unto this day.”

The images were burned with fire and treated as the cursed thing they are. So Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel.
docs/study/2-kings/10.md|2 Kings 10:28-3:
“Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.” Jehu stood; he executed judgment on the house of Ahab and destroyed Baal, and the Most High promised his children to the fourth generation would sit on the throne. Still he fell, for he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam.

And there was no excuse: “God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.” The Most High provides a way to escape. Jehu took no heed.

“All, except David and Ezekias and Josias, were defective: for they forsook the law of the most High, even the kings of Juda failed.”

Jehu is counted among the defective. He destroyed Baal out of Israel, and the Most High commended him for doing to the house of Ahab all that was in his heart. Yet he departed not from the golden calves in Beth-el and in Dan, and “took no heed to walk in the law of the Lord God of Israel with all his heart.”

Only David, Hezekiah and Josiah stand apart. A man may do great things and still turn away and stay in sin.

“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” Many will say they prophesied, cast out devils and “done many wonderful works”, and the answer will be, “I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”

Jehu did wonderful works in the Lord’s name. He destroyed Baal out of Israel. But he did not do the will of the Father with all his heart; he kept the golden calves. Great works do not stand in the place of walking in the law.
docs/study/2-kings/11.md|2 Kings 11:4-8|:
“And ye shall compass the king round about, every man with his weapons in his hand: and he that cometh within the ranges, let him be slain: and be ye with the king as he goeth out and as he cometh in.”

In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest brought the captains into the house of the Lord, took an oath of them and showed them the king’s son. He set them by watches and companies so the house would not be broken down, and this is the order that crowned it: every man armed around the king, anyone coming within the ranges slain, and the guard with him as he went out and came in.
docs/study/2-kings/12.md|2 Kings 12:1-3|:
“How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent?”

None can call on the Lord unless they believe, none believe unless they hear, and none hear without a preacher who is sent to guide and instruct. That is Jehoash: he “did that which was right in the sight of the Lord all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him.”

No one comes to the truth alone. The Most High set up a structure of instruction, and a person must be taught the word rather than claiming private revelation.
docs/study/2-kings/12.md|2 Kings 12:9-16:
“Deliver all things in number and weight; and put all in writing that thou givest out, or receivest in.”

That is how the money for the house was handled. Jehoiada set a chest with a hole bored in the lid beside the altar, and when there was much money the king’s scribe and the high priest came up, “and told the money that was found in the house of the Lord”, and gave it into the hands of them that did the work.

This is why records must be kept, especially where money is concerned. All things touching the body must be put in writing.
docs/study/2-kings/14.md|2 Kings 14:1-6|:
Chronicles gives the same king, twenty and five years old, reigning twenty and nine years in Jerusalem, his mother Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. And it says plainly what Kings means: “he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart.”

That explains the words in Kings, “yet not like David his father.” Amaziah did right, but he did not serve with a perfect heart, and so he was not counted like David.

“The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.”

When the kingdom was confirmed in his hand, Amaziah slew the servants who had slain the king his father. “But the children of the murderers he slew not”, because this is the law of Moses. Kings quotes it word for word from the book of the law. Every man is put to death for his own sin.

“All, except David and Ezekias and Josias, were defective: for they forsook the law of the most High, even the kings of Juda failed.”

Amaziah did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, “yet not like David his father”, and the high places were not taken away. He is among the defective kings of Judah. Only David, Hezekiah and Josiah are set apart.
docs/study/2-kings/15.md|2 Kings 15:1-7|:
“Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the room of his father Amaziah.”

Azariah is Uzziah. Kings says Azariah son of Amaziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign; Chronicles names the same king Uzziah and gives his life and acts in greater detail. Kings itself points there: “are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?” For the fuller account of the king who did right, left the high places standing, and was smitten a leper, read 2 Chronicles 26.
docs/study/2-kings/15.md|2 Kings 15:8-12:
The Most High told Jehu, “Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes, and hast done unto the house of Ahab according to all that was in mine heart, thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel.”

Zachariah the son of Jeroboam is that fourth generation. He reigned six months, did evil, departed not from the sins of Jeroboam, and Shallum conspired against him and slew him. And Kings says it outright: “This was the word of the Lord which he spake unto Jehu, saying, Thy sons shall sit on the throne of Israel unto the fourth generation. And so it came to pass.”
docs/study/2-kings/16.md|2 Kings 16:1-4|:
“Ye shall utterly destroy all the places, wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree.” Their altars overthrown, their pillars broken, their groves burned, their graven images hewn down. “Ye shall not do so unto the Lord your God.”

Ahaz did the very thing the law forbade. He “sacrificed and burnt incense in the high places, and on the hills, and under every green tree.” He made his son to pass through the fire “according to the abominations of the heathen, whom the Lord cast out from before the children of Israel.”

The nations’ places of worship were to be utterly destroyed, not imitated. Ahaz walked in the way of the kings of Israel and imitated them.
docs/study/2-kings/16.md|2 Kings 16:10-1:
The priests “serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.”

The true altar was made after the pattern of heavenly things given through Moses. Ahaz went to Damascus to meet the king of Assyria, saw a heathen altar he admired, and sent Urijah the priest “the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof.” He traded the pattern shown in the mount for the fashion of the nations.

Then he moved the brasen altar from before the Lord, made the new altar the place of all the offerings, and kept the brasen altar “for me to enquire by.” Moses was warned to make all things according to the pattern, and Ahaz did the opposite.
docs/study/2-kings/17.md|2 Kings 17:13-1:
Israel was warned, “Lest ye corrupt yourselves, and make you a graven image”, the likeness of male or female, beast, fowl, creeping thing or fish. “And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them.”

They did every part of it. They “made them molten images, even two calves, and made a grove, and worshipped all the host of heaven, and served Baal.” They corrupted themselves exactly as the law said not to, and the Most High testified against them by all the prophets and seers before he brought the judgment.

“He that believeth in the Lord taketh heed to the commandment; and he that trusteth in him shall fare never the worse.”

True belief is tied to obedience. Israel hardened their necks “like to the neck of their fathers, that did not believe in the Lord their God”, and the proof they did not believe is that they rejected his statutes and his covenant.

To believe in the Most High is to take heed to the commandments. Those who claim belief while breaking the commandments do not truly believe.
docs/study/2-kings/17.md|2 Kings 17:18-2:
“They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked me to anger with their vanities: and I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.”

Israel provoked the Most High with their vanities, and he was very angry and “removed them out of his sight.” He “rejected all the seed of Israel, and afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of spoilers, until he had cast them out of his sight.” This foretells their rejection among the nations.

That rejection is why the seed of Israel are later called heathens and Gentiles in the New Testament, and it resolves much of the struggle over Jews and Gentiles there.
docs/study/2-kings/17.md|2 Kings 17:35-4:
The law says, “if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee.”

The curses come from forsaking the Most High, so no man can buy or redeem the nation out of its condition. No nation and no treaty can do it. The covenant said, “the Lord your God ye shall fear; and he shall deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies.” Only turning to the Most High can.

“Howbeit they did not hearken, but they did after their former manner.” The settler nations feared the Lord and served their graven images to this day, and as a nation Israel does the same, serving the gods of the nations. So the curses stay on them.
docs/study/2-kings/17.md|2 Kings 17:7-12:
“Ye shall utterly destroy all the places, wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree.” Overthrow their altars, break their pillars, burn their groves, hew down their graven images.

The law had already commanded Israel to destroy such high places, not build them. Instead Israel “built them high places in all their cities, from the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city. And they set them up images and groves in every high hill, and under every green tree.” They walked in the statutes of the heathen and served idols, “whereof the Lord had said unto them, Ye shall not do this thing.” That is why the captivity came.
docs/study/2-kings/18.md|2 Kings 18:5-8|:
“Keep therefore the words of this covenant, and do them, that ye may prosper in all that ye do.”

Hezekiah “clave to the Lord, and departed not from following him, but kept his commandments, which the Lord commanded Moses. And the Lord was with him; and he prospered whithersoever he went forth.”

Prospering here does not mean a mansion or luxury. It is the blessing that comes from keeping and doing the commandments: the Most High with him, rebelling against the king of Assyria and serving him not, and smiting the Philistines even unto Gaza.
docs/study/2-kings/18.md|2 Kings 18:9-12:
The law says, “if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee.”

Samaria was besieged in Hezekiah’s fourth year and taken at the end of three years, and the king of Assyria carried Israel away into Halah, Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. Israel was carried away in stages, not all at once.

The reason is given again, in the words of the curse: “Because they obeyed not the voice of the Lord their God, but transgressed his covenant, and all that Moses the servant of the Lord commanded, and would not hear them, nor do them.” The captivity comes because Israel would not hearken.
docs/study/2-kings/19.md|2 Kings 19:20-2:
“Also Judah kept not the commandments of the Lord their God, but walked in the statutes of Israel which they made. And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, and afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of spoilers.”

That is why Assyria had power to come up at all. The Most High answers Sennacherib, “Hast thou not heard long ago how I have done it, and of ancient times that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps.” He gave Assyria the very ability to lay the cities waste, for his own purpose, because his people kept not his commandments.

But Assyria boasted with the multitude of his chariots, the same as a nation today boasting of its army, military and political system, and lifted his eyes against the Holy One of Israel. So the spoiler is turned back: “I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest.”

Micah prophesied in the same time: “Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof.” Samaria is made a heap and her idols laid desolate.

That is the work the Most High formed of ancient times and brought to pass through Assyria, “that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps.” Samaria fell to Assyria by his hand. Yet when Assyria raged against him and came against Jerusalem, the virgin the daughter of Zion “hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn.” Israel laughs at the enemy, for it is already written that they lose.
docs/study/2-kings/19.md|2 Kings 19:35-3:
Tobit lived in Nineveh in this same time: “if the king Sennacherib had slain any, when he was come, and fled from Judea, I buried them privily; for in his wrath he killed many.”

Sennacherib fled from Judea after the angel of the Lord smote his camp, and returned to dwell at Nineveh, and there in his wrath he slew many Israelites. Tobit buried them in secret. When a Ninevite complained of him to the king, he hid himself for fear of death, “Then all my goods were forcibly taken away, neither was there any thing left me, beside my wife Anna and my son Tobias.”

“And there passed not five and fifty days, before two of his sons killed him, and they fled into the mountains of Ararath; and Sarchedonus his son reigned in his stead.”

Tobit records the same murder of Sennacherib by his sons that Kings gives: “Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia.
