And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.” Sarchedonus is Esarhaddon. Two witnesses to one history, and the word of verse 7 fulfilled.

“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.”

Israel did not lift a finger: “the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand.” A score is twenty, so that is a hundred and eighty-five thousand, all dead corpses by morning.

The battle is the Most High’s to fight for his people. This is praying for the death of the enemy and for righteous judgment, and leaving it to his spirit, not to might or power.
docs/study/2-kings/20.md|2 Kings 20:1-7|:
“For it was neither herb, nor mollifying plaister, that restored them to health: but thy word, O Lord, which healeth all things.”

Isaiah said, “Take a lump of figs”, and they laid it on the boil, and Hezekiah recovered. Remedies and herbs go together with prayer. But it was not the figs that healed him. Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed, and the word came, “I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will heal thee.”

It is neither herb nor plaster that heals, but the word of the Most High. Our healing is in his hand.
docs/study/2-kings/20.md|2 Kings 20:12-1:
The king of Babylon told Ashpenaz “the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring certain of the children of Israel, and of the king’s seed, and of the princes”, children without blemish, skilful in wisdom, able “to stand in the king’s palace”, to be taught “the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.” “Now among these were of the children of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.”

That is Isaiah’s word fulfilled: “of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” Daniel and his companions, of the king’s seed, were put under the master of the eunuchs and made eunuchs in that palace.

“Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart.”

Berodach-baladan king of Babylon “sent letters and a present unto Hezekiah.” The gift did its work. “Hezekiah hearkened unto them, and shewed them all the house of his precious things”, the silver, gold, spices, precious ointment and all his armour: “there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not.”

A gift destroyeth the heart. Because of the present, Hezekiah trusted his enemies and let them in to see everything he owned, and that is why Isaiah declared it would all be carried into Babylon.

“For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother’s womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men.”

Some are born eunuchs and some are made eunuchs of men. Daniel and his companions were made eunuchs of men, after they were grown, when they were carried to Babylon. So Isaiah’s word that Hezekiah’s sons “shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon” came to pass as it was spoken.
docs/study/2-kings/21.md|2 Kings 21:10-1:
“My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee”, “seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.”

Because Judah rejected the knowledge of the law, the Most High rejects them: “I will forsake the remnant of mine inheritance, and deliver them into the hand of their enemies.” They have provoked him to anger “since the day their fathers came forth out of Egypt, even unto this day.” He bore with this wickedness for hundreds of years, and now it is rejection for rejection.

“Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge: and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst. Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure.”

Hell here means captivity. Having no knowledge, the people go into captivity, and it opens its mouth without measure: “their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it.”

That is the evil the Most High brought on Jerusalem and Judah, such that “whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle”: the remnant of his inheritance delivered into the hand of their enemies.

“I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down: And I will lay it waste”, and “I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.”

Israel is his vineyard, and this is the same desolation promised over Jerusalem for Manasseh’s wickedness: “I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.” What was done to Samaria reaches Judah. The hedge comes down, and the remnant of his inheritance becomes “a prey and a spoil to all their enemies.”
docs/study/2-kings/21.md|2 Kings 21:16-1:
“Wherefore the Lord brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon.”

The rest of the acts of Manasseh are written in the chronicles, and this is part of what Kings leaves out. The captains of the king of Assyria carried him bound to Babylon, which was then a province under Assyria. There he repented and prayed, and the prayer of Manasseh is recorded in the Apocrypha, prayed while he was held captive in Babylon.

It also shows the power struggle beginning, with Assyrian kings ruling over Babylon.

“In the twelfth year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor, who reigned in Nineve, the great city.”

Nebuchadnezzar, a Babylonian, reigns over the Assyrians in Nineveh. In Manasseh’s day the captains of the king of Assyria carried him to Babylon, then a province under Assyria. Later the order is turned: Babylonian kings rule over Assyria. Babylon is rising to take all that Assyria held.
docs/study/2-kings/22.md|2 Kings 22:8-13:
The law says, “if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee.”

This is the wrath Josiah heard when the book was read. Manasseh and Amon were so wicked that the very book of the law had been lost, until Hilkiah found it in the house of the Lord. The king was meant to read the law before all the people, and the wicked kings had not done it.

When Shaphan read it before him, Josiah rent his clothes and sent to inquire of the Lord, “for great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.” The curses were written concerning them, and they had come.
docs/study/2-kings/23.md|2 Kings 23:1-3|:
Josiah sent, saying, “Go ye, enquire of the Lord for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book.”

Having seen why the wrath was kindled, the king did what the fathers had not done. He stood by a pillar and made a covenant before the Lord “to walk after the Lord, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.”

The Lord answered, “Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read: Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods”, “therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched.”

That word stood behind the gathering. Knowing the evil written in the book was coming because they forsook him and burnt incense to other gods, Josiah read all the words of the book of the covenant in the ears of the people, and made the covenant to walk after the Lord and keep his commandments with all their heart and soul.

“And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.”

That found book is the book Josiah read to the nation. He gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets and all the people, small and great, “and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the Lord.” Our forefathers had the Bible, and the king read it openly.
docs/study/2-kings/23.md|2 Kings 23:10|J:
“The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin: To whom the word of the Lord came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.” It came also in the days of Jehoiakim, “unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month.”

Jeremiah was a prophet during this very time of reform. What he says about Topheth speaks to the same place Josiah defiled.

The Lord says, “they have built the high places of Tophet, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart.”

Topheth was the place where the people sacrificed their children. It had to be defiled because Israel would not stop the evil on its own, and Josiah “defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.”

And the Lord said what it would become: “it shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter: for they shall bury in Tophet, till there be no place. And the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.”
docs/study/2-kings/23.md|2 Kings 23:11-1:
“For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.” He “went not fully after the Lord, as did David his father. Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon.”

In his old age Solomon built these high places, and they stood until Josiah: “the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had builded for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Zidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon, did the king defile.”

Josiah tore down the corruption Solomon began. He broke the images, cut down the groves and filled their places with the bones of men. This is repentance in action: cleaning house, getting rid of every idol and evil that causes a people to go off from the Lord and fall under punishment.
docs/study/2-kings/23.md|2 Kings 23:15-1:
The man of God “cried against the altar in the word of the Lord, and said, O altar, altar, thus saith the Lord; Behold, a child shall be born unto the house of David, Josiah by name; and upon thee shall he offer the priests of the high places that burn incense upon thee, and men’s bones shall be burnt upon thee.”

He named Josiah before he was born. Now Josiah broke down the altar at Beth-el and the high place Jeroboam made when he set up the golden calves, burned it and stamped it small to powder. Turning himself, he spied the sepulchres, took out the bones, “and burned them upon the altar, and polluted it, according to the word of the Lord which the man of God proclaimed.”

When he learned which sepulchre belonged to the man of God who came from Judah and proclaimed these things, he said, “Let him alone; let no man move his bones.”
docs/study/2-kings/23.md|2 Kings 23:21-2:
“And Josias held the feast of the passover in Jerusalem unto his Lord, and offered the passover the fourteenth day of the first month.”

Josiah commanded all the people, “Keep the passover unto the Lord your God, as it is written in the book of this covenant”, and he kept it in its appointed time, the fourteenth day of the first month. Reading the book of the law brought the nation back to keeping the appointed feasts in order, just as the feast is kept in order today.

“And Jeconias, and Samaias, and Nathanael his brother, and Assabias, and Ochiel, and Joram, captains over thousands, gave to the Levites for the passover five thousand sheep, and seven hundred calves.”

The magnitude of the offering shows how great and well ordered this Passover was. “Surely there was not holden such a passover from the days of the judges that judged Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel, nor of the kings of Judah.”
docs/study/2-kings/23.md|2 Kings 23:4-5|:
“And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the Lord thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven.”

Israel was not to be driven to worship the sun, moon and stars, which the Lord divided to the other nations. Yet the kings of Judah ordained idolatrous priests, and there were those “that burned incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the host of heaven.” Josiah put them down.

Hearing the law cut him, just as a person is cut when they first hear the truth and realize what they have been doing wrong.

“The graven images of their gods shall ye burn with fire: thou shalt not desire the silver or gold that is on them”, “for it is an abomination to the Lord thy God. Neither shalt thou bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cursed thing like it.”

Judah had brought the abomination into the very house of the Lord: “all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven.” Josiah had them brought forth out of the temple, “and he burned them without Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron, and carried the ashes of them unto Beth–el.”

When Josiah read the law, the fear of the Lord came upon him and he saw why the nation was under judgment. He did what the law said to do with the cursed thing: burn it with fire and get it out of the house.
docs/study/2-kings/24.md|2 Kings 24:1-4|:
Jeremiah was told, “Set up the standard toward Zion: retire, stay not: for I will bring evil from the north, and a great destruction.” That evil from the north is the army of Babylon, the very bands the Lord sent against Judah.

In the days of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim served him three years and then turned and rebelled. So the Lord sent “bands of the Chaldees, and bands of the Syrians, and bands of the Moabites, and bands of the children of Ammon” against Judah “to destroy it, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by his servants the prophets.” The warning from the north was that word, now fulfilled.

It did not come by chance: “Surely at the commandment of the Lord came this upon Judah, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh”, and for the innocent blood he shed, “which the Lord would not pardon.” The Lord warned of a great destruction, and then he brought it.
docs/study/2-kings/24.md|2 Kings 24:13-1:
Isaiah told Hezekiah, “Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the Lord.”

Here it is fulfilled. Nebuchadnezzar “carried out thence all the treasures of the house of the Lord, and the treasures of the king’s house, and cut in pieces all the vessels of gold which Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the Lord, as the Lord had said.” The robbing of the temple is exactly what Isaiah prophesied: nothing left.

And not only the treasures. He carried away all Jerusalem, the princes, the mighty men of valour, ten thousand captives, “and all the craftsmen and smiths: none remained, save the poorest sort of the people of the land.” Jehoiachin, the king’s mother, his wives and his officers went to Babylon too. Babylon wanted the craftsmen and smiths to build for it what they had built in their own land, for conquering nations have always used Israel’s skill and industry.
docs/study/2-kings/24.md|2 Kings 24:17-2:
In “the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah”, when “the king of Babylon’s army besieged Jerusalem”, Jeremiah was “shut up in the court of the prison”. Zedekiah had shut him up for prophesying that the Lord would give the city into the hand of the king of Babylon.

Jeremiah warned him plainly: “Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes shall behold his eyes”. He would be led to Babylon, “and there shall he be until I visit him, saith the Lord: though ye fight with the Chaldeans, ye shall not prosper.”

That is the Zedekiah of this passage. The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s father’s brother, king in his stead and changed his name to Zedekiah. He reigned eleven years and “did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.” And “through the anger of the Lord” it came to pass that Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon, until the Lord had cast Judah out from his presence. He was warned, he rebelled anyway, and he could not prosper against the Chaldeans.
docs/study/2-kings/3.md|2 Kings 3:1-3|1:
Jehoram “cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin”. Here is that sin. Jeroboam “made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” He set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, “And this thing became a sin: for the people went to worship before the one, even unto Dan.”

Jehoram the son of Ahab wrought evil, “but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made.” He put away Baal, but not the calves. The house of Ahab had reared up images and led the kingdom into idolatry, and even the son who took down Baal “departed not therefrom”: he held on to Jeroboam’s golden calves, the sin that made Israel to sin.
docs/study/2-kings/3.md|2 Kings 3:20-25|:
“The Lord shall cause thine enemies that rise up against thee to be smitten before thy face: they shall come out against thee one way, and flee before thee seven ways.” That is the promise to Israel when the nation keeps his commandments, and here it is in the field against Moab.

The Moabites came out one way. Rising early, they saw the sun on the water “as red as blood” and said, “This is blood: the kings are surely slain, and they have smitten one another: now therefore, Moab, to the spoil.” They ran toward the camp expecting to gather the plunder of dead men. Instead “the Israelites rose up and smote the Moabites, so that they fled before them”, and Israel went forward smiting them even into their own country, beating down the cities, stopping the wells and felling the good trees.

This is a testament to how great a people Israel was when the hand of the Lord was with them. When Israel was in its right mind and its prayers went forth, the Lord fought for them and their enemies were smitten before their face. That is part of why the heathen nations, and Moab in particular, have hated Israel to this day.
docs/study/2-kings/4.md|2 Kings 4:8-17|G:
Abraham and Sarah “were old and well stricken in age”, and “Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” The Lord answered, “Is any thing too hard for the Lord? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.”

The Shunammite stands where our mother Sarah stood. She was a great woman who fed the man of God and made him a little chamber on the wall, and Elisha wanted to bless her: “thou hast been careful for us with all this care; what is to be done for thee?” She had no child, and her husband was old. When Elisha told her, “About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son”, she did not believe it, just like Sarah: “Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid.” The same words, “according to the time of life”, are in both promises.

And the same answer holds: nothing is too hard for the Lord. Sarah had her son, and “the woman conceived, and bare a son at that season that Elisha had said unto her, according to the time of life.”
docs/study/2-kings/5.md|2 Kings 5:25-27|:
“To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:” everything has its time, receiving included.

Gehazi went in and stood before his master, and when Elisha asked, “Whence comest thou, Gehazi?” he answered, “Thy servant went no whither.” Elisha said, “Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards, and sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and maidservants?” It was not the season for it.

Because Gehazi took in a time that was not the time to receive, “The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever.” He went out from Elisha’s presence “a leper as white as snow.”

“A time to get, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;” That is what Elisha explained to Gehazi: there was a time to receive the gifts, and this was not it.

Gehazi was hasty to grasp. He lied to his master, but Elisha’s heart went with him, and for taking out of season the leprosy of Naaman cleaved to him and to his seed for ever.

This shows how Israel thought then, and how the nation still thinks now: hasty to grasp things by unjust means instead of waiting for the time to get.
docs/study/2-kings/6.md|2 Kings 6:13-17|:
“The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.” That is what the young man saw when his eyes were opened.

The king of Syria sent “horses, and chariots, and a great host” by night to Dothan to fetch Elisha, and they compassed the city about. The servant rose early, saw the host, and cried, “Alas, my master! how shall we do?” Elisha answered, “Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” He prayed, “Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see”, and “behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.”

Round about the man of God, just as the psalm says the angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him. When Israel goes out to war, there is more with them than with their enemies, for the angels of the Lord are with them.
docs/study/2-kings/6.md|2 Kings 6:24-31|:
“And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the Lord thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee:” That is the curse on a disobedient Israel, and in Samaria it came to pass.

Ben-hadad king of Syria besieged Samaria, and the famine was so great that “an ass’s head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver.” A woman cried to the king on the wall and told him, “This woman said unto me, Give thy son, that we may eat him to day, and we will eat my son to morrow. So we boiled my son, and did eat him”. The next day the other woman hid her son.

The siege, the straitness, the enemy distressing them, and mothers eating the flesh of their sons: the curse fulfilled. The king had no help to give, “If the Lord do not help thee, whence shall I help thee?” He rent his clothes, the people saw “he had sackcloth within upon his flesh”, and he swore that the head of Elisha would not stand on him that day.
docs/study/2-kings/8.md|2 Kings 8:20-24|:
Isaac told Esau, “Behold, I have made him thy lord, and all his brethren have I given to him for servants”. Esau lifted up his voice and wept for a blessing, and Isaac answered, “by thy sword shalt thou live, and shalt serve thy brother; and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck.”

Edom is Esau. From the days of David and Solomon, Edom had been in subjection to Judah, serving his brother. Then in Jehoram’s days “Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah, and made a king over themselves.” Joram went over to Zair and smote the Edomites that compassed him about, “Yet Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah unto this day.”

That revolt is the word spoken to Esau fulfilled: when he gained the dominion, he broke the yoke from off his neck. It is a pattern that reaches all the way to Edom’s later rise.
docs/study/2-samuel/1.md|2 Samuel 1:11-1:
“And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the Lord your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.”

When the news came, “David took hold on his clothes, and rent them; and likewise all the men that were with him”, and they mourned, wept and fasted until even for Saul, for Jonathan, “and for the house of Israel; because they were fallen by the sword.” The renting of garments was the sign of mourning.

But the Most High looks for a rent heart and not rent garments only. True repentance is inward, not just an outward show, and it is the heart turned unto the Lord that he is looking for.
docs/study/2-samuel/1.md|2 Samuel 1:17-2:
“A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.” So was Jonathan to David, knit at the soul.

David cried, “I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.” Jonathan was that friend closer than a brother.

The lament is a prophecy given in the spirit, almost a eulogy: “Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions.” Before the devil jumped on Saul he was good, and the two of them were good together. And they died only when the Most High said it was time; that is the only way any of Israel’s forefathers died.

“Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.” That is how Israel fights in the last days: with the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus, not the bow or the gun.

David taught the children of Judah the use of the bow in his day, but the redemption of Israel does not come by force of arms. This is spiritual war and not physical, and the saints hold it with patience, keeping the commandments and the faith.

“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.”

David “bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow”, and his lament is “written in the book of Jasher.” The book of Jasher is not in the canon because the Most High did not will us to have it; he put in the book exactly what he wanted his people to read in the last days.

And the bow is not how this walk goes in the last days. It is not by might nor by power, but by the Spirit of the Lord. The captivity is not overthrown by rising up with the bow or the gun; this is spiritual war and not physical. There is nothing wrong with knowing how to defend yourself, but the redemption of Israel does not come by force of arms.
docs/study/2-samuel/1.md|2 Samuel 1:5-10:
“And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau’s son; and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek”. Amalek came of Eliphaz the son of Esau, so the Amalekites are the seed of Esau.

That is who came to David from mount Gilboa. The young man said Saul asked him who he was, “And I answered him, I am an Amalekite.” He told how he found Saul leaning upon his spear with the chariots and horsemen following hard after him, and Saul said, “Stand, I pray thee, upon me, and slay me: for anguish is come upon me”. So he slew him, “and I took the crown that was upon his head, and the bracelet that was on his arm”, and brought them to David. In the earlier account Saul fell upon his sword but did not die at that moment.

Their lineage is written in Genesis, and it is a thing to know when reading of Israel’s enemies: the Amalekite standing over Saul was of the seed of Esau.
docs/study/2-samuel/10.md|2 Samuel 10:1-:
“Then Nahash the Ammonite came up, and encamped against Jabesh–gilead”. When the men of Jabesh asked him for a covenant, he answered, “On this condition will I make a covenant with you, that I may thrust out all your right eyes, and lay it for a reproach upon all Israel.”

That is the Nahash whose son Hanun now reigned over the children of Ammon. David said, “I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me”, and sent his servants to comfort him for his father.

Remember who the children of Ammon were. They had been warring with Israel, and they got smashed and put under tribute back in the days of Saul.
docs/study/2-samuel/10.md|2 Samuel 10:6|:
David had already dedicated unto the Lord “the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued; Of Syria, and of Moab, and of the children of Ammon, and of the Philistines, and of Amalek, and of the spoil of Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah.”

So when “the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David” and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob and of Zoba, of king Maacah and of Ish-tob, they were calling on nations David had already subdued. Syria, Ammon, Rehob and Zobah are all in that list of the spoil.

Once they saw David did not like what happened, they knew David was a man of war and Israel a people of war, so they sought help. They simply tried to get the men who had always been beefing with Israel to come against Israel yet again.
docs/study/2-samuel/10.md|2 Samuel 10:7-:
“They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks:”

That is Joab at the gate of Ammon. With the children of Ammon in array at the entering in of the gate and the Syrians by themselves in the field, “the front of the battle was against him before and behind”. So he chose of all the choice men of Israel against the Syrians and gave the rest into the hand of Abishai his brother against Ammon: “If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will come and help thee.”

This is how much of a warrior nation Israel is: Joab put his troops in a battle array to fight two enemies at one time. That warrior mentality is already etched inside us. We just have to keep the commandments so it can come back out, as it is going to according to Joel 2.
docs/study/2-samuel/11.md|2 Samuel 11:14:
“Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly. And all the people shall say, Amen. Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person.”

David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah himself: “Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.” Joab assigned him to a place where he knew valiant men were, “and Uriah the Hittite died also.”

David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. He smote his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing. And he took reward to slay an innocent person: the reward was that woman, and he slew an innocent man who had done nothing. Both curses fall on this deed.
docs/study/2-samuel/12.md|2 Samuel 12:13:
The Most High is “Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children”.

David confessed, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan answered, “The Lord also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die.”

That is both halves of Exodus 34:7. David got pardoned, but he did not get cleared. The punishment was still coming: one part the men of Israel dying in battle, the other his son having to die and his house having nothing but trouble. The judgment of David was that child being put to death.
docs/study/2-samuel/12.md|2 Samuel 12:24:
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.”

David’s sorrow was godly sorrow, and it worked repentance. Through the judgment, “David comforted Bath–sheba his wife”, and she bare a son, “and he called his name Solomon: and the Lord loved him.” The Lord sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, who called his name Jedidiah, “because of the Lord.”

David was still loved and still forgiven, and that shows repentance. Through David’s judgment Solomon was still able to be born; it was all part of the plan of the Most High. The backup master plan behind everything was Christ, who still had to be born through David’s lineage.

“For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.”

David fell, and he rose up again. He was judged, he repented, and the Lord still loved him and gave him Solomon, whom Nathan called Jedidiah because of the Lord. Even the mighty among us can fall and yet rise back up.

“My flesh trembleth for fear of thee; and I am afraid of thy judgments.”

David had felt the judgment of the Most High. He was pardoned, but the child that was born to him surely died, as Nathan said. His repentance was not a light thing; it came from a man afraid of the Lord’s judgments. Out of that repentance Solomon was born, and the Lord loved him.
docs/study/2-samuel/13.md|2 Samuel 13:12:
“But if a man find a betrothed damsel in the field, and the man force her, and lie with her: then the man only that lay with her shall die: But unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing; there is in the damsel no sin worthy of death: for as when a man riseth against his neighbour, and slayeth him, even so is this matter:”

Tamar told Amnon, “Nay, my brother, do not force me; for no such thing ought to be done in Israel: do not thou this folly.” She herself calls it folly, a sin, a thing that ought not to be done in Israel. “Howbeit he would not hearken unto her voice: but, being stronger than she, forced her, and lay with her.”

The law settles it: the man who forces a damsel is worthy of death, and there is no sin in her. Any man talking about forcing a woman is wicked. This shows plainly from the scriptures that rape is not good in the Bible. It is the same as murder.
docs/study/2-samuel/14.md|2 Samuel 14:4-:
“The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer: when he meeteth him, he shall slay him.”

That is the law the woman of Tekoah built her story on. Joab had her act as a widow whose two sons “strove together in the field, and there was none to part them, but the one smote the other, and slew him.” Now the whole family said, “Deliver him that smote his brother, that we may kill him, for the life of his brother whom he slew”. By that law they would slay her last son and “quench my coal which is left”, leaving her husband “neither name nor remainder upon the earth.”

She knew, as Joab knew, that David was merciful, so she framed it around the revenger of blood to draw out his mercy. She asked the king “that thou wouldest not suffer the revengers of blood to destroy any more, lest they destroy my son”, and David swore, “As the Lord liveth, there shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth.”
docs/study/2-samuel/15.md|2 Samuel 15:30:
“And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.”

That is why it mattered when “one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David, weeping as he went up mount Olivet, prayed, “O Lord, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”

And he did not stop at praying. He sent his friend Hushai the Archite back to the city to say unto Absalom, “I will be thy servant, O king”, so he could hear Ahithophel’s counsel and intervene: “then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.” Everything he heard would go to Zadok and Abiathar the priests and on to David by their two sons. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.
docs/study/2-samuel/16.md|2 Samuel 16:20:
“For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.”

What came on David from Absalom and Ahithophel came for his own faults, as the Most High spoke in chapter 12; none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. There is no glory in being buffeted for your faults. The suffering that is acceptable with God is to do well, suffer for it, and take it patiently.

The Most High told David by Nathan, “Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun. For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.”

Here it is. Ahithophel counselled Absalom, “Go in unto thy father’s concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father”. So “they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.” The ten concubines David left, on the roof of the house, in the sight of the sun.

This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen. What David did secretly was done before all Israel, by evil raised up out of his own house, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did.

He is “Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children”.

David repented and was forgiven, yet the judgment spoken in chapter 12 still came to pass on the roof of his own house, when his son went in unto his concubines in the sight of all Israel. The Most High keeps mercy and forgives, but by no means clears the guilty.

So even when we come in and repent, we still must remember the fear of the Most High, for there is but one step between us and death.
docs/study/2-samuel/17.md|2 Samuel 17:1-:
Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give counsel among you what we shall do.” Ahithophel answered, “Go in unto thy father’s concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.” That was already wicked counsel, before he ever asked for twelve thousand men.

Ahithophel was David’s own counselor turned traitor, being the devil the Bible speaks of, working deceit and betrayal from inside the gates of Israel. And “the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.” That tells you he was very influential and had the gift of gab, so persuasive that his advice sounded almost biblical.

So when he said, “Let me now choose out twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David this night”, to come upon him “while he is weary and weak handed” and “smite the king only”, Absalom was hearing it from the man everyone listened to. He wanted the victory and the bragging rights of being the one who killed King David.

“Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war.”

The Most High’s own people rise up as an enemy. Ahithophel was David’s own counselor, working betrayal from inside the gates of Israel, and here he asks to pursue David that same night and smite the king only.

The enemies Christ said to forgive are the enemies of our people.
docs/study/2-samuel/17.md|2 Samuel 17:15:
This is a Psalm of David when he fled from Absalom his son: “Lord, how are they increased that trouble me! many are they that rise up against me. Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God.” But “thou, O Lord, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.”

That is this night. Hushai sent word by Zadok and Abiathar: “Lodge not this night in the plains of the wilderness, but speedily pass over; lest the king be swallowed up, and all the people that are with him.” Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited by En-rogel and a wench carried the word to them. A lad saw them and told Absalom, so they hid in a well in a man’s house in Bahurim, and a woman spread a covering over the well’s mouth and ground corn upon it to camouflage it. She told Absalom’s servants, “They be gone over the brook of water”, and the pursuers returned to Jerusalem.

The Most High put his spirit on certain people to orchestrate his plan. Often when a man tries to do evil to another, it falls back on him, for he that diggeth a pit shall fall therein.

“I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the Lord sustained me. I will not be afraid of ten thousands of people, that have set themselves against me round about.” David arose and all the people with him passed over Jordan, and “by the morning light there lacked not one of them that was not gone over Jordan.” “Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: thy blessing is upon thy people.”
docs/study/2-samuel/17.md|2 Samuel 17:23:
“All unrighteousness is sin”. To be unrighteous is to not keep the commandments, and sin is the transgression of the law.

Ahithophel walked in unrighteousness, and his own evil pursued him to the end: he put his household in order, “and hanged himself, and died, and was buried in the sepulchre of his father.”

“And it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments before the Lord our God, as he hath commanded us.”

That is what it means to be righteous: to observe to do all the commandments of the Lord. So when the scripture says good shall be repaid to the righteous, this is who it means. David was righteous and good was repaid to him, while Ahithophel the sinner was pursued by his own evil until he hanged himself.

“Evil pursueth sinners: but to the righteous good shall be repayed.”

When Ahithophel “saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, and arose, and gat him home to his house, to his city, and put his household in order, and hanged himself, and died”. The evil counsel he devised reared its head around and bit its author. Evil pursued the sinner.

And to the righteous good was repaid. David did not want to war against his own son, yet good was repaid to him, while Ahithophel was pursued by his own evil.
docs/study/2-samuel/17.md|2 Samuel 17:5-:
“But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him.” Promotion comes from the Most High, not from a man taking the seat himself.

Absalom tried to take the seat, stealing the hearts of Israel at the gate and rising up against his own father. But God sets the members in the body as it pleases him, and he had not set Absalom on that throne. That is why the counsel that would have won it for him was defeated, and evil came upon Absalom instead.

Absalom “prepared him chariots and horses, and fifty men to run before him”, stood beside the way of the gate, and told every man who came to the king for judgment, “See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.” Then he said, “Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!” So he stole the hearts of the men of Israel at the gate.

That is how Absalom came to be sitting with Ahithophel and Hushai, asking how to take his father. He took the seat himself. But the Lord was not with him: the Lord was working with Hushai and David, while Satan was in the spirit of Absalom and Ahithophel.

When David came to the top of the mount, Hushai the Archite met him “with his coat rent, and earth upon his head”. David sent him back: “if thou return to the city, and say unto Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; as I have been thy father’s servant hitherto, so will I now also be thy servant: then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.” Whatever he heard out of the king’s house he was to tell Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and send to David by their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan. The name Hushai means loyal to the king.

That is the man Absalom called when he wanted a second opinion: “Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he saith.” Hushai was a counterintelligence agent, a spy planted in righteousness, always siding with King David.

So he told Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel hath given is not good at this time.” He reminded him that his father and his men were mighty men, “chafed in their minds, as a bear robbed of her whelps in the field”, war ready and strategic, and that David “will not lodge with the people” but moves by night. He warned that if some were overthrown at the first, even he “whose heart is as the heart of a lion, shall utterly melt”, for all Israel knew David was a mighty man. David and his mighty men were on another level; none of Absalom’s thousands could compare to them.

Then he counselled that all Israel be gathered “from Dan even to Beer–sheba, as the sand that is by the sea for multitude”, with Absalom going to battle in his own person. It was deliberately inaccurate counsel that would waste time gathering troops and give David room to escape. Hushai did exactly what David sent him back to do: he defeated the counsel of Ahithophel.

“There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand.”

Ahithophel had his device and Hushai had his. “And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” But it was not Absalom’s choosing that decided it: “For the Lord had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the Lord might bring evil upon Absalom.” The counsel of the Lord stood.

There is safety in a multitude of counselors, but only where the counsel is according to thus saith the Lord. A counselor who does not go to the scriptures is not one you should want.
docs/study/2-samuel/18.md|2 Samuel 18:6-:
At “the time when kings go forth to battle”, David sent Joab out against the children of Ammon, “But David tarried still at Jerusalem.” From the roof he saw Bath-sheba, sent and took her, and when she was with child, “David sent to Joab, saying, Send me Uriah the Hittite. And Joab sent Uriah to David.”

Joab was David’s nephew and the go between in the matter of Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah. Joab knew David’s dirt, which is why he often defied the king’s orders.

And here he defied them. The man who saw Absalom hanged in an oak would not touch him for a thousand shekels, “for in our hearing the king charged thee and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Beware that none touch the young man Absalom.” Joab said, “I may not tarry thus with thee”, took three darts, “and thrust them through the heart of Absalom, while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.”

Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder. He could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bare Joab’s armour compassed about and smote Absalom and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.
docs/study/2-samuel/19.md|2 Samuel 19:16:
When king David came to Bahurim, Shimei the son of Gera, of the family of the house of Saul, “came forth, and cursed still as he came. And he cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David: and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.” He cried, “Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial”.

That was David in a low state, fleeing Jerusalem, surrounded by his mighty men, and Shimei cursed him to his face. Now the king was coming back, and the same Shimei hasted down with a thousand men of Benjamin and fell down before him at Jordan: “Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem”. He confessed, “For thy servant doth know that I have sinned”.

Abishai said, “Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?” But David rebuked the sons of Zeruiah as adversaries: “shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? for do not I know that I am this day king over Israel?” He said to Shimei, “Thou shalt not die”, and swore it. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.
docs/study/2-samuel/19.md|2 Samuel 19:31:
Eleazar said, “it becometh not our age, said he, in any wise to dissemble, whereby many young persons might think that Eleazar, being fourscore years old and ten, were now gone to a strange religion”. Eleazar was a very aged man, being fourscore years and ten.

Like Barzillai at fourscore, Eleazar at fourscore and ten is counted very aged, far short of the hundred and twenty years the Most High first set. The Lord kept cutting our lifespan down because of sin.

“And the Lord said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.” The Most High set man’s days at a hundred and twenty years.

Barzillai the Gileadite was “a very aged man, even fourscore years old”. At eighty he asked, “How long have I to live, that I should go up with the king unto Jerusalem?” He could no longer taste what he ate or drank, nor hear “the voice of singing men and singing women”. He would go only a little way over Jordan, and asked to turn back, “that I may die in mine own city, and be buried by the grave of my father and of my mother.”

Man’s days were set at a hundred and twenty years, yet at fourscore Barzillai was already very aged and ready to die.

“The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.” A man is very aged at seventy and eighty.

Barzillai was fourscore, the span given by reason of strength, and his strength was labour and sorrow: “can I discern between good and evil? can thy servant taste what I eat or what I drink? can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women?” He would not be a burden to the king, so he sent Chimham over with David in his place, and the king kissed him and blessed him, and he returned unto his own place.
docs/study/2-samuel/2.md|2 Samuel 2:12-2:
“The Lord is a man of war: the Lord is his name.”

At the pool of Gibeon, Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men now arise, and play before us. And Joab said, Let them arise.” To play there means to compete and battle one another. The Lord is a man of war, and contests of strength like this were known among his people and done in that day.

Twelve of Benjamin and twelve of David’s servants “caught every one his fellow by the head, and thrust his sword in his fellow’s side; so they fell down together”, and that place was called Helkath-hazzurim. Then “there was a very sore battle that day; and Abner was beaten, and the men of Israel, before the servants of David.”

Asahel, “as light of foot as a wild roe”, meaning he was fast, pursued Abner and would not turn aside, though Abner warned him again and again: “wherefore should I smite thee to the ground? how then should I hold up my face to Joab thy brother?” When he refused, Abner smote him “with the hinder end of the spear” under the fifth rib, “that the spear came out behind him”. A strong thrust is needed to drive a spear through a man, and Abner was strong. As many as came to the place stood still. The lesson is to take heed to the warning and not keep testing a man.
docs/study/2-samuel/21.md|2 Samuel 21:1-:
“When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.” And “neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error”.

That is the lesson of the famine. It lasted “three years, year after year”, and when David enquired, “the Lord answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.” The Gibeonites “were not of the children of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites; and the children of Israel had sworn unto them”, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal. Saul broke his word.

David asked, “wherewith shall I make the atonement, that ye may bless the inheritance of the Lord?” The blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through this famine. They would have “no silver nor gold of Saul, nor of his house”, but asked for seven of his sons to hang up unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul. Saul did not pay what was vowed, and the whole house paid for it.

“But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.” Christ simplified it.

Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay. Saul went back on his word after he had given his yea to the Amorites, and the Lord sent three years of famine for it, until seven of Saul’s sons were given up to be hanged unto the Lord. The lesson the Most High is teaching Israel here is to pay what you vow.
docs/study/2-samuel/21.md|2 Samuel 21:15:
“It is God that girdeth me with strength, and maketh my way perfect. He maketh my feet like hinds’ feet, and setteth me upon my high places. He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.” That is the strength the Most High gave David in his youth.

Now David was getting up in age. The Philistines had war again with Israel, “and David waxed faint.” Ishbi-benob, of the sons of the giant, “thought to have slain David. But Abishai the son of Zeruiah succoured him, and smote the Philistine, and killed him.” Then David’s men swore, “Thou shalt go no more out with us to battle, that thou quench not the light of Israel.” It was time for him to sit on the throne.

His servants finished the work. At Gob and at Gath the sons of the giant fell: Sibbechai the Hushathite slew one, Elhanan slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite, “the staff of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam”, and Jonathan the son of Shimea, David’s brother, slew a man of great stature “that had on every hand six fingers, and on every foot six toes”. These were tall men, one about eight or nine feet, not the twenty foot giants of fairy tales. Goliath had kin, and “These four were born to the giant in Gath, and fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants.”
docs/study/2-samuel/22.md|2 Samuel 22:1-:
“Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.”

David sang this song “in the day that the Lord had delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies, and out of the hand of Saul”: “The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; The God of my rock; in him will I trust”. He called the Lord his shield, the horn of his salvation, his high tower, his refuge and his saviour: “thou savest me from violence.”

This is heavy. Like Judas Maccabee, Simon, Jonathan and all our forefathers, the first thing David did in trouble was turn to the Most High. They trusted in God and not in man. Today many of our people have it backwards: they trust in a vote and in man, and then call on God.
docs/study/2-samuel/22.md|2 Samuel 22:17:
“Go not after thy lusts, but refrain thyself from thine appetites.” David kept himself back from his iniquity all his days.

That is what he meant when he sang, “I was also upright before him, and have kept myself from mine iniquity.” He refrained himself and held back his flesh, and the Lord recompensed him for it.

“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble. Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.”

David sang, “The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness: according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me. For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not wickedly departed from my God.” All the Lord’s judgments were before him, and he did not depart from his statutes. His hands were clean, and the Lord delivered him.

Submit to God, resist the devil, draw nigh to God, cleanse your hands and purify your hearts: that is the very thing we need in these last days.

“The Lord said, Verily it shall be well with thy remnant; verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well in the time of evil and in the time of affliction.” The Most High delivers those he delights in.

David sang, “He delivered me from my strong enemy, and from them that hated me: for they were too strong for me. They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the Lord was my stay.” And, “He brought me forth also into a large place: he delivered me, because he delighted in me.”

The enemy was too strong for David, but in the time of evil the Lord was his stay and his help. When your ways please the Lord, he will deliver you.

“For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again”. That is what David did after his fall.

David held back his flesh. The one time it overtook him he was judged, and he got right back on track, for a righteous man falls and rises again. So he could still sing, “Therefore the Lord hath recompensed me according to my righteousness; according to my cleanness in his eye sight.”
docs/study/2-samuel/22.md|2 Samuel 22:26:
“I will go and return to my place, till they acknowledge their offence, and seek my face: in their affliction they will seek me early.” The afflicted people is Israel.

David sang, “And the afflicted people thou wilt save: but thine eyes are upon the haughty, that thou mayest bring them down.” Israel is the people the Most High leaves in affliction till they acknowledge their offence and seek his face, and it is the afflicted people he saves.

“For thou art my lamp, O Lord: and the Lord will lighten my darkness. For by thee I have run through a troop”: a troop is a body of some two hundred men or more.

“For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.”

David sang, “With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful, and with the upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright. With the pure thou wilt shew thyself pure; and with the froward thou wilt shew thyself unsavoury.” What a man soweth, that shall he reap.

We all need mercy, so we must show mercy to one another, forgiving and not bearing grudges, that the Lord be merciful with us in the day of judgment. And we rejoice when mercy is extended in the day we deserved punishment.
docs/study/2-samuel/22.md|2 Samuel 22:31:
“But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.” That is what Israel did.

David knew where his strength came from: “God is my strength and power: and he maketh my way perfect.” This is what Israel forgot. We waxed fat and kicked, forgot the Most High and where our strength came from, and began to say we are lords ourselves.

But our strength comes from the Most High, who is merciful enough to let us take a breath and blink our eyes every moment.

“As is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel. He played with lions as with kids, and with bears as with lambs. Slew he not a giant, when he was yet but young?” And “he called upon the most high Lord; and he gave him strength in his right hand to slay that mighty warrior, and set up the horn of his people.”

That is the man who sang, “He teacheth my hands to war; so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.” Not bent, but broken. David knew a lion and a bear were nothing to a man trained by the Most High.

The Most High made David’s feet “like hinds’ feet” and set him upon high places. He gave him “the shield of thy salvation: and thy gentleness hath made me great.” His repentance enlarged his steps, “so that my feet did not slip.”

“For the Lord is great, and greatly to be praised: he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the Lord made the heavens.” There is no other God.

David sang, “As for God, his way is perfect; the word of the Lord is tried: he is a buckler to all them that trust in him. For who is God, save the Lord? and who is a rock, save our God?” A buckler is a shield. There is no other God save the Lord, and no rock save our God.

This is the answer to the Muslims and Negroes practicing Islam who try to make this rock into a cobblestone. It is talking about the Most High God of Israel, not a stone. The gods of the nations are idols; the Lord made the heavens.
docs/study/2-samuel/22.md|2 Samuel 22:47:
“And that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom, that they are double to that which is! Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth.” The secrets of wisdom are double to that which is: the scriptures often carry a double meaning, speaking of that time and of what is to come.

David’s song is twofold, and David is prophesying. “It is God that avengeth me, and that bringeth down the people under me, And that bringeth me forth from mine enemies”: it speaks of David in that moment and of us who are yet to come.

And God exacteth of us less than our iniquity deserves. The Most High requires of us far less: to repent, keep the commandments, and keep the faith in his son Jesus the Christ. For this David gives thanks “among the heathen” and sings praises unto his name, for “He is the tower of salvation for his king: and sheweth mercy to his anointed, unto David, and to his seed for evermore.”
docs/study/2-samuel/22.md|2 Samuel 22:8-:
“Son of man, thou dwellest in the midst of a rebellious house, which have eyes to see, and see not; they have ears to hear, and hear not: for they are a rebellious house.”

That is why we cannot understand the Lord’s voice in the thunder. The Lord thunders from heaven and the Most High utters his voice, but we dwell in the midst of a rebellious house, with ears to hear that hear not. We no longer have that spirit upon us, so his voice sounds like clouds clashing, the way Esau tells it.

“He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his discretion. When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens”, and “he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures.”

David sang, “The Lord thundered from heaven, and the most High uttered his voice. And he sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them.” What we hear as thunder is the Most High speaking. Esau says the thunder is only clouds clashing; the scripture says it is the voice of the Lord, and after his voice there is a multitude of waters, meaning the rain that follows.

The one who made the earth by his power rules all of it: “the channels of the sea appeared, the foundations of the world were discovered, at the rebuking of the Lord, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.” His power over creation is total.

Christ prayed, “Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again. The people therefore, that stood by, and heard it, said that it thundered: others said, An angel spake to him. Jesus answered and said, This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes.”

The people heard the voice of the Father and called it thunder. That shows the thunder is the Most High speaking, just as David sang, “The Lord thundered from heaven, and the most High uttered his voice.” We hear it, but we cannot comprehend it because we no longer have that spirit upon us.

“And the Lord came down in the pillar of the cloud, and stood in the door of the tabernacle, and called Aaron and Miriam”. He came down in a cloud to speak, just as David describes.

David sang, “He bowed the heavens also, and came down; and darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: and he was seen upon the wings of the wind. And he made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies.” That is how the Most High travels, shielded in the darkness of the cloud, the same way he came down and spoke to Moses face to face.
docs/study/2-samuel/23.md|2 Samuel 23:1-:
“Hear therefore, O ye kings, and understand; learn, ye that be judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, ye that rule the people, and glory in the multitude of nations. For power is given you of the Lord, and sovereignty from the Highest, who shall try your works, and search out your counsels.”

In his last words David says, “The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake to me, He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God.” Rulers hold a small power from the Most High until the King comes, and the Highest will try their works and search out their counsels. So the one who rules must be just in his judgments, in the fear of the Most High. This is how you are a great leader.

And such a ruler “shall be as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth, even a morning without clouds; as the tender grass springing out of the earth by clear shining after rain.”

David could say this because “The Spirit of the Lord spake by me, and his word was in my tongue.” David was a prophet, the sweet psalmist of Israel, and the book of Psalms are songs of prophecy.
docs/study/2-samuel/24.md|2 Samuel 24:1-:
The same story told in Chronicles names who stood behind the numbering: “And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.” Second Samuel says the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel and “he moved David against them”; Chronicles says Satan provoked him. Both are true.

The Most High wanted to judge Israel, and he used Satan to provoke David to do it. That is how he accomplished his judgment. The numbering was not the king's job but the work of the Levites, which is why Joab asked, “why doth my lord the king delight in this thing?”

Notwithstanding, “the king’s word prevailed against Joab”, and the captains went out to number the people. Joab did not see what was behind it all: verse one, “the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel.” It was of the Most High that this happened.
docs/study/2-samuel/4.md|2 Samuel 4:9-12:
“Let all things be done decently and in order.” Rechab and Baanah slew Ish-bosheth in his own house upon his bed, a man at rest, asleep. It was not even a man-to-man contest for the kingdom. That is not how the Most High brings his purpose to pass, and he is not the author of vengeance taken out of order.

The Most High has his own way of doing things, and his people are not to put the cart before the horse. The kingdom was coming to David, but not by murder done in his name.

So David asked, “shall I not therefore now require his blood of your hand, and take you away from the earth?” They were slain, their hands and feet cut off, and they were hanged up over the pool in Hebron, while the head of Ish-bosheth was buried in the sepulchre of Abner. They received judgment for taking a man's life that was not ordained of the Lord nor commanded by the king. This is why David is called a man after the Most High's own heart: he did not accept wickedness done in his name or let the murderers slide.

David was the same at the end of his life. He charged Solomon concerning Joab: “thou knowest also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, and what he did to the two captains of the hosts of Israel, unto Abner the son of Ner, and unto Amasa the son of Jether, whom he slew, and shed the blood of war in peace.”

Joab shed blood out of order, in a time of peace, just as Rechab and Baanah slew a righteous person upon his bed. So David said, “Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace.” The doer of evil was rewarded according to his wickedness.

David never let blood shed wickedly slide, not in Ish-bosheth's day and not in Joab's. The same man who slew the messenger in Ziklag, and who hanged Rechab and Baanah over the pool in Hebron, required Joab's blood through his son.
docs/study/2-samuel/5.md|2 Samuel 5:1-5|:
When the tribes came to Hebron they said, “Also in time past, when Saul was king over us, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel.” This is where that began: “Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house.”

Saul made David his armourbearer and captain of his host. So even while Saul was king, David was the one leading Israel out to war and bringing them in, and the people remembered it when they came to make him king over all Israel.

“And David went out whithersoever Saul sent him, and behaved himself wisely: and Saul set him over the men of war, and he was accepted in the sight of all the people.”

That is what the tribes meant when they said David was the one “that leddest out and broughtest in Israel.” Saul set him over the men of war, and David fought many wars. The Lord had already said to him, “Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be a captain over Israel.” He was a captain before he was a king.

So when all the elders came to Hebron and anointed him king over Israel, it was the people who had already accepted him in their sight making it official over the whole nation.

“And the women answered one another as they played, and said, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”

David had fame among the people while Saul was still king. That is why the tribes could say, “Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh”: we are kinsmen, related to thee, and we know thee. They remembered the man who led them out and brought them in.

So all the elders came to the king to Hebron, and “they anointed David king over Israel.” He was thirty years old, a young man, and he reigned forty years: seven years and six months over Judah in Hebron, and thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem.
docs/study/2-samuel/5.md|2 Samuel 5:17-2:
At Baal-perazim “they left their images, and David and his men burned them.” David knew the law: “The graven images of their gods shall ye burn with fire: thou shalt not desire the silver or gold that is on them, nor take it unto thee, lest thou be snared therein: for it is an abomination to the Lord thy God.”

He did not keep the Philistines' gods as spoil or desire the silver and gold on them. He burned them, exactly as the law commanded, lest a man be snared by them.

The law goes on: “Neither shalt thou bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cursed thing like it: but thou shalt utterly detest it, and thou shalt utterly abhor it; for it is a cursed thing.”

That is why David and his men burned the images the Philistines left behind. To carry them home would have brought an abomination into the house and made a man a cursed thing like it. David knew the law and kept it, even in the heat of victory.

“The Lord is a man of war: the Lord is his name.” When the Philistines came up to seek David, he did not go to war on his own strength. He enquired of the Lord, “Shall I go up to the Philistines? wilt thou deliver them into mine hand?” He knew where his power lay.

The Lord answered, “Go up: for I will doubtless deliver the Philistines into thine hand.” And when David smote them he gave the Lord the victory: “The Lord hath broken forth upon mine enemies before me, as the breach of waters.” So he called the place Baal-perazim.

The Philistines had already lost their champion Goliath, and still they came to challenge this man. But the victory was the Lord's, because the Lord is a man of war. No war did Israel win alone.
docs/study/2-samuel/5.md|2 Samuel 5:22-2:
“And all people of the earth shall see that thou art called by the name of the Lord; and they shall be afraid of thee.”

That was the blessing on Israel when they obeyed, and it was on David. He did “as the Lord had commanded him”, and the Lord went out before him. The nations that came against him saw a people called by the name of the Lord, and they were smitten and afraid.

“The Lord shall cause thine enemies that rise up against thee to be smitten before thy face: they shall come out against thee one way, and flee before thee seven ways.”

The Philistines rose up against David twice in the valley of Rephaim, and twice the Lord caused them to be smitten before him. The second time the Lord himself went out before David, and the host was smitten from Geba to Gazer. David knew this promise from the law, and because he knew it, he knew the Lord was his power source.

“And I will give peace in the land, and ye shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid: and I will rid evil beasts out of the land, neither shall the sword go through your land.”

The Philistines came up yet again and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim. The Most High hardened the hearts of the nations, so it was of God that they came back. But David was not afraid, because he meditated in the law and knew the promise: peace in the land, and none to make Israel afraid. The Lord was his power source.

“And five of you shall chase an hundred, and an hundred of you shall put ten thousand to flight: and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword.”

David leaned wholly on that promise. When he enquired this time, the Lord gave him war strategy: “Thou shalt not go up; but fetch a compass behind them, and come upon them over against the mulberry trees.” David sought counsel again rather than assume the last answer.

When he heard “the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees”, then “shall the Lord go out before thee, to smite the host of the Philistines.” The Lord fought before him, and David smote the Philistines from Geba until he came to Gazer. That is how a few chase an hundred and an hundred put ten thousand to flight.

David said it himself: “For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall.”

David knew his power source. That is why he enquired of the Lord before going up against the Philistines, and why he waited for the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees before he moved. It was by his God that he ran through the host of the Philistines, not by his own strength.

“He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.”

David's strength was of the Most High. The Lord taught him war in the plainest way at the mulberry trees: go not up, fetch a compass behind them, and move when you hear the sound in the tree tops. David did so, “as the Lord had commanded him”, and smote the Philistines from Geba to Gazer. The hands were David's, but the Lord taught them to war.
docs/study/2-samuel/5.md|2 Samuel 5:6-10:
David took the strong hold of Zion from the Jebusites. They thought to put a stipulation on him, “Except thou take away the blind and the lame, thou shalt not come in hither”, thinking he could not come in at all. They did not reckon with a man who had already slain his ten thousands. “Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion.” When the scripture says nevertheless, it means the thing will be done regardless of what stands against it.

Our forefathers were aggressive toward the nations in that time period. David was a man after God's own heart who would not let any nation stand in the way of the Lord's people, and “the Lord God of hosts was with him.”

But that is not the time we are in now. “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” We are at peace with all men. We do not break the laws of the land, for this is at present a spiritual battle and not a physical one.
docs/study/2-samuel/6.md|2 Samuel 6:1-5|:
“Again, David gathered together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.” Not everyone is a warrior, and not everyone goes to the front lines. But everyone in the body is important in some way.

“Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary.” The members that seem more feeble are needful, and on them more honor is bestowed. Every part in the body has honor.

So it was when David went up from Baale of Judah to bring up the ark of God. There were the chosen men, there were Uzzah and Ahio driving the new cart, and there was “all the house of Israel” playing before the Lord on harps, psalteries, timbrels, cornets and cymbals. Every one had a part.
docs/study/2-samuel/6.md|2 Samuel 6:6-11:
“And the Lord said unto Moses, Speak unto Aaron thy brother, that he come not at all times into the holy place within the vail before the mercy seat, which is upon the ark; that he die not.”

Only chosen men could come near the ark. The Lord set many stipulations upon it, even after the two sons of Aaron died for offering strange fire. Even Aaron, the high priest, could not come before the mercy seat at all times, lest he die. The Most High is holy and not to be handled carelessly.

So when the oxen shook the cart and Uzzah put forth his hand and took hold of the ark, “the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error.” Grabbing it was a natural reaction, but the Most High had already declared the ark holy and untouchable.

Before Aaron could come into the holy place, “He shall put on the holy linen coat, and he shall have the linen breeches upon his flesh, and shall be girded with a linen girdle, and with the linen mitre shall he be attired: these are holy garments; therefore shall he wash his flesh in water, and so put them on.”

Everything in that day had to be done to a T. If the high priest had to be washed and clothed in holy garments before coming near the mercy seat, Uzzah could not lay his hand on the ark at the threshingfloor. The Lord was not playing about his commandments.

We owe thanks that there is mercy through Christ.

“My flesh trembleth for fear of thee; and I am afraid of thy judgments.”
